  • The table grows with every run and unit; Delta's own OPTIMIZE and VACUUM apply. A retention command is a later concern.
  • Lease times rely on the clocks of the writers, as with the other stores.
  • The contract's cross-process lock test starts a second JVM, so it runs only with PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK_HEAVY=1. CI does not set it yet: on GitHub runners the child JVM stalled for over 240 s while resolving the Delta packages, before it reached the lock. Lock exclusion between writers is still covered in one process (the eight-thread race), and it rests on the same Delta commit check whether the writers share a JVM or not. Running the test in CI, for example with the Delta jars pre-resolved into a local directory, is a follow-up.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amends ADR-0008.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: pipeloom 0.5 adds an orchestrator plugin that deploys a plan as a Databricks job. The core must stay free of any orchestrator, yet the plugin needs four things from it: a place for deploy options that the plan carries without changing its identity, a manifest that is byte-identical across compiles so a deployed copy can be compared, a way to add CLI commands, and secrets that resolve at run time without entering any recorded output. ADR-0004 (discovery), ADR-0010 (events and artifacts), ADR-0013 (run identity) and ADR-0014 (secrets by reference) each say something about these, and this ADR amends them. It covers the 0.5 core change: the first half is the deploy block, the stable manifest, plugin commands and secrets; the second half is the orchestrator id, pipeloom finalize and the link fallback for write_json_once.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Deploy options as a model key or a new top-level section. Compute is a runtime setting a target may override, so a separate section would need its own precedence rules.
  • A deploy runtime key bound against the existing renderers plugin group. One precedence rule (target over top level), one options model per plugin, no new group of specs.
  • Resolve ${secret:...} at load time. Simple, but the value would reach the plan, the manifest and compile output.
  • Resolve it when the options of a plugin are bound for execution. The value lives in the plugin object only.
  • Commands through a new plugin spec group. A command is a click object, not a PluginSpec, so a spec would add nothing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
deploy is a runtime key (RuntimeSettings.deploy, a plugin block). Binding checks it against the renderers group: the kind must exist, and its options must validate against the spec's config_model, with line marks. The core never calls a renderer factory. The validated options, kind included, are recorded as PlanMetadata.deploy and written to the manifest under metadata.deploy, which is left out when the target has no deploy block. It is not in _HASHED_METADATA, so editing it leaves the plan hash unchanged. The JSON Schema shows deploy as a oneOf on kind, like the other plugin blocks.

manifest_bytes(plan, stable=True) blanks generated_at and invocation_id and empties the selection (select, exclude, selected), so one project and target always give the same bytes. write_manifest takes the same flag.

pipeloom.commands is a ninth entry-point group. Its entries name a click command and are discovered from metadata only: the module is imported when the command is invoked, never to list it, and --help lists plugin commands without importing them. A built-in command beats an entry point of the same name, and of several distributions providing one name the first by distribution name wins; both cases print a warning to stderr. A command that fails to import becomes a stub that prints the error and exits 1, so the rest of the CLI keeps working. PIPELOOM_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD hides every plugin command. plugins list --group commands lists them, and --check imports them. The group has no PluginSpec, so it is not part of GROUPS, only of the Group literal.

${secret:provider/path} references resolve only when a command executes, while the options of the plugins it builds are bound (run and finalize). BoundPlugin.create(secrets) re-validates the options as written with each reference replaced, and the resolved value is registered with the redactor before any plugin that holds it is built. Providers come from the secret_providers group, are built once per invocation with default options, and a failure of any kind is PLX109 naming the provider and path, never a value. Compile, validate and the manifest only ever see the reference text. A resolved value is masked everywhere text leaves the process: the event bus, run_results.json (finalize), per-unit attempt files and state store rows (the runner), and the message of an internal error. Under boundary: task each unit process resolves and masks on its own. A plugin factory that fails while it holds resolved options is reported as PLX109 with a masked message and no chained traceback. The naming plugin is built at compile time and therefore never resolves secrets.

Only a reference written literally in the YAML resolves. The loader records the span of each one, also under secret-like keys, whose ${env:...} and ${var:...} are otherwise left alone. $${secret:provider/path} is the escape: it renders as the text ${secret:provider/path}, is never resolved and never asks for its provider, so an unknown provider is not an error there. Text that arrives through ${env:...} or ${var:...} and happens to look like a reference never resolves either. The built-in env provider reads the process environment, not the env mapping given to the API, so through the API ${secret:env/X} and ${env:X} can read different environments; the CLI passes the process environment to both.

docs.title: Orchestrator ids and pipeloom finalize
docs.text:
run --orchestrator-id KEY=VALUE (repeatable, a later duplicate wins) puts the ids into the runtime context, every attempt file, the orchestrator_ids of each results row and of run.identity, and the context of every event as orchestrator_id.<key> (event context holds strings only). Keys match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}, values are 1 to 256 printable characters, anything else is exit 2. A process-boundary child gets the same flags. They win over the ids an identity provider supplies.

pipeloom finalize closes a run an orchestrator drove unit by unit. Per unit in scope (the whole plan by default, or -s/--select and --exclude) the precedence is: attempt file, else the external state from --unit-states (pipeloom.unit_states/1: skipped, cancelled, failed or excluded, with optional reason, code, message and orchestrator_ids), else skipped with the new reason not_run. excluded drops the row. An external failed row carries the given code (default PLX106) and message; an external skipped has the reason given, default upstream_failed. The run is failed when any row is failed, timed out or skipped as upstream_failed (or fail_fast); otherwise cancelled when any row is cancelled; otherwise succeeded. not_run and any other skip reason count for nothing. This differs from run, where a stop request makes the run cancelled even after a failure: an orchestrator's join task must not hide a failure behind a cancellation, so finalize puts failure first (status_of(failure_first=True)). Exit codes are 0, 1 and 130. Finalize binds plugin options like run (secrets resolve and are masked in every artifact), records the run, runs the intermediate cleanup, emits run.completed and rewrites the same results when repeated. It takes the run lock like run but only to detect a live pipeloom run: when the lock is held for the same run id and the run record is still running it refuses with PLX105 (exit 1, like run), because in-flight units would be counted as not run and cleanup could delete their intermediates; a lock held for another run id, a lock without a running record (finalize never records running, so a crashed finalize does not block its retry), or no lock lets it proceed. Unit invocations never take the lock, so an orchestrated run is unaffected. A unit with no attempt file and no state is upstream_failed (with the failed upstream, walking the unit graph in topological order) when an upstream row failed, timed out or was skipped for that reason, else not_run. An unreadable or invalid --unit-states file is exit 2, reported before anything runs (the file is read once). The command's own options are recorded in the invocation event as given, so the states file appears as a path and its content (a message may hold a secret) never does.

write_json_once falls back to os.open(O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_WRONLY) plus a write when os.link fails with EPERM, ENOTSUP, EOPNOTSUPP, EXDEV or ENOSYS, as on FUSE volumes. It stays exclusive, so the first terminal attempt file still wins, but the file is not created atomically: a reader can briefly see a partial file, and a crash mid-write leaves one (the writer removes it on an exception).

The plugin API stays (0, 4). Every change is additive for plugins: a new runtime key, a new entry-point group read only by the CLI, and BoundPlugin.create gaining an optional argument that plugins never call.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: An orchestrator plugin can carry its options in the manifest without touching the plan hash, and can ship a manifest whose bytes do not depend on when it was compiled. A project with a deploy block fails with PLR204 where the renderer plugin is not installed, which is the point. Masking is by exact value: a plugin that transforms a secret (encodes or truncates it) before logging it defeats the redactor, and values shorter than four characters are never masked. A ${secret: reference in a place the core does not bind as plugin options (model SQL, vars) stays literal.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended by ADR-0049: the unit-states schema, the unit graph and the orchestrator protocol.

docs.title: ADR-0035: Databricks rendering and job lifecycle
Context
docs.text:
pipeloom 0.5 deploys a plan as a Databricks job. ADR-0011 sketched the job shape and ADR-0012 the orchestrator modes, and both left facts to verify. ADR-0034 gave the core the hooks (a deploy block, a stable manifest, plugin commands, pipeloom finalize). This ADR covers the plugin side. It is written in halves: the first is rendering, which is pure and needs no workspace, and the wrapper and bundle command that need none either; the second half (deploy, run, repair, find by tag, upload) arrives with the client and amends this record. It amends ADR-0011 and ADR-0012.

Facts checked against the public Jobs API documentation: a task key is 1 to 100 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_-]; jobs/create, reset, update and runs/submit all accept at most 1,000 tasks; a job has at most 10 environments; an environment has an environment_version (a string, 1 to 6) and dependencies; a job run's result comes from its leaf tasks.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• A databricks executor. ADR-0020 picks executors by boundary, and Databricks is an orchestrator, not a boundary. Rejected.
  • Per-model compute as a model key. Compute is a runtime setting a target may override, so a model key would need its own precedence. Rejected for target-level compute_rules with selectors.
  • Grouping only above the task limit. The shape of the job would change when the 1,001st model is added. Rejected: grouping applies whenever task_grouping is set.
  • Tasks call the core CLI directly. Needs an environment where the pipeloom script exists, and cannot turn a start time or an empty run id into arguments. Rejected for a plugin wrapper entry point.
  • Rendering through the SDK dataclasses. They lag the API and drop fields such as environment_version. Rejected for stdlib frozen dataclasses that mirror the subset we use.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The plugin pipeloom-databricks registers the databricks kind in the renderers group. Its options (DatabricksDeployOptions) are the validated deploy block: pipelines (each a selection of units and one job), named computes (serverless or job_cluster), compute_rules (the first matching rule wins), task_grouping (none, by_tag, by_folder) and passthrough job settings. The spec imports no Databricks or Spark library. Rendering is a pure function of the plan, the options and a few locations the caller supplies (project root, manifest path, the target's artifacts root, whether its state store is shared, cancel_grace); the core needs no new input for it.

A job is named pipeloom_<project>_<pipeline>_<target> and carries the tags pipeloom_job (<project>.<pipeline>.<target>), pipeloom_plan_hash, pipeloom_settings_hash (sha256 of the canonical settings without that tag) and pipeloom_version. User tags are merged and ours win. Equal settings hashes mean a deploy is a no-op.

Tasks run a plugin wrapper: python_wheel_task with package pipeloom_databricks and entry point pipeloom_databricks_task. Parameters are --opt=value strings, so an empty value stays one argument. They carry dynamic references ({{job.parameters.pipeloom_run_id}}, {{job.id}}, {{task.name}}, {{job.start_time.timestamp_ms}}); the start time is passed as milliseconds because the iso_datetime format is undocumented. A one-time run (runs/submit) gets the run id, the full-refresh flag and the start time as literals and no job references. It may use serverless compute only.

Each unit is a task named by its unit id; with grouping, a group is a task named tag_<first tag> (tag_untagged) or dir_<folder of the model file> (dir_root). Group dependencies come from unit parents; groups that wait for each other are PLD003. A group must run on one compute. A finalize task, pipeloom__finalize, depends on every leaf, runs with run_if: ALL_DONE, one retry and a 1,800 s timeout, on the default compute. Tasks are sorted by key, finalize last. Retries and the retry delay are the model's (a group takes the largest); timeout_seconds is the model timeout plus cancel_grace plus 300 s, summed over a group whose every member has a timeout. Serverless tasks set disable_auto_optimization: true, because auto-optimization retries a failed task on top of max_retries (found by the live workflow, amended 2026-11-05).

Task keys replace characters outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] with _. A key above 100 characters, a key shared by several ids and a key equal to the finalize key are shortened to 91 characters, _ and 8 hex characters of the sha256 of the raw id; every id in a collision gets the suffix, so keys do not depend on order. A job above 1,000 tasks, finalize included, is PLD001 with a hint to set task_grouping or split pipelines. PLD002 stays reserved and is never emitted, because submit and create share the limit. Invalid options for the plan or target are PLD004 (environment version 1, an unknown compute, more than 10 serverless environments, a key in settings that pipeloom owns (name too) or a pipeloom_ tag, a ${secret: reference, an artifacts root that is unset or relative, a state store that is not shared, a group on two computes, an ephemeral run on a job cluster, an unknown pipeline or one that selects no unit). A compute rule that matches no model is the warning PLD005.

The wrapper (pipeloom_databricks.task, a [project.scripts] entry plus a lazy function of the same name in the package, so both Databricks lookups find it) has the subcommands unit and finalize. It rejects any parameter that still holds {{ (PLD013, exit 1), turns an empty run id into dbx-<job run id>, turns the run start into --run-started-at (the job run's start_time from the Jobs API, falling back to start_ms with a warning when the call fails or the run is one-time: the live workflow showed that {{job.start_time}} is the start of the latest repair, so a repaired task would otherwise fail with PLX108; amended 2026-11-05), and calls pipeloom run or pipeloom finalize in the same process, so an active Spark session stays the active one. A group task recomputes its members with build_tasks from the shipped manifest (an unknown group exits 1). It passes databricks_job_id, databricks_job_run_id, databricks_task_key and databricks_task_run_id as orchestrator ids and exits with the core's code. Finalize scopes the run to the units of its pipeline, spelled as unit: selectors, because the shipped manifest has an empty selection and a bare finalize --manifest would scope no unit.

After a unit task the wrapper sets the task value pipeloom (v, run_id, status and, per unit, status, attempt, rows written, duration, target version, error code and warning count) read from the newest attempt files. Above 32,768 bytes units are dropped from the end and truncated is true. Task values are documented for notebooks only, so setting one is best effort: a failure prints one line on stderr and never changes the exit code. Only task_values.py (with the client modules) imports databricks.sdk, and only on a Databricks runtime.

pipeloom databricks bundle --target T --out DIR [--pipeline NAME]... [--bundle-root PATH] [--check] writes, per pipeline, pipeloom_<project>_<pipeline>_<target>.job.yml (with a header comment saying it is generated) and the stable .manifest.json into a bundle. Paths are bundle variables: ${workspace.file_path}/<project dir relative to the bundle root> and ${workspace.file_path}/<out relative to the bundle root>/<file>. The bundle root is --bundle-root or the nearest folder above --out with databricks.yml; none, or a project or output folder outside it, is exit 2. --check writes nothing and exits 1 listing the files that differ. The plugin registers the group in pipeloom.commands.

Amended 2026-11-20 (Databricks CLI versions). Databricks CLI 1.3.0 made the direct deployment engine GA and the default, and 1.20.0 removed the Terraform engine. The golden job files were checked with databricks bundle validate on CLI 1.18.0 and raise no unknown-field warning; the fields are Jobs API fields that both engines accept. The command writes no bundle.databricks_cli_version: pipeloom has no technical need for a floor, one would make bundle validate fail on older CLIs whose bundles work today (a break for a minor release under ADR-0016), and an included file overrides the root's value, so it would also loosen a range the user set in databricks.yml. Users who want a floor set it there. pipeloom never invokes the CLI, so there is no runtime version check and no diagnostic code.

pipeloom_databricks.testing.jobsim.simulate_job runs a rendered job locally: it substitutes the references, runs the tasks in dependency order through the wrapper, and honors run_if, only and a repair (rerun). The Spark engine's active mode, when DATABRICKS_RUNTIME_VERSION is set and no session is active, attaches with builder.getOrCreate() and no conf, because a wheel task starts without a session; it never configures or stops that session.

Run, repair and finalize states (second half). run finds the job by tag and compares its pipeloom_settings_hash tag with the local render: a missing job is PLD007 and a different hash PLD008, unless --ensure deploys first. --select and --exclude resolve on the plan, intersect the pipeline's units and become only (task keys, groups deduplicated, plus finalize); a partly selected group runs whole with a warning, and an empty selection is exit 2. With --run-id the start carries idempotency_token = sha256("<job_id>:<run_id>"). --ephemeral uploads as deploy does and submits with the token sha256(run_id); a selection prunes the submitted tasks and finalize waits for the selection's leaves. A repair of a finished run reruns tasks that ended FAILED, TIMEDOUT, CANCELED, UPSTREAM_FAILED, UPSTREAM_CANCELED or MAXIMUM_CONCURRENT_RUNS_REACHED plus finalize, passes latest_repair_id from the run history and the run's job parameters (without them {{job.parameters.pipeloom_run_id}} resolves to its empty default and the repair starts a new pipeloom run; amended 2026-11-05), and a run still active is PLD014. After a repair --wait keeps polling until the run reports the new repair id. The finalize wrapper calls connect(profile=None, env=os.environ) and get_run, and maps each unit without an attempt file: EXCLUDED and DISABLED (what serverless reports for a task left out by only) to excluded, UPSTREAM_FAILED and UPSTREAM_CANCELED to skipped (upstream_failed), CANCELED and TIMEDOUT to cancelled, FAILED to failed with PLD011 and the termination message. The map goes to core as --unit-states. A client error prints one warning and passes no states, so those units count as not run. A one-time run has no job run id in its task parameters, so its finalize asks for nothing.

Output is byte-deterministic: JSON with 2-space indent, ASCII only and LF, keys in field order; bundle YAML from yaml.safe_dump without key sorting. Environment dependencies default to the pinned distributions (pipeloom, pipeloom-databricks and every plugin in the plan, name==version, sorted).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The job is a plain JSON document that a person can read, diff and send to the Jobs API unchanged, and rendering is testable with goldens and no workspace. The renderer needs three inputs the plan does not hold (artifacts root, state sharing, cancel grace), which the caller reads from the bound target. Tasks of a pipeline ignore dependencies on units outside it. Platform behaviors that only a live run can confirm (references in wheel task parameters, only with an ALL_DONE finalize) are guarded by the wrapper and checked by the manual workflow, not here.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted (first half: rendering, wrapper and bundle command; second half: run, repair and finalize states). Amended in 0.9 by ADR-0050.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: With Python-first authoring (ADR-0050) the upload set of deploy and run --ephemeral is pipeloom.yml, the .py file of every node, every *.py under python_paths, the properties YAML files under model_paths (not read at run time, uploaded so the folder mirrors the project) and the stable manifest. A task never runs discovery: it imports the one module named by the node's callable. Modules found through model_packages are not uploaded; they must be installed in the job environment (for example through the compute's dependencies), and the plugin guide says so.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Deploying a job needs a workspace: list and create jobs, upload the project, read the current user. Later releases of the plugin also run and repair jobs and read secrets. The plugin must be testable without a workspace, must never use a credential the user did not choose, and must not break when the installed SDK lags the API.

Facts checked against public documentation. The Jobs API 2.2 paths used are jobs/list, jobs/create, jobs/reset, jobs/run-now, jobs/runs/submit, jobs/runs/get (with include_history, paginated by next_page_token over tasks), jobs/runs/list and jobs/runs/repair. Workspace import (POST /api/2.0/workspace/import) takes base64 content, a 10 MB limit and overwrite. Its format values are SOURCE, HTML, JUPYTER, DBC, R_MARKDOWN, AUTO and RAW; only AUTO is described in prose ("imported depending on an analysis of the item's extension and the header content"), and RAW has no description anywhere in the REST reference, the SDK reference or the CLI reference. Sources: https://docs.databricks.com/api/workspace/workspace/import and https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/cli/reference/workspace-commands.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• The typed SDK methods (w.jobs.create(...)). They lag the API and drop fields such as environment_version. Rejected.
  • A hand-written HTTP client. Would re-implement authentication, retries and error mapping. Rejected.
  • The SDK's api_client.do. Authentication, retries and errors come from the SDK, and the JSON is ours, unchanged.
  • Workspace import format RAW. Probably stores a plain file, but nothing public says so. Rejected until documented.
  • Picking the DEFAULT profile when nothing is set. Convenient, and a way to deploy to a workspace the user did not mean. Rejected.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The plugin owns a small DatabricksClient protocol with JSON-shaped records (JobSummary, RunInfo, TaskRunInfo, DirEntry) and one error type, ApiError (HTTP status, error code, message). SdkClient implements it with WorkspaceClient.api_client.do for every call; the endpoints are the ones listed above plus GET /api/2.0/preview/scim/v2/Me, the workspace mkdirs, list and delete, GET /api/2.0/fs/files<path> (volumes) and GET /api/2.0/secrets/get. A task run's state is read from status when present and from the legacy state otherwise; a termination code that is not a result state name counts as FAILED. get_secret returns the base64 value exactly as the API does. SDK errors become ApiError, with the message passed through the redactor of the connection, which registers the token and client secret it was built with.

Workspace files are stored with import format AUTO: it is the only documented format that does not turn the content into a notebook unless the file has a notebook header or a notebook extension. The upload set therefore refuses such files (PLD012): a Databricks notebook header (# Databricks notebook source, -- ..., // ...), an .ipynb file, a file above 10 MB, or one outside the project folder. If RAW is documented as a plain-file format, switching is one constant (IMPORT_FORMAT).

databricks.sdk is imported lazily and only in client/sdk.py, client/connect.py and task_values.py; import-linter enforces it. The dependency is bounded databricks-sdk>=0.50,<1, and the SDK client tests run against 0.50.0 as well as the locked version.

The connection is chosen in this order, and never by guessing: --profile; a profile the user set in DATABRICKS_CONFIG_PROFILE; DATABRICKS_HOST with DATABRICKS_TOKEN or DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET; runtime authentication when DATABRICKS_RUNTIME_VERSION is set; otherwise PLD010. Without a profile the SDK gets a config_file in a fresh temporary folder where no file exists, so it cannot fall back to a DEFAULT profile in ~/.databrickscfg. Host and credentials come from the mapping the caller passes, not from ambient state. A hidden group option --client-factory MODULE:ATTR replaces all of this with a zero-argument callable that returns a client; tests and case files use it.

pipeloom_databricks.testing.fake.FakeDatabricks is an in-memory client: jobs, a workspace tree with modification ticks, runs, secrets, a call log and injectable failures. Tests of the plugin run with every DATABRICKS_* variable removed, DATABRICKS_CONFIG_FILE pointing at nothing and databricks.sdk.WorkspaceClient, databricks.sdk.core.Config and databricks.sdk.config.Config replaced by functions that fail, so a test that builds a real client fails. Only the connect tests put recorders in their place.

Direct deploy (pipeloom databricks deploy) uploads the project to <workspace_root>/<project>/<pipeline>/<target>/<hash[:12]>, where the hash covers every uploaded path and its bytes and the stable manifest. The default workspace_root is /Workspace/Users/<current user>/.pipeloom. A folder holding the marker _pipeloom/complete, written last, is never uploaded again. The job's parameters name that folder, so a changed project changes the settings hash; equal hashes leave the job alone, otherwise the job is created (found by its pipeloom_job tag, by name first and by a scan of all jobs second; two matches are PLD006) or reset. The upload set is pipeloom.yml, the model and source files of the plan, the *.py files below python_paths (skipping dot entries, __pycache__, venv, .venv, dist, build, node_modules, folders with pyvenv.cfg and the artifacts root) and the stable manifest, so data files, wheels and credentials stay local. The workspace API gives folders no modification time, so folders are ordered by the modification time of their marker file, which every deploy that points the job at a folder writes again. The current folder and the two newest others are kept (the newest other is the folder the job used before), older ones are deleted, a folder that cannot be inspected is never deleted, and a failed delete is a warning. API failures are PLD009. --dry-run prints the settings and creates no client.

Secrets and Unity Catalog use the same connection rules. The databricks secret provider resolves ${secret:databricks/<scope>/<key>} through get_secret: the client is built on the first reference and kept for the life of the provider (one per invocation), it calls connect with no profile, so a profile is never chosen, and it decodes the base64 value as UTF-8. A path that is not <scope>/<key>, a missing connection, an API error or an undecodable value is PLX109 naming the provider and the path, never the value (the blueprint's PLX108 was taken). The unity catalog subclasses the Spark session catalog: identifiers are always catalog.schema.name with the catalog from the options when naming leaves it empty, and ensure_namespace checks databaseExists first so a principal without CREATE SCHEMA can still write to an existing schema. Both specs import neither the SDK nor Spark at module level.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Fields the SDK does not know yet reach the API intact, and the plugin does not depend on SDK dataclasses. A deploy never reaches a workspace the user did not name. The protocol is small enough to fake completely, so deploy, run and repair are tested without a network. list_dir returns DirEntry with a modification time (the blueprint's tuple has none); it is meaningful for files only, which is why pruning reads the marker file.

Unconfirmed until the manual workflow runs against a workspace: that AUTO keeps a plain .py or .yml as a file, that the workspace API accepts a path with the /Workspace prefix, that tasks can read the uploaded folder through that prefix, and the mapping from termination_details.code to a result state. The job reset overwrites edits made in the UI; use the settings passthrough instead. Revisit RAW when it is documented.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0037: Airflow packaging and rendering
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 13, The Airflow plugin

Amends ADR-0005 and ADR-0012.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pipeloom 0.6 runs a plan from Apache Airflow. ADR-0005 set the distribution layout and ADR-0012 sketched the Airflow modes and left versions and mechanics open. This ADR covers packaging and rendering, which are pure and need no Airflow; the execution modes, the artifact store and the Databricks mode arrive in later records and amend this one.

Facts checked against the public Airflow sources and PyPI metadata: 3.3.2 is the latest stable release and 3.2.0 is the first with Python 3.14 support; core requirements carry no platform markers and Airflow does not support Windows; airflow.sdk exports DAG, TaskGroup, BaseOperator, BaseSensorOperator and Asset; the DagBag lives in airflow.models.dagbag on 3.1 and in airflow.dag_processing.dagbag on 3.3; AirflowSkipException is in airflow.sdk.exceptions. Airflow 3 parses the DAG file before every task.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The open questions of the 0.6 plan, each with the option chosen first.

  • Floor. Airflow >=3.2,<4 (first with Python 3.14, tested in CI), or >=3.1, or >=3.0 as ADR-0012 wrote.
  • Dependency. Airflow as an extra with a runtime check (as pyspark in ADR-0031), or a hard dependency.
  • Artifact store. A shared POSIX path with a sentinel for a missing result, or fsspec URIs in the core, or an XCom relay of attempt files.
  • Run id. A hash of NUL-separated parts with the group id, or the literal dag_id plus run_id.
  • Shared Databricks polling. A deferred launch snapshot, or an in-memory hub per triggerer.
  • CI. Make the airflow job a required check after two green runs on main.
  • Deferrable pods. Forbidden in 0.6, or supported through trigger_reentry.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
pipeloom-airflow is a workspace member that depends on pipeloom~=X.Y.0 and has no hard Airflow dependency. The extra airflow pulls apache-airflow>=3.2,<4; the floor is checked when a DAG is built (PLA005). Its pure modules (configs, loading, rendering, command lines, state mapping, ids) run on every CI cell. The root extra airflow pins the plugin. Importing the package imports nothing (PEP 562) and a test proves airflow stays out of sys.modules.

One import seam: only pipeloom_airflow._compat and _compat_k8s import airflow or kubernetes. Import-linter forbids the core from importing the plugin or Airflow, and the pure modules from importing Airflow, Kubernetes or the Databricks SDK; indirect imports are allowed because the subprocess test covers them.

Rendering is a pure function of a loaded plan and the configs. There is one Airflow task per unit; group_by (none, folder, tag) only nests visual task groups. Ids: unsafe characters become _; an id above 200 characters, a colliding id or one equal to a reserved id (pipeloom_finalize, pipeloom_launch) ends in _ and 8 hex of the sha256 of the raw name. The run id is af- plus 16 hex of the sha256 of dag_id, run_id and, inside a task group, the group id, separated by NUL, so two inputs never concatenate alike and two groups of one DAG run never share a run. Model retries become Airflow retries; a unit invocation keeps retries=0; max_attempts is retries + 1; the execution timeout is the model timeout plus cancel_grace plus 300 s, with the core default of 30 s for the grace because the manifest does not carry it.

A plan loads from a stable manifest, or by compiling the project (PROJECT). PROJECT results are cached on disk under a key that is the sha256 of the canonical JSON of the cache schema, the installed pipeloom* versions, the target, the variables and the path, size and mtime of pipeloom.yml and every file under model_paths and python_paths (dot entries, __pycache__ and the artifacts root skipped). An entry also stores a fingerprint (sha256 per name) of the environment variables the plan read, and a hit needs equal fingerprints, so a secret value never lands on disk. An entry is two files, <key>.entry.json and <key>.manifest.json (a stable manifest), written to a temporary name and replaced into place; the newest 8 are kept. A cache that cannot be read or written is PLA006 and the project still compiles. Compiling runs no user code (ADR-0003).

Asset URIs follow a template (default pipeloom://{project}/{target}/{relation}) whose values are percent-encoded. Case files for the PLA codes use a new python: kind (module:function returning diagnostics), so they run without Airflow. Airflow-importing tests will run in a separate airflow CI job on Ubuntu, and DAG-bag parses in a subprocess with an explicit environment and a throwaway AIRFLOW_HOME. The recommended option of the other open questions is recorded here and applies to the later records: a shared POSIX artifact root with a PLA004 sentinel, a deferred launch snapshot for shared polling, the airflow job required after two green runs on main, and no deferrable pods.

Deviations from the 0.6 plan, all in this first half. PLA004 and PLA005 are active from the start, because pure modules emit them (states, version). A MANIFEST load checks only the target, since the configs carry no expected project name. The cache key reads pipeloom.yml as plain YAML for model_paths, python_paths and artifacts roots, so an interpolated root is not skipped (the key only becomes more sensitive). A cache entry names the sha256 of its manifest, so interleaved writers that share a key cannot pair one writer's entry with another's manifest; a mismatch is a miss. DATABRICKS mode needs pipeloom-databricks, which this distribution does not declare; without it the render reports PLA001. finalize takes its unit states from --unit-states PATH. The core flag --unit-states-json for small documents arrived with the Kubernetes mode, which emits it for its finalize pod (see ADR-0038); the LOCAL and VIRTUALENV finalize task still uses --unit-states.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: A machine that renders or parses a DAG needs the extra, and the pure code is testable everywhere. Airflow internals drift between minors, so every Airflow import sits in two modules. A project compile can run at task start when the cache misses; the stat-based key keeps that rare. The plugin does not record model_paths in the plan, so folder groups use the folder every rendered model shares as the model path. The DOCKER mode is PLA001 until it exists.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. A second half, covering the execution modes and the artifact store, follows with the operators. Amended in 0.9 by ADR-0050.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: With Python-first authoring (ADR-0050), "compiling runs no user code" holds only for model modules whose decorator arguments are static. A PROJECT load imports the dynamic model modules, and only those, inside the DAG processor, so their top-level code runs at parse time. PROJECT unit tasks pass no manifest and compile in every task (CoreCommand), so dynamic modules are also imported on workers. The PROJECT cache key also covers the directories of the packages named in model_packages, walked like model_paths. MANIFEST stays the default and recommended mode and imports nothing at parse or run time except the one module of the unit being run.

docs.title: ADR-0038: Airflow execution modes and artifact store
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 13, The Airflow plugin

Amends ADR-0012, ADR-0020 and ADR-0037.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-0037 renders a plan into one Airflow task per unit but runs nothing. A task must now run its unit, report the outcome to Airflow in a way its retries understand, stop cleanly when Airflow kills it, and a last task must close the pipeloom run. Airflow 3 parses the DAG file before every task, and its workers may be separate machines.

Checked on Airflow 3.3.2 (and 3.2.2 for the floor): a DAG subclass with its own __init__ builds and serializes (DagSerialization.serialize_dag), as astronomer-cosmos does; RuntimeTaskInstance.get_task_states(dag_id, task_ids=, run_ids=) returns {run_id: {task_id: state}}; airflow.sdk.exceptions has AirflowFailException; TaskGroup(parent_group=None) passed explicitly does not attach to the enclosing group.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Artifact store. One shared POSIX directory for every task and the finalize task, with a sentinel for a unit whose task succeeded but whose result is not visible; or fsspec URIs in the core; or relaying attempt files through XCom.
  • Process model. A child process per task running the core CLI; or running the core in the worker process.
  • Retries. Map the core's retry classification to Airflow exceptions; or let Airflow retry every failure.
  • DAG class. Subclass DAG and TaskGroup; or a factory returning a plain DAG.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The target's artifacts.root must be one directory that every unit task and the finalize task see (any path under the LocalExecutor, a network volume otherwise). fsspec is deferred: create-once files and atomic replace are not portable across its backends, and state stores and filesystem catalogs need shared storage anyway.

Each unit task runs python -m pipeloom run --log-format json --select unit:<id> with the DAG run's run id and orchestrator ids, in a new session (its own process group), with sys.executable (local) or the interpreter of virtualenv_dir (virtualenv; a missing interpreter fails without retry). Child events are logged line by line. Exit 0 succeeds; 2 fails without retry; 130 fails with retry; 1 fails without retry when the unit's terminal error is permanent and retry_on is transient, else with retry. Model retries and retry_delay become the task's; the execution timeout is the model timeout plus the cancel grace plus 300 s, so the core times out first. on_kill sends SIGTERM to the process group and SIGKILL after the cancel grace.

The finalize task (pipeloom_finalize, trigger rule all_done, one retry) reads the states of the unit tasks, maps them to unit states (a success or failed task without an attempt file becomes a failed unit with PLA004) and runs pipeloom finalize --unit-states <temp file>. Exit 1 fails it without retry, so the DAG run fails when the pipeloom run failed.

PipeloomDag subclasses DAG and PipeloomTaskGroup subclasses TaskGroup; both build the plan in their constructor. Errors raise PipeloomAirflowError, which Airflow shows as the file's import error; warnings go to the pipeloom_airflow logger. The Airflow version is checked first (PLA005): _compat reads the apache-airflow distribution version before it imports anything from Airflow, so a missing Airflow, an Airflow 2 or a 3.1 is PLA005 at import, never an ImportError.

Deviations from the 0.6 plan. A stable manifest carries an empty selected, and pipeloom finalize --manifest without a selector keeps it, so the core would see no unit in scope and drop every external state; without a render selection the finalize task therefore passes --select unit:<id> for every rendered unit. The core behavior is reported as a follow-up rather than changed here. The databricks mode reports PLA001 until its operators arrive.

Kubernetes mode (PR38). PipeloomKubernetesOperator and PipeloomKubernetesFinalizeOperator subclass KubernetesPodOperator of the cncf-kubernetes provider (extra kubernetes, >=10.25,<11, also in the airflow dependency group; it needs Airflow 2.11 or later, so the 3.2 floor holds). Only _compat_k8s imports the provider and the kubernetes client, and dag.py imports the operators only in this mode; a missing provider is PLA001. The pod gets KubernetesConfig.image and namespace, the user's pod_kwargs, ExecutionConfig.env as pod environment (the pod_kwargs entry wins), and the cancel grace as the termination grace period. The name is pipeloom-<task id> as a DNS label (the provider adds a random suffix), do_xcom_push is false and deferrable is forced false (also rejected in pod_kwargs and operator_args as PLA002), so a deferrable pod is not supported in 0.6. The interpreter KubernetesConfig.python is the pod command, the core arguments are set in execute after templating (the run id never sits in a templated field) and the child logs as text. retry_on is not enforced: Airflow sees only the pod's result. The finalize pod passes the compact unit states inline with the new pipeloom finalize --unit-states-json TEXT (same document and errors as --unit-states; both together exit 2); above 120 KiB it fails with PLA002 (one Linux exec argument is capped at 128 KiB); the compact form shortens the PLA004 messages to stay small. It keeps trigger rule all_done and one retry, so a failed run finalizes twice with the same result.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Units on unshared storage fail loudly through PLA004, but state stores and filesystem catalogs on unshared paths still misbehave; PLA007 and the docs mitigate that. A task costs a child interpreter start on top of the DAG parse. Airflow-importing tests run in a separate CI job and in WSL, with a throwaway home and sqlite database checked by the test conftest.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0039: Airflow DATABRICKS mode
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 13, The Airflow plugin

Amends ADR-0012, ADR-0035 and ADR-0036.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0037 renders one Airflow task per Databricks task key, but DATABRICKS mode reported PLA001. The units run inside a Databricks job, so Airflow must start that job, show each task's result, and fail the DAG run when the pipeloom run fails. Airflow workers and triggerers are long-lived shared processes: they must not pick up a Databricks profile or DATABRICKS_* variables meant for something else, and a deferred task must not store a secret.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Client. The Databricks Airflow provider, which pulls the SQL connector, pandas and pyarrow; or pipeloom_databricks.api with the Airflow connection mapped by pipeloom.
  • Polling. Every sensor defers on its own trigger (one API call per task per interval); or the launch defers on one whole-run trigger and the sensors read its final snapshot; or an in-memory hub per triggerer.
  • A cleared launch. Start a new run; or find the run by its pipeloom run id and attach to it, repairing it when a task failed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• No provider dependency. The extra databricks adds pipeloom-databricks~=X.Y.0. pipeloom_databricks.api.connect_explicit(host, auth_type, token | client_id and client_secret) builds the SDK configuration with the auth type set and a config file that does not exist, so neither ~/.databrickscfg nor a worker's DATABRICKS_* variables change the auth. The connection fields follow the provider's convention (host; token in the password or extra.token; extra.service_principal_oauth with the client id as login and the secret as password). Azure-only extras and missing values are PLD010, naming the connection id and never a value. Secrets go through Airflow's mask_secret; the trigger serializes only the connection id.
  • The launch compiles the project on the worker (PLX103 when its plan hash is not the DAG's) and calls start_or_attach: no run with the DAG run's pipeloom run id goes through run_job (PLD007, PLD008, or a deploy with databricks_ensure_job; the run id is the idempotency key); an active or succeeded run is attached; an ended run with failed, cancelled or skipped tasks is repaired, and each rerun key's next attempt number is recorded as its baseline. An existing run is continued as it was started, without the drift check.
  • databricks_poll has two modes. per_task is the default: the launch returns {v, run_id, job_id, job_run_id, run_page_url, repair_id, baseline, action} right after run-now or repair, and each sensor makes one synchronous get_run; without a verdict it defers on DatabricksRunTrigger(task_key=key) with the sensor's timeout, which is ExecutionConfig.databricks_timeout. The trigger polls every interval, retries a transient ApiError (429, 5xx, status 0) up to 5 times in a row with sleeps of one, two, then four intervals, and yields an error event on any other API error or when the retries run out. shared: the launch defers on DatabricksRunTrigger(task_key=None) until the run is over (after a repair, until that repair is over, with the rules of wait_for_run), and execute_complete adds the run's snapshot to that XCom; sensors read it and make no API call. No process-global state is kept in the triggerer. Every deferral carries timeout=ExecutionConfig.databricks_timeout (default 24 hours, PLA002 unless positive), because execution_timeout is reserved and the trigger itself never gives up; a timed-out launch fails that try, and its retry finds the same run and attaches to it.
  • Verdicts: SUCCESS is success; SKIPPED, EXCLUDED and UPSTREAM_* are skipped; FAILED, TIMEDOUT, CANCELED, INTERNAL_ERROR and MAXIMUM_CONCURRENT_RUNS_REACHED fail once the attempt is the last one Databricks makes or the run is over; while the run is active an attempt below its baseline is ignored; a task an ended run does not list was skipped, and any other state of an ended run is a failure. A failed sensor raises AirflowFailException with the task message and the run page URL; sensors have no retries.
  • Graph: pipeloom_launch -> one sensor per key (plan edges, asset outlets) -> pipeloom_finalize, a sensor on the job's pipeloom__finalize task with trigger rule all_done, which fails when Databricks finalize failed (it exits 1 on a failed run).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A DAG in DATABRICKS mode needs the project files and pipeloom-databricks on the worker that runs the launch, and pipeloom-airflow[databricks] on the triggerer.
  • per_task costs one API call per waiting sensor per interval, so a wide DAG should raise databricks_poll_interval or use shared, where one call per interval is made but a sensor's result shows only when the whole run is over.
  • The blueprint's airflow_e2e dag.test() of a DATABRICKS-mode DAG is deferred: the test client factory builds a new in-memory FakeDatabricks for each client the launch and the trigger make, so a run started by one is unknown to the other, and nothing in the fake plays the job's tasks to an end. It needs a file-backed fake that advances runs, which arrives with the live-workflow step of PR41. The launch, trigger and sensors are covered in process instead (tests/airflow/test_databricks_*.py), and the DAG file parses in a real DagBag.
  • Repair baselines assume Databricks numbers a repaired task's attempt after the earlier ones; only a live workspace confirms it, and the terminal-run rules keep a wrong guess from hanging a sensor.

docs.title: ADR-0040: Per-model catalog
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 3, Pipeline

Amends ADR-0022.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A model chooses its schema, but the catalog of its relation comes only from the target: the catalog option of the naming strategy, or the catalog option of the catalog plugin. A project that keeps each layer in its own catalog (for example pipeloom_bronze.tpch.orders and pipeloom_gold.tpch.revenue_by_region) cannot say so in YAML. The two path catalogs, filesystem and delta_path, also ignore the catalog of a target, so a catalog name set on them had no effect.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Where the catalog is resolved.
  • Pass the model's catalog through the NamingStrategy protocol. Strategies could rewrite catalogs, but the protocol changes and the plugin API goes from (0, 4) to (0, 5), which breaks every installed plugin until it is rebuilt.
  • Resolve it in the core, after the strategy returns. The protocol and the API stay. Strategies cannot rewrite a model's catalog.
  • Path catalogs.
  • Map the catalog to a leading directory: <root>/<catalog>/<schema>/<name>/. A target with no catalog keeps the old layout.
  • Add a diagnostic for a catalog on a path catalog. It is explicit, but it needs a new code, and it rejects a layout that has a natural meaning.
  • Keep ignoring it. Nothing changes, but two layers in different catalogs would collide in one directory without a warning.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• ModelSettings and ResolvedModelConfig gain catalog: str | None, next to schema. It cascades like every other setting: model file, then folder _defaults.yml, then defaults.models.
  • Compile calls naming.relation(name, schema, identity) as before. When the resolved model catalog is set, it replaces the catalog of the returned TargetRef; when it is unset, the strategy's catalog option stays. NamingStrategy and API_VERSION do not change, and strategies keep transforming only the schema (prefix, per_user).
  • SparkSessionCatalog and UnityCatalog already use target.catalog or self.catalog and need no code change. pipeloom creates schemas, never catalogs: a catalog must exist.
  • FilesystemCatalog and DeltaPathCatalog lay a table out at <root>/<catalog>/<schema>/<name>/ when the target has a catalog, and at <root>/<schema>/<name>/ when it has none. ensure_namespace follows the same rule, and the catalog goes through the same directory-name check as the schema.
  • PLP412 (quarantine clash) compares (catalog, schema, name). No new diagnostic code.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The resolved config gains a field, so node checksums and plan hashes change once, for every project, when it moves to this version.
  • A naming strategy that has to rewrite catalogs (for example a per-user catalog) needs the protocol extended and a plugin API bump. It is not needed yet.
  • A local Spark session needs each catalog registered in its conf (spark.sql.catalog.<name>) before a run; on Databricks the catalogs and the USE CATALOG grants must exist.
  • Layout change on path catalogs: a project whose naming option set a catalog on filesystem or delta_path now gets that catalog as a directory. It either moves its tables or removes the option. The CHANGELOG carries the migration note.
  • A source with a three-part table: a.b.c is split into catalog, schema and name, so on a path catalog it now reads <root>/a/b/c instead of <root>/b/c. Such a source either moves its files under a directory named after the catalog, or is written as b.c.
  • PLP412 compares the effective catalog and schema: the model's own value, else the catalog and schema options of the naming strategy.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended in 0.9 by ADR-0050.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: catalog keeps its meaning and cascades through the layers of ADR-0050: the @model decorator, then the config of a properties entry, then the models: tree of pipeloom.yml (+catalog) from the folder nearest the model up to the root, then the project root +catalog, then the built-in default. _defaults.yml and defaults.models are removed with the legacy YAML path before 0.9.0; until then they map onto the folder and project layers. The rest of this decision (the catalog replaces the naming strategy's, path catalogs lay tables out under it) does not change.

docs.title: ADR-0041: pipeloom init
docs.text: Architecture: Section 3, Architecture overview

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A new user starts from an empty folder and has to write pipeloom.yml, a target, a catalog, a state store and the model files by hand, copying from the quickstart or the TPC-H examples. dbt solves the same problem with dbt init, which asks a few questions and writes a working project. pipeloom has no such command, and the CLI list in the architecture does not include one.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Where the templates live.
  • Inside the core package, pipeloom/scaffold/templates/, shipped in the wheel. Nothing to download, and the version of the templates always matches the installed core.
  • In each engine plugin, through a new entry-point group. Each plugin owns its template, but init would have to import a plugin before the user picked an engine, and a new group changes the plugin API.
  • A remote template repository (cookiecutter style). Flexible, but it needs network access and a new dependency.
  • How the user picks values.
  • Flags plus click prompts for what the flags leave out, prompting only when stdin is a terminal.
  • Flags only. Scriptable, but a first-time user has to read --help first.
  • What --force does with existing files.
  • Keep every existing file and report it as skipped.
  • Overwrite. Fast to retry, but it can destroy user work without a warning.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• pipeloom init [DIRECTORY] writes a project from templates inside the core package. The templates are plain text files with {{key}} placeholders, rendered with string replacement. The core imports no engine to do it.
  • Each engine is a stack of template folders (common, local, sql, then the engine's own folder); a later folder's file replaces an earlier one with the same path. polars, spark and databricks get SQL models; pandas gets Python models, because pandas has no SQL (PLC502).
  • polars, pandas and spark read a six-row CSV written into data/, so the project runs with no download. databricks reads samples.tpch.orders, which every workspace has, and gets a unity catalog, a state table, an artifacts root on a volume and a serverless deploy block, with comments that say what must exist before the first deploy.
  • Every layer writes to its own schema (bronze, silver, gold) through the folder _defaults.yml, not its own catalog, so local Spark needs no extra catalog configuration.
  • The generated YAML is block style; only short scalar lists such as tags: [bronze] stay inline.
  • Flags --name, --engine, --catalog, --no-input and --force. Prompts run only when stdin is a terminal and --no-input is not given, and only for values the flags leave out.
  • --force allows a non-empty directory and never overwrites: an existing file is kept and listed on stdout as skipped. A directory that already holds pipeloom.yml is refused even with --force.
  • A bad name, a bad engine, --catalog with an engine other than databricks, an existing project and a non-empty directory without --force are click usage errors (exit 2). No diagnostic code is added: init reads no project.
  • init writes no event stream: there is no project, target or sink configuration to send events to.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Templates ship with the core and change with it. A template that stops validating is caught by the tests, which validate and run (polars, pandas) or validate and compile (spark, databricks) every generated project.
  • The databricks template pins the deploy dependencies to the installed pipeloom version.
  • A plugin cannot add its own template yet. When one needs to, an entry-point group can be added then.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended in 0.8 (editor setup, pipeloom new model), in 0.9 by ADR-0050 and in 1.1 (duckdb template, pipeloom demo).

docs.title: Amendment (0.8): editor setup and pipeloom new model
What changed
docs.text:
• Every YAML file init writes starts with a # yaml-language-server: $schema=<url> modeline: project.json for pipeloom.yml, defaults.json for _defaults.yml and models.json for model files. The _defaults.yml templates lacked it. The URLs are the published schemas under SCHEMA_BASE_URL (pipeloom.config.schema); a test checks the templates against that constant.
  • init writes .vscode/settings.json, which maps yaml.schemas to the three schemas by glob (pipeloom.yml, models/**/_defaults.yml, and models/**/*.yml minus _defaults, with .yaml variants), and .vscode/extensions.json, which recommends redhat.vscode-yaml. Completion then works with only the YAML extension. --force keeps existing files as before.
  • pipeloom new model NAME [--sql|--python] [--folder PATH] adds one model file to a project. It loads the project (load stage only), so it knows the project name, python_paths, the existing model names and the engine kind of the default target. The default kind is Python when that engine is pandas (no SQL, PLC502), SQL otherwise; a flag wins.
  • It writes <first model path>/<folder>/<name>.yml with the models.json modeline and one block-style entry. SQL gets a select 1 as id body; Python gets python: <project>_models.<name>:build and a stub <python_paths[0]>/<project>_models/<name>.py with def build(ctx: Any, **inputs: Any) -> Any, which satisfies PLK602 for any alias. Both carry a commented inputs: example. The package __init__.py is created when missing.
  • It prints the written paths on stdout and writes no events. A project that does not load exits 1 with its diagnostics. A bad name, a name or file that already exists, --sql with --python, a --folder outside the model path and a Python model without python_paths in pipeloom.yml are usage errors (exit 2). No diagnostic code is added.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Append the model to an existing file: rejected. Rewriting YAML drops comments, and keeping them needs a round-trip YAML dependency. One file per model was chosen.
  • A --ref or --input flag to declare inputs: left out to keep the roadmap's interface. A commented inputs: example shows the shape.
  • A template engine or generator framework: a few inline scaffold strings are enough.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Authors get completion and validation squiggles in VS Code without installing a pipeloom extension. The schemas come from the published docs site, so completion needs network access the first time.
  • The .vscode templates ship in the wheel with the other templates.
  • New files stay valid by construction: tests run validate on generated models for polars and pandas and check every generated YAML against the exported JSON Schemas.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: With Python-first authoring (ADR-0050) pipeloom new model NAME [--sql|--python] [--folder PATH] writes one file, models/<folder>/<name>.py, with a decorated function and no YAML entry. With --sql the body returns ctx.sql("select 1 as id"); with --python it returns a frame stub. The default stays --python on pandas and --sql otherwise. The usage error for a Python model without python_paths goes away, because python_paths defaults to ["."]. init writes one .py model per layer, a models: tree in pipeloom.yml instead of _defaults.yml, and models/silver/_properties.yml; .vscode/settings.json maps project.json to pipeloom.yml and properties.json to models/**/*.yml, and the defaults.json and models.json globs go away. These templates change with the examples, after the discovery and resolve changes of ADR-0050. As built, the --python stub raises NotImplementedError, because the frame type depends on the engine; the name check also counts decorated models; and a Python keyword or ctx, model or ModelContext as NAME is a usage error, since NAME becomes the function name.

docs.title: Amendment 1.1: the duckdb template and pipeloom demo
What changed
docs.text:
• ENGINES gains duckdb: layers common, local, sql, duckdb. The template reads the same CSV, writes the same three SQL models, and targets the duckdb engine and catalog (target/warehouse.duckdb) with no extension. Its models/silver/_properties.yml adds one unit test for orders_clean, so pipeloom build has a unit test, three models and data tests to run. The default engine of init stays polars: only a new major version may change a default.
  • pipeloom demo [DIRECTORY] renders that template into DIRECTORY (default pipeloom_demo), then runs build and docs generate in process through the CLI commands over pipeloom.api, so events and diagnostics reach stderr as they do for those commands. It prints the project path, the site path (target/docs/index.html) and the next commands, and exits 0. A DIRECTORY that exists and is not empty is a usage error (exit 2) and nothing is written. There is no --force: a demo never mixes with user files.
  • The demo requires the duckdb engine and never falls back to another installed engine. Without it, the command stops before writing anything with PLU004 (exit 1) whose hint is pip install "pipeloom[duckdb]". The message lists the engine plugins that were found, so an environment with only polars sees why the demo did not run. The check reads entry-point metadata only (the core imports no plugin).
  • PLU004 is in the plugin layer, active since 1.1, with a case file and goldens.
  • CI installs the built core and pipeloom-duckdb wheels into a fresh venv and runs pipeloom demo on Linux, macOS and Windows, then checks target/docs/index.html.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Fall back to polars or any installed engine: rejected. The output would depend on the machine, the sample would need one template per engine kept passing, and the CI check could pass on an engine nobody meant to demo.
  • Bundle DuckDB in the core dependencies: rejected. The core keeps no engine dependency; the duckdb extra and the one-line install hint carry the same ease.
  • --force on demo: left out; use a new folder.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• uvx --from "pipeloom[duckdb]" pipeloom demo is the whole first run. A user with only the core gets one clear error instead of a validate failure about an unknown engine kind.
  • The duckdb template is covered by the same layout and YAML-style tests as the others, plus a build test.

docs.title: ADR-0042: Selection by state and --defer
docs.text: Architecture: Section 7, Error codes, and section 11, Artifacts

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A developer who changes one model wants to build that model and what depends on it, and to read the parents they did not touch from production instead of rebuilding them in their own schema. dbt does this with --state, state:modified, result: and --defer. pipeloom has the pieces: compile --stable writes a manifest with a checksum for every node and the relation each persisted model is written to, and every run writes run_results.json. It has no way to compare against them or to read from them.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• How state:modified decides a node changed.
  • Compare the node checksum of the reference with this project's. The checksum covers the canonical model config and the body bytes. It already leaves out the relation, which is computed separately from the naming strategy, so a dev project and a prod reference compare equal when nothing changed. Changing the checksum to drop target values is not needed.
  • The checksum misses rewired inputs, because they live in PlanNode.inputs. The comparison key is therefore the checksum plus the sorted alias to unique id pairs.
  • How --defer points a read at the reference.
  • Rewrite the relations of the plan before it runs. This changes plan_hash and the manifest, so a deferred run and a plain run of the same project would no longer share a plan. Rejected.
  • Swap the read spec when the runner resolves a read. The plan, its hash and the manifest stay the same. Chosen.
  • Whether --defer checks that the reference relation exists.
  • Check each one first. It costs a catalog round trip per parent and cannot know what this target may read.
  • Trust the reference, as dbt does with --favor-state, and let a missing table fail as PLM204 with a hint that names the reference relation. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• --state DIR on run, compile, ls and graph. DIR/manifest.json is required and DIR/run_results.json is optional; the artifacts root (target) works as is, because finalize copies both there. A relative DIR is relative to the project dir.
  • artifacts/reference.py loads the reference. A missing folder, an unreadable manifest, a manifest of another project (the target may differ), or run results that are unreadable, have another schema or belong to another project are PLX110 (exit 1).
  • state:modified selects a node that is absent from the reference or whose key differs, plus the persisted models that inline a modified ephemeral model. state:new selects a node absent from the reference. Other values are PLG305. + operators work as for any method.
  • result:fail|skip|cancelled|succeeded matches the status of the model's row in the reference run results: fail is failed or timed out, skip is skipped for any reason. Ephemeral models never match, as with unit:.
  • A state: or result: atom without --state is PLG307, and a result: atom when the folder has no run results is PLG308. Both are usage errors (exit 2).
  • run --defer needs --state (a click usage error without it). Every persisted model that the run does not build is read from reference.nodes[uid].relation. Sources are never deferred, and ephemeral parents are inlined as always.
  • An intermediate parent, a parent missing from the reference, or one with no relation there is read from this target, and PLX112 warns. It counts under --warn-error.
  • PLX111 (exit 2) refuses --defer for a unit invocation, for an effective boundary: task, and when the reference catalog kind differs from this target's or is missing. --manifest runs may defer.
  • The run results record args.state and args.defer. model.input_read gains relation and deferred, both additive.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Variables and environment values interpolated into a model's config sit inside its checksum, so changing one marks the node modified. A source change is not detected, because a source has no checksum. A Python model's checksum covers its module file, not the modules it imports.
  • A manifest records the catalog kind only. With a filesystem catalog, the reference's root must be the same as this target's for deferred reads to find the tables.
  • Task-boundary defer is refused in 0.8: each unit would run in a child process that does not know the reference. Use --boundary process.
  • state:modified on a project with no changes matches nothing, so PLG303 warns, and a run with --warn-error fails.
  • Defer trusts the reference. A parent that was never built there, or that this target cannot read, fails the child with PLM204 and a hint that says so.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended in 0.9 by ADR-0050.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: With Python-first authoring (ADR-0050) the checksum formula keeps its shape: the resolved config, the callable, a NUL byte and the bytes of the model's module file, plus columns without their description. The resolved config now includes what properties files and the models: tree of pipeloom.yml set, so a change in either marks the node modified. The body is always a module file, and editing any function in it marks every model of that file modified; this is conservative and accepted. Checksums and plan hashes change once for every project.

docs.title: ADR-0043: Docs site
docs.text: Architecture: Section 1, Principles and non-goals; Section 3, Architecture overview

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pipeloom writes everything a browser needs to show a project: manifest.json (nodes, sources, edges, bodies, resolved configs) and run_results.json (status, rows, bytes and errors per model). The only way to see the graph is pipeloom graph --output mermaid, and nothing lets a reader browse models. dbt solves this with dbt docs generate and dbt docs serve.

The architecture lists "a scheduler service or UI" as one non-goal. The roadmap splits it: a scheduler, or a UI that writes, needs authentication, a database and a daemon, while a read-only view over files pipeloom already writes needs none of that. The roadmap also planned the graph with "one pinned and vendored JavaScript library". This ADR decides that, and the other points that shape the site.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Non-goal scope.
  • Keep all UI out. Nothing changes, but the observability work stays invisible and users keep writing their own viewers.
  • Narrow it to "a scheduler service, or any UI that starts, schedules or changes runs". A read-only viewer is allowed and the risky half stays out.
  • Site shape.
  • Multi-file: an HTML shell that fetches manifest.json at load. Smaller HTML, but fetch on file:// fails in some browsers, so it needs a server.
  • One self-contained index.html. It opens from disk, by double click or as an attachment.
  • Graph.
  • A vendored library: cytoscape.js (about 400 KB, no dependencies) or mermaid (about 3 MB with bundled dependencies). Interactive, but it adds license and update work, makes the output hard to test byte for byte, and grows the core wheel.
  • A layout computed in Python and written as inline SVG. Static, but deterministic, offline by construction and testable with a golden file.
  • Templating.
  • Jinja. Familiar, but a new dependency in a core that bans Jinja for models and keeps a short dependency list.
  • The standard library: html.escape and string building.
  • Input.
  • Always compile the project. Simple, but it needs the project's plugins and environment.
  • Also accept --manifest PATH, so CI can render a manifest produced elsewhere.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The non-goal becomes "a scheduler service, or any UI that starts, schedules or changes runs". pipeloom docs generate and pipeloom docs serve are read only.
  • The site is one index.html, written to --out (default <project-dir>/target/docs), which holds exactly that file. All CSS and the little JavaScript are inline. A Content-Security-Policy meta tag (default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data:) stops the page from loading anything external. Colors follow prefers-color-scheme.
  • The HTML is rendered in Python with the standard library, and manifest.json is not embedded: the HTML is the rendering, and the manifest stays the data contract. The output is deterministic. It holds no wall-clock time, so the compile timestamp is not shown.
  • The graph deviates from the roadmap's vendored library. It is an inline SVG laid out by a pure Python module (pipeloom.docs.layout): layer = longest path from the roots, order inside a layer from (path, name) then four alternating barycenter sweeps with stable tie-breaks, fixed node size, each layer centered, and one cubic Bezier per edge with no dummy nodes. Reasons: no license or update work, a golden-testable output, offline by construction, and a smaller core wheel. A few lines of vanilla JavaScript add zoom buttons and a model filter; with JavaScript off the page still works. The interactive graph is left to pipeloom ui (1.1), which ships as its own distribution.
  • Content: a header (project, target, version, short plan hash and, with results, the last run), the graph, a filterable model table, one section per model (relation, materialization, strategy, tags, inputs, parents, children, expectations, resolved config, body, last result with the pipeloom explain CODE hint) and one section per source. Model contracts (columns) arrive in 0.9 and are shown then.
  • Inputs: by default the command compiles like pipeloom compile (--project-dir, --target, --vars, --plugin, --log-format), reports diagnostics on stderr and exits 1 on errors. --manifest PATH renders an existing manifest (PLX107 and exit 1 when unreadable). Results come from --run-results PATH, else from the run_results.json at the root of the artifacts root when it exists; with --manifest and no flag there are none. A results file that is not pipeloom.run_results/1, or belongs to another project, is a usage error (exit 2). Results with a different plan_hash still show per unique_id, with a note in the header. No diagnostic code is added.
  • pipeloom docs serve runs the standard library ThreadingHTTPServer over --dir (default <project-dir>/target/docs) on --host (default 127.0.0.1) and --port (default 8000). A missing index.html is a usage error. It never opens a browser and stops cleanly on Ctrl+C. make_server lives in pipeloom.docs.serve so tests can run it on port 0.
  • pipeloom.docs is a core package above plan, artifacts, graph and diagnostics in the import-linter layers, beside runtime: it imports neither runtime nor a plugin.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The core wheel gains no dependency and no bundled asset. The site works from file://, in an air-gapped network, and as a CI artifact.
  • The graph cannot pan, zoom to a node or collapse groups. Large projects scroll. Layout quality is that of a simple layered drawing, and long edges can cross nodes; pipeloom ui is the place for an interactive graph.
  • Output is byte-stable for a given manifest and results, so the SVG of the shop fixture is a golden file and layout changes show up in review.
  • The page grows with the project: every model's SQL and config is in the HTML. A project with thousands of models gives a large file.
  • Widening the read-only exception to pipeloom ui still needs its own ADR for the server choice.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0044: Model contracts
docs.text: Architecture: Section 4, Configuration, section 9, Schema change, and section 10, Data quality

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A model's output schema is whatever its body returns. on_schema_change (ADR-0026) only compares the batch with the existing target, so a first build, an overwrite or a full refresh accepts any schema, and a downstream consumer learns about a changed type from its own failure. dbt calls the fix a model contract: declared columns with a type and a nullability, enforced at build time, where an enforced contract must match the column set exactly (dbt model contracts). pipeloom already has a logical type vocabulary (pipeloom.engine.types: int64, decimal(18,2), timestamp[us, UTC], ...) that every engine reports through EngineSession.schema, and an evaluate primitive that counts nulls the same way on every engine (ADR-0028).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Column set.
  • Exact: every declared column is present, no other column is. The written table is what the contract says.
  • Subset: declared columns must be present, others pass. Extra columns reach the table unseen, which is what a contract is meant to stop.
  • Types.
  • Exact equality of the logical type string.
  • Accept a batch type that widens to the declared one and cast it. Needs a cast step before the schema policy and makes the written type depend on the cast.
  • Nullability.
  • Read the engine's schema nullability. polars and pandas do not track it, and Spark marks most computed columns nullable.
  • Count nulls with EngineSession.evaluate and a not_null check per non-nullable column: one aggregation, the same semantics on every engine, and the expectation suite already compares each engine with the reference.
  • Where the check runs. Before the expectations, or after them on the rows that will be written.
  • Hashes. Keep columns out of the node checksum and plan hash, or add it only when it is declared.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Config. A model may declare columns, a list of name, dtype and nullable (default true). It is a model key, not a default: _defaults.yml and defaults.models cannot set it. dtype must be a logical type name of pipeloom.engine.types (LOGICAL_TYPE_PATTERN, also in the JSON Schema); a duplicate column name is rejected. Both are PLS102 at L1.
  • Exact match. The batch must have exactly the declared column names (case-sensitive, order ignored) and each column's logical type must equal the declared dtype string. No widening and no cast: the user casts in the body, so the type is visible where it is produced. Engines report fixed forms (Spark timestamps are always timestamp[us, UTC]), so a project that targets several engines declares the form they share.
  • Nullability. For every column with nullable: false, one evaluate call counts rows with a null (NaN counts as null, as in expectations). A lazy relation is persisted first, as the quality step does. Engines need the quality capability; PLC510 now also covers a non-nullable contract column on an engine without it. Every built-in engine has it.
  • Order. The contract is checked after the expectations, on the kept rows, and before the schema policy, the quarantine write, align and the write. An expectation that drops null rows therefore runs before the contract checks the column. A violation is PLM208, permanent (never retried under retry_on: transient), and nothing is written, the quarantine table included.
  • Schema-change policy. Unchanged. The contract checks the batch; on_schema_change still compares the batch with the target. With a contract the batch schema is fixed, so the policy only acts when the target drifted or the contract itself changed.
  • Materializations. Tables, incremental models and intermediate models are checked. Views and ephemeral models produce no batch of their own, so columns on them is PLP414 (L4). Python and SQL models are treated the same.
  • Manifest and hashes. nodes[].columns is an additive field of pipeloom.manifest/1, present only when a model declares columns. The node checksum and the plan hash cover it only then, so a contract change selects the node under state:modified and changes the plan hash, while a project without contracts keeps byte-identical manifests, checksums and plan hashes.
  • Docs site. A model page shows a Columns table when the node has a contract.
  • Codes. PLM208 (runtime) and PLP414 (L4) are new in 0.9. PLM209 stays free.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A contract stops a changed output before any write, on every engine, at the cost of one schema call and, with non-nullable columns, one aggregation per write.
  • Exact types are strict across engines: a polars body that yields timestamp[ns] fails a timestamp[us] contract until it casts. This is deliberate; a widening mode can be added later as an option.
