  • Lineage, the OpenLineage schema facet and column-level lineage can read nodes[].columns without running anything.
  • Contracts do not check sources, and they carry no column descriptions yet.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended in 0.9 by ADR-0050.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: With Python-first authoring (ADR-0050) columns comes from the @model decorator (a list of Column(...) or plain mappings) or from the columns of a properties entry. It stays a model key: the models: tree of pipeloom.yml cannot set it, as _defaults.yml and defaults.models could not. When both set it, the decorator's list replaces the properties list whole; the lists are never merged column by column. ColumnConfig gains an optional description, kept out of the node checksum and the plan hash, so editing a description neither marks a model modified nor makes a deployed job stale. Where descriptions appear in the manifest and on the docs site is settled later in 0.9, outside the plan hash. Every model is a Python function, so the line about Python and SQL models no longer applies. PLP414 does not change.

docs.title: ADR-0045: Unit tests, post-write data tests and pipeloom build
docs.text: Architecture: Section 4, Configuration, section 5, Validation, section 7, Execution, and section 10, Data quality

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Expectations (ADR-0009, ADR-0028) judge each batch before it is written, and contracts (ADR-0044) fix its schema. Neither answers two questions users ask of a transformation. Does the body compute the right rows for a known input, without a warehouse? And does the written table hold together as a whole, for example every foreign key finds its parent? dbt answers the first with unit tests (given input rows, expect output rows, run on the warehouse without building parents) and the second with data tests (not_null, unique, relationships) run after the build; dbt 1.8 renamed the model key tests to data_tests to stop the two being confused (dbt unit tests, dbt data tests). dbt build runs both in DAG order.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Naming. A bare tests key, or unit_tests and data_tests.
  • Where cases live. On the model only, or also in separate files, with or without a new discovery path.
  • Hashes. Cases in the plan and manifest, or kept out of both.
  • Where a case runs. Through the full unit runner with a throwaway catalog, or by calling the body directly with in-memory inputs.
  • Comparing rows. Ordered or as a multiset; with or without float tolerance; in the core or per engine.
  • Data tests. As expectations with a new action, or as a separate list run against the written table.
  • build. A new scheduler that interleaves test nodes, or test followed by run with data tests on.

docs.title: Naming and config
docs.text:
1. unit_tests holds cases, data_tests holds post-write checks. There is no bare tests key. The roadmap text uses these names.
  2. Under Python-first authoring (ADR-0050, point 15) unit tests live in the model's properties entry, as unit_tests: beside description, config, columns and data_tests, and never on the decorator: rows are data, not code. The diagnostics point at the properties file. While the legacy YAML path coexists with Python-first (ADR-0050, point 19), a YAML model entry may also declare unit_tests:, and any YAML file under model_paths may hold a top-level unit_tests: list whose entries name their model with model: (a missing model: is PLS105); both go away with the legacy path. There is no new discovery path and no new project key. unit_tests is a model key, not a setting: the models: tree cannot set it.
  3. A case is {name, given: {alias: {rows | csv, columns?}}, expect: {rows | csv, columns?}}. A given key is an input alias, which for a decorated function is the parameter name. rows and csv are mutually exclusive (PLS108). Every input alias of the model must be given, and only input aliases (PLR208). CSV paths are relative to the project dir and read with the standard csv module; an empty field is null. Case names are unique per model (PLR208); an unknown model: is PLR208.
  4. Cases stay out of PlanNode, the manifest, the node checksum and the plan hash. Manifests and plan hashes are byte-identical with or without unit tests.

docs.title: Types and comparison
docs.text:
1. A given column's type comes from the given columns, else from the upstream model's ADR-0044 columns, else from inference. Inline values infer boolean, int64, float64, string, date, timestamp[us] and timestamp[us, UTC] from their YAML type (a quoted date stays a string). CSV columns infer int64, then float64, then string; dates and timestamps must be declared. An all-null column with no declared type is PLX115.
  2. Comparison lives in pipeloom.quality.rows, because the core may not import pipeloom.testing; pipeloom.testing.reference re-exports it. The compared columns are the keys of expect; extra output columns are ignored, a missing one fails the case. Expected values are cast to the output column's logical type. Rows compare as a multiset: order is ignored, duplicates count. Null equals NaN, floats are normalized to 12 significant digits, a naive timestamp is read as UTC, and decimals compare exactly. The diff lists missing and unexpected rows: 10 of each in the message, 50 in the event.

docs.title: Running a case
docs.text:
1. Given rows become relations through EngineSession.from_rows(rows, schema). A SQL body runs through the existing session.sql(body, inputs), which scopes the aliases to that query; a Python body is called as build(ctx, **inputs) with is_incremental=False and the model's frame_api. The result is read back with EngineSession.to_rows(rel), which returns plain Python values. No materializer runs, no namespace is created and nothing touches the catalog or the state store. Ephemeral parents are not inlined: their alias is given like any other input.
  2. pipeloom test takes --select, --exclude, --state, --target, --vars, --plugin, --project-dir and --log-format. It runs the cases of the selected models in plan order, takes no lock, writes no artifacts and creates no run id. Each case emits unit_test.passed or unit_test.failed; unit_tests.completed closes the invocation with the counts. A case whose rows differ is PLX114, a case that cannot run (a missing or unreadable CSV, a value that does not cast, an untyped all-null column, an engine without from_rows or to_rows, a body that raises) is PLX115. Both travel as the code of unit_test.failed, which carries the diff, and count as errors of the invocation. Exit codes: 0 when every case passed, 1 when one failed, 2 for a usage error, 130 when stopped.

docs.title: Engine protocol
docs.text: 1. Plugin API (0, 5) gains from_rows(rows, schema) -> Relation, to_rows(rel) -> list[dict] and orphans(rel, column, parent, field) -> int on EngineSession. They are additions to 0.5 before 0.9 ships, so a third-party 0.5 engine without them fails only when it is used, with PLX115, mirroring PLX117. pipeloom.engine.portable has a narwhals to_rows and an anti-join orphans that polars and pandas reuse; from_rows uses each engine's own logical-type map (polars polars_dtype, pandas arrow_type), because a narwhals Decimal cannot carry a precision on every backend. MemoryEngine keeps plain rows. Spark builds a StructType from its logical-type map for createDataFrame, reads timestamps back through unix_micros so they come out as aware UTC whatever the session time zone, and counts orphans with a left_anti join.

docs.title: Data tests (implemented in the second half of 0.9)
docs.text:
1. data_tests: [{name, check: {not_null | unique | relationships: {column, to: {ref | source}, field}}, on_violation: warn | fail}] is a model key like columns. The decorator sets it with data_tests= (a list of pipeloom.DataTest objects or mappings) and properties set it with data_tests:; the decorator list (or, on the legacy path, the YAML model entry's) replaces the properties list whole. Being a model key, the models: tree and its root +keys cannot set it, which keeps a relationship next to the model it describes. Diagnostics point at the list that won (ResolvedModel.data_tests_at). PlanNode.data_tests is left out of the manifest when absent; the node checksum and the plan hash cover it only when declared (the ADR-0044 pattern).
  2. A relationships violation is a child row whose non-null column (NaN counts as null) matches no field value of the parent; parent nulls never match. to is read like an input, through the runner's read and source specs, so --defer, intermediates and per-model catalogs behave the same; an unreadable parent is PLM204. The judge treats relationships like unique: the violation count is the value. to reuses PLR201 and PLR203 for unknown names.
  3. Data tests run inside the unit after the write and the watermark commit and before the attempt file, and also on the replay path, so a retry that replays the write token tests again. They read the whole written table, incremental models included. Tables, incremental, intermediate and view models take them; data_tests on an ephemeral model is PLP415, as is a relationships to that names the model itself, a descendant, an ephemeral model, an intermediate model, or that closes a cycle among edges of both kinds (inputs and relationships). An intermediate parent is rejected because its table exists only while a run that builds it is in progress: a run that selects the child alone would fail with PLM204.
  4. Results are entries of results[].expectations with scope: "table". From 0.9 every entry carries scope: batch entries get "batch", filled in when old commit_meta replays. The change is additive. warn adds to warnings[]; a fail is PLQ303, permanent: the unit fails, its descendants are skipped, the run exits 1, and the data stays written. PLC510 also covers data tests on an engine without quality.

docs.title: build
docs.text: 1. pipeloom build runs the unit tests of the selected models first; any failure stops it with exit 1 before a run id exists and before any write, and invocation.completed counts each failed case as an error (RunOutcome.extra_errors). Then it runs run with data tests on. Relationship parents become extra scheduling edges at run time only (UnitGraph.from_parents); run and unit_parent_map are unchanged. build takes run's user-facing flags. run gets a hidden --data-tests true|false that the process executor passes to its children; args.data_tests is recorded in run_results, and retry --from inherits it.

docs.title: Non-goals for 0.9
docs.text:
1. The Airflow and Databricks renderers do not pass --data-tests yet. pipeloom test does not run data tests against existing tables. init templates are unchanged.

Since the legacy model path was removed in 0.9 (ADR-0050), cases come only from properties entries of resolved models, so a properties entry for an unknown model is PLR209 and PLR208 covers the case itself (a missing or unknown input alias, a duplicate case name). There are no SQL bodies: a model that calls ctx.sql runs it through the same translate and session.sql path as pipeloom run (point 7).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A body is testable on a laptop in milliseconds, on every engine, with the same properties file. A plain pytest call on the decorated function also works. The contract suite runs one passing and one failing case per engine.
  • Unit tests never change a manifest or a plan hash, so adding them selects nothing under state:modified.
  • Data tests scan the whole written table on every build, incremental models included; on_violation: warn is available where that is too slow.
  • Type inference can surprise (a CSV id read as int64 where a string was meant); declaring columns on the given is the fix the guide documents.
  • scope on every expectation entry changes the run_results goldens and event payloads, additively.
  • Third-party 0.5 engines without the new methods fail only when a test runs.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The roadmap (section 3, End-to-end observability) asks for a pipeloom-openlineage sink in 0.9: unit events become OpenLineage run events with the job <project>.<model> and a parent run facet for the pipeloom run, datasets come from the manifest, the facets cover schema, output statistics, data quality assertions and errors, the transport is the openlineage-python client, and Marquez is the reference backend. Under Airflow the operators implement get_openlineage_facets_on_complete, so the Airflow OpenLineage provider reports the tasks with the DAG as parent, and the sink must stay silent there or every unit is reported twice (roadmap risk "Duplicate OpenLineage events under Airflow").

A sink only sees events (ADR-0010). Events name units and relations but not the plan: the inputs of a unit, its source locations, its contract and its file are in the manifest. One pipeloom run can span many processes: a pipeloom run, process-boundary children whose events the parent forwards, one unit invocation per orchestrator task, and pipeloom finalize (ADR-0034). Each process builds its own sinks. The plugin API is (0, 5) and not yet released (ADR-0047), so additive changes stay in (0, 5).

Models are moving from YAML files with SQL or Python bodies to @model-decorated Python functions (ADR-0050, in progress). SQL bodies go away before 0.9.0, and node fields may be renamed.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Read the manifest from disk in the sink. The sink would guess the artifacts root and the run folder, and a unit invocation reads the manifest from --manifest, which can sit anywhere.
  • Put datasets on the events. Every unit event grows lineage fields that only one sink reads.
  • A sink hook that hands over the plan. Chosen: plan_ready(PlanInfo), optional, called once per invocation that has a plan.
  • Schema from the contract only. Most models declare no contract.
  • Schema from what was written. Chosen, through an additive model.written.columns field; the contract fills in when the write path does not know the columns.
  • Random run ids per process. The finalize process and the unit tasks of one run would report unrelated OpenLineage runs.
  • uuid5 run ids derived from the pipeloom ids. Chosen: every process derives the same ids without talking to the others.
  • The sql job facet. SQL bodies go away with the Python-first pivot; the facet would describe a body pipeloom no longer has.
  • The sourceCodeLocation job facet. Chosen: the model's file and line, which both authoring styles have.
  • Inside Airflow, the sink and the provider both emit. Duplicate jobs and runs in the backend.
  • Inside Airflow, only the provider emits. Chosen as the default (inside_airflow: skip), with emit for setups without the provider.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Core hook (additive in plugin API (0, 5)). pipeloom.events.bus.PlanInfo(manifest, project_dir) holds the run's manifest as manifest_dict(plan) returns it (pipeloom.manifest/1) and the absolute project dir. EventBus.plan_ready(info) calls plan_ready(info) on every enabled sink that defines it; sinks without it are skipped, and a failure counts against the sink's failure budget like a failed delivery. BufferedSink queues the plan in order with the events and never drops it. pipeloom run calls the hook right after run.started (a unit invocation, which emits no run.started, calls it at the same point), and pipeloom finalize calls it before run.completed. A process-boundary child reports to its parent only, so the parent's sinks get the plan once.

model.written.columns (additive in pipeloom.event/1). The table's columns after the write, as the schema policy resolved them (name, dtype, nullable; scd2 tables include their validity columns). Null on the intermediate path, for views and for replayed writes.

Distribution. pipeloom-openlineage (module pipeloom_openlineage, sink kind openlineage, root extra openlineage) depends on openlineage-python>=1.52.0,<2. The floor is what apache-airflow-providers-openlineage requires, so the sink and the provider can share one client inside an Airflow image. The spec imports no OpenLineage code; the client is built at the first event that needs it, from transport when given (an openlineage-python transport config), else from OPENLINEAGE_URL or openlineage.yml as the client reads them. A transport that still holds a ${secret:...} reference (a command that never resolves secrets) sends nothing.

Options. namespace (default pipeloom.{target}; {project} and {target} are filled in), dataset_namespace (default: the job namespace), transport, and inside_airflow: skip|emit (default skip).

Jobs and runs. The pipeloom run is the job <project>; each persisted model is the job <project>.<model>. Run ids are uuid5 values in a fixed pipeloom namespace: run:{project}:{run_id} for the run and unit:{project}:{run_id}:{unit_id}:{attempt} for one attempt of a unit; the project keeps two projects that pass the same --run-id apart. pipeloom_openlineage.sink.run_uuid and unit_uuid are the only place that computes them, so the Airflow operators use the same functions. Every unit run carries the parent facet (and its root) pointing at the pipeloom run.

Event mapping. run.started is START of the run job. unit.started is START of the unit run; unit.succeeded is COMPLETE; unit.failed and unit.timed_out are FAIL with the errorMessage facet (the code and message, and the full traceback as stackTrace); unit.cancelled is ABORT, and a unit cancelled or skipped before it started has no OpenLineage run. Each attempt of a retried unit is its own run. run.completed is COMPLETE, FAIL or ABORT by its status, with an errorMessage facet listing the failed units; a run.completed with replay: true is skipped, since the first finalize reported it. A run driven by an orchestrator gets no START for the run job: its unit tasks report their runs with the parent facet, and finalize reports the end.

Datasets. Inputs of a unit are the inputs of all its nodes, minus the ephemeral models it inlines. A model input is its catalog relation (catalog.schema.name) in dataset_namespace. A source with a table is that table in dataset_namespace; a source with a location follows the OpenLineage naming spec: a URI with a host (s3://bucket/raw/s) has scheme://host as namespace and the path without its leading slash as name (raw/s); a file: URI has namespace file and the absolute path as name; any other scheme without a host (dbfs:/Volumes/c/s/v/x) has the scheme as namespace and the path as reported; a plain relative path is joined to the project directory under namespace file. The output is the persisted model's relation.

Facets. jobType (BATCH, integration PIPELOOM, JOB for the run, MODEL for a unit); sourceCodeLocation (type file, path the node's file relative to the project dir, url the same with #L<line> when the manifest has the line); schema on the output, from model.written.columns, else from the contract; outputStatistics on a completed output (rowCount and size from unit.succeeded); dataQualityAssertions from the unit's model.quality_evaluated results (assertion is the expectation kind, success means no failed rows, severity is the action). The spec defines dataQualityAssertions as an input dataset facet. pipeloom checks the rows it writes, so the sink puts it in the output dataset's facets, where Marquez shows it on the dataset; the sink casts the type. No sql facet.

Manifest access. The sink reads only metadata.project, metadata.target, units, nodes[].file, line, inputs, relation and columns, and sources[].location and table, each through one small accessor function, so a rename of node fields in the Python-first pivot touches one place.

No duplicates under Airflow. Events of a unit run by an Airflow task carry orchestrator_id.airflow_dag_id in their context. With inside_airflow: skip the sink ignores every such event, the run events included, and the provider reports the task. The Airflow operators implement get_openlineage_facets_on_complete through a mixin, by execution mode: LOCAL and VIRTUALENV capture the child's events and build the same inputs, outputs and facets as the sink; KUBERNETES returns the static datasets from the manifest; DATABRICKS relies on the sink in the Databricks task (its events carry no Airflow ids). A test runs one task with the sink configured and asserts one set of events.

Reference check. examples/marquez/compose.yml (compose project pipeloom-marquez: API on 15000, admin on 15001, web on 13000, Postgres without a host port) and uv run --all-packages python tools/marquez_check.py [--keep] run a project against Marquez and check five things: the jobs, the lineage edges against the manifest, the schema fields, the quality assertions and the parent run ids. It needs Docker and is run by hand before a release, not in CI.

Release. release.yml gets publish-pipeloom-openlineage (environment pypi-openlineage), joins the known list and the outputs loop, and github-release waits for it. CI type-checks and tests the plugin like the others.

Codes. None. PLX116 stays unused.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Lineage works for pipeloom run, process-boundary runs and runs an orchestrator drives task by task, with stable ids across processes and retries of finalize. Sinks that want the plan get it without reading files, and third-party sinks keep working unchanged. The columns field and the hook are additive, so the plugin API stays (0, 5). Column-level lineage, dataset version facets and an input statistics facet are left for later; the sql facet is not planned. The Airflow mixin, the Marquez compose file and its check, and the docs guide land with the second half of this item.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0047: Run history and the webhook sink
Context
docs.text:
Every state store already records one RunRecord per run, and every run writes runs/<run_id>/run_results.json under the artifacts root, but nothing lists them: to find the last failed run a user opens folders by hand. The roadmap (section 3, End-to-end observability) asks for StateStore.list_runs in the plugin API at version (0, 5), a pipeloom runs command over it, and a webhook sink that tells a chat channel or a pager when a run fails, with stdlib HTTP only.

Plugins implement StateStore structurally: they do not subclass the protocol, so a default method body on the protocol never reaches them. While the plugin API major is 0 the core accepts only plugins built for its exact version (ADR-0016, ADR-0017). The event bus already disables a sink that fails failure_budget times in a row and emits one sink.disabled event (PLE401), but it resets the count on every delivered event, and a webhook ignores most events, so a streak of failed posts is never consecutive from the bus's point of view.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• History from the state store only. One source, but runs whose store was lost, or that ran on another machine with a local sqlite file, cannot be listed.
  • History from run_results.json only. Works without a store, but needs a readable artifacts root and parses one file per run.
  • Both, the store by default and the artifacts on request. Chosen.
  • Page by timestamp. Two runs can start in the same microsecond, and the user has to copy a timestamp.
  • Page by run id. A run id is what ls prints and what show and retry --from take.
  • Webhook budget in the bus. The bus would have to know which events a sink ignores.
  • Webhook budget in the sink. The sink knows what it posted; the bus keeps reporting.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Plugin API (0, 5). StateStore gains list_runs(project, target, limit, before=None) -> tuple[RunRecord, ...]. API_VERSION becomes (0, 5). During 0.x the match stays exact, so every first-party plugin moves with the core (they declare API_VERSION) and a plugin built for (0, 4) fails with PLU001; ADR-0016 does not allow a compatibility window before 1.0.

Order and paging. list_runs returns the runs of one project and target, newest first, ordered by (started_at, run_id) descending, at most limit (at least 1). before is a run id: the result starts with the run that comes right after it in that order. A before that names no run of that project and target raises UnknownRun (a LookupError).

Default for stores that lack it. The core never calls the method directly: pipeloom.state.types.list_runs(store, ...) calls it when the store has it and otherwise raises ListRunsUnsupported, which the CLI reports as PLX117 with a hint to use --artifacts. This is the default the roadmap asks for, placed where a structural plugin cannot skip it.

Implementations. A shared helper, page_runs, orders and pages a sequence of records, so the stores agree on ties. The sqlite store selects the project's and target's rows, the json store reads runs/*/run.json, and the Spark plugin's table store selects the run rows of that project and target. Each call reads the whole history of one project and target; that is fine for thousands of runs, and a store can push the order and the limit down later without changing the contract. The state store contract suite gains the ordering, paging and unknown-cursor tests, so the Spark table store is checked by the same tests in CI.

pipeloom runs. A command group with ls and show RUN_ID. It takes no lock and changes no run. Building the store may still create it (the sqlite file, the json store's folder and marker, the Delta table), as every other command does; opening stores read only is left for later. The commands:

  • runs ls prints the last runs of the bound target, --limit N (default 20), --before RUN_ID for the next page, --target, and --output text|json like ls. Text is one tab-separated line per run: run id, status, started at, duration and unit counts. JSON is a list of the state records as the json store writes them.
  • runs show RUN_ID prints one run and its unit attempts; --output json prints {"run": ..., "units": [...]}.
  • --artifacts on both reads <artifacts root>/runs/*/run_results.json of the bound target instead of the store, keeps the documents of this project and target, and skips folders without a readable pipeloom.run_results/1 document (a run that is still running or crashed). Units then come from the results rows.
  • An unknown run id (show, --before) is PLX118. Both codes exit 1 and go through the event bus to stderr; results go to stdout.

The webhook sink. A built-in sink, kind webhook, with these options:

  • secret_url: the URL, given as ${secret:provider/path}. The name is secret-like, so a literal URL is PLS104. Only http and https are accepted. The URL is never logged, printed or put in an error message; the bus also masks it as a resolved secret.
  • events (default [run.completed]): event types to post. A run.completed event is posted only when its status is in statuses (default [failed]).
  • min_level (default none): also post any event at or above this level (warning or error). It is off by default so that a failed run posts exactly once.
  • timeout (default 10 seconds) per request, and max_failures (default 3).

The body is one JSON object, {"text": ..., "event": ...}: text is a one-line summary (for a failed run, the run id, the status and the first failed units with their codes) that Slack and Teams incoming webhooks render, and event is the full redacted event envelope for anything else. It is sent with urllib.request as a POST with Content-Type: application/json; any 2xx answer is a success. No new dependency.

The failure budget lives in the sink: a failed post raises an error that names only the HTTP status or the exception type. After max_failures failed posts in a row the sink stops posting and fails every later delivery with one fixed message, so the bus disables it and emits one sink.disabled warning (PLE401), at the latest when the bus closes. The sink is meant to run with buffered: true, so a slow endpoint never holds up the run. A sink built without secret resolution (commands that never run, such as validate) still holds the reference and posts nothing.

Retried finalize. pipeloom finalize exits 1 for a failed run, and orchestrators retry it (the Databricks finalize task has max_retries=1), so one run can be finalized twice by two processes, and a sink cannot remember the first post. run.completed therefore gains an additive field, replay (default false). Finalize sets it when the state store already held a finished record of the run id with the same status, and no unit attempt of the run started after that record's ended_at; finalize never records running, so that record comes from an earlier finalize or a finished pipeloom run. The attempt check matters for a Databricks repair, which reruns units under the same run id and finalizes again: its new attempts start after the first finalize, so a repair that fails again is no replay and posts again. Comparing the set of failed units instead would miss a repair that fails on the same unit. A repaired task that fails before its unit starts writes no attempt file and counts as a replay; the orchestrator reports that failure itself. The event is still emitted, so the console, jsonl and run files report the retry as before, and the webhook skips run.completed events with replay: true. pipeloom run always sets false, because it runs units again. A first finalize whose post failed is not posted again by its retry; the sink.disabled warning of the first one is the signal.

Codes. PLX117 (state store cannot list runs) and PLX118 (run not found) join a new _ACTIVE_09 table. PLX119 stays free.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Run history works on every built-in store and on the Spark table store, and on any artifacts root without a store. Third-party state stores must add list_runs and rebuild for (0, 5); until they do, PLU001 stops them. A store that declares (0, 5) but lacks the method still runs pipelines, and runs reports PLX117 for it. Alerting needs no new dependency, and a broken webhook costs at most max_failures timeouts per invocation. Paging pushdown in the stores, filters by status, and alert templates are left for later.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended in 0.9 by ADR-0050.

docs.title: Amendment 0.9 (ADR-0050)
docs.text: Plugin API (0, 5) also carries EngineCapabilities.sql_dialect: str | None = None, the engine's sqlglot dialect for ctx.sql (ADR-0050). (0, 5) is not released yet, so the version does not change.

docs.title: ADR-0048: Airflow WATCHER mode
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 13, The Airflow plugin

Amends ADR-0012 and ADR-0038. No core change.

Status: Accepted (2026-11-16, after the live check on the Astro example: a green run, then a failed unit cleared with Downstream and rerun on try 2).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: In LOCAL, VIRTUALENV and KUBERNETES modes every unit is its own Airflow task and its own process: each one starts Python, imports the engine, binds the project and checks the plan hash. On a wide DAG of short models that start-up cost dominates, and the core scheduler, which already runs units in parallel with in-process retries, goes unused. A user wants one pipeloom run for the whole selection and still one Airflow task per model, with its state, retries, logs and asset events.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• One task for the run. A single task runs pipeloom run. Cheap, but the graph, per-model state and asset events are lost.
  • Producer and watchers. One producer task runs the selection; one deferrable watcher per unit reads the files the run writes and reports that unit. The watchers cost a triggerer slot each instead of a worker slot.
  • Producer pushes states. The producer sets the state of the unit tasks through the Airflow API. It needs API credentials on the worker and breaks the retry semantics of the unit tasks.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Config: ExecutionMode.WATCHER = "watcher". New ExecutionConfig fields: watcher_workers (--workers of the producer's run; None keeps the target's), watcher_poll_interval (10 seconds), watcher_timeout (86400 seconds: the producer's execution_timeout and each watcher's deadline for one try) and watcher_artifacts_root (an absolute path that overrides the root read at parse time). virtualenv_dir is optional, as in VIRTUALENV. Watchers always defer, so there is no deferrable switch. RECHECK_S = 300 and VISIBILITY_GRACE_S = 120 are constants. PLA002 also covers a worker count below 1, a non-positive poll interval or timeout, and a WATCHER selection made only of unit: selectors (the producer would run in unit mode). PLA007 is not reported: one process runs every unit.
  2. Retries: the producer has Airflow retries=0, because the core scheduler applies the model retries in process, and a producer try above 1 is skipped, so it runs once per DAG run. Each watcher gets the model's retries and retry_delay. A failure the producer already reported fails the watcher without a retry; a rerun's failure maps exit codes as LOCAL does.
  3. Graph: the producer pipeloom_run is a root task with no edge to the watchers. Watchers follow the plan edges, so a failed unit leaves its descendants upstream_failed. Each watcher has one asset outlet per model, and group_by nests watchers. pipeloom_finalize (trigger rule all_done) runs after the producer and every leaf. The producer's priority_weight is the task count plus 2, with weight_rule="absolute", so it starts first.
  4. Producer command: python -m pipeloom run --log-format json, the project and plan arguments (--manifest in MANIFEST mode, always --expect-plan-hash), the rendered --select and --exclude, --run-id, --run-started-at, --full-refresh, the orchestrator ids, --vars and --workers when set. An empty rendered selection is passed as --select name:*: a run without selectors keeps the selection a non-stable manifest recorded at compile time, while the DAG renders every unit. Exit 0 or 1 is a success (the results belong to the watchers; finalize fails the DAG run when the pipeloom run failed), once runs/<run id>/run_results.json is visible under the resolved root within the grace, else PLA008. Exit 2 or 130 fails the producer.
  5. Artifacts root: resolved at parse time from <project_dir>/pipeloom.yml read as plain YAML, as the core does: targets.<t>.artifacts replaces the top-level block whole, root falls back to target, and a relative root is joined to the execution project dir. An unreadable pipeloom.yml, or a ${...} reference in the root without the override, is PLA008. The project is never bound on the worker for this (it would import user modules and break MANIFEST mode). The triggerer must mount the root at the same path.
  6. Watcher state machine. Inputs are the unit's files and the producer's task state. The producer is in progress while its state is not terminal and the files hold no final verdict. At try 2 or later, when the producer is not in progress, the watcher reruns its unit (same run id, unit mode, one attempt). Otherwise the files decide: the latest attempt succeeded is a success; timed out or cancelled is a failure; failed with no retry left under the unit's policy (should_retry of the core) is a failure. With no final attempt and run_results.json present: a skipped row runs the unit here (its parent was rerun), a cancelled row is a failure, and a terminal row without its attempt file is invisible (PLA004 after the grace). With no results and the producer ended, PLA009 after the grace, which fails the try so a watcher with retries reruns the unit. Else the watcher defers. On success it logs the attempt summary and the tail of the unit's log; on failure the code, message and trace excerpt.
  7. Trigger: PipeloomWatcherTrigger(run_dir, unit_id, retries, retry_on, poll_interval, recheck_after) reads files only, every interval, in a thread. It yields done, run, invisible (after the grace) or, after recheck_after, pending, on which the watcher checks the producer's state on a worker and defers again with the remaining deadline. The trigger never reads task states (a triggerer deadlock fixed in Airflow 3.2.2).
  8. Shared storage: the watcher lists the unit folder and also opens attempt-1 up to attempt-<retries + 1> by name, since an NFS listing can lag behind a file. Partial or invalid JSON is not visible. Waiting is bounded by the grace.
  9. Rerun and finalize: a unit invocation takes no lock and writes no results; pipeloom_finalize, cleared with Downstream, merges the new attempt and overwrites the producer's run_results.json.
  10. Codes: PLA008 (WATCHER artifacts root not resolved) and PLA009 (WATCHER producer ended without run results).
  11. OpenLineage (ADR-0046): the producer's child carries the Airflow ids, so the openlineage sink stays silent by default. Each watcher reports its unit to the Airflow provider through the operator hooks, with the static datasets of the manifest, as KUBERNETES does; a watcher that reruns its unit reports the facets of its own child, as LOCAL does. The producer reports nothing.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One process start per DAG run instead of one per unit, and the core scheduler's parallelism and in-process retries apply. Watchers hold triggerer slots, not worker slots, while they wait.
  • The triggerer needs pipeloom-airflow and the artifacts root mounted at the same path as the workers. On NFS, lookupcache=positive and a low acdirmax keep the grace short.
  • If a producer's worker dies, its child may keep running; PLA009 and a watcher retry can then run a unit twice.
  • A watcher retry after a watch timeout can rerun a unit the producer finished meanwhile.
  • To confirm on a live Airflow: try_number rises after a clear, an upstream_failed task goes back to try 1, and a watcher can defer again from execute_complete.

docs.title: ADR-0049: Artifact schemas, the unit graph and the orchestrator protocol
Context
docs.text:
Principle 3 of the architecture says the artifacts are the contract: an orchestrator, a catalog or a dashboard reads manifest.json, run_results.json, the event stream and the attempt files, and never imports pipeloom. The roadmap's export theme for 1.0 asks to publish that contract. Today only the config files have JSON Schemas (schema/v1/project.json, models.json, defaults.json). The artifacts are described in prose in docs/reference/artifacts.md and pinned by golden tests, and the reference page says a schema "will follow once the field set stops moving". 1.0 is that point.

Two orchestrator plugins exist (Databricks and Airflow), and each one re-derives the same facts from the manifest: which units exist, their parents, their relations and the command line of each unit. Kestra, Argo or GitHub Actions would each need the same code again. ADR-0034 already defines the behavior an orchestrator relies on (run --select unit:<id> --run-id --expect-plan-hash, finalize --unit-states), and ADR-0038 defines retries and the shared artifacts root, but nothing states it as one protocol.

The artifacts come from two kinds of code. Events are pydantic models (pipeloom.events.model): an Event envelope and one EventPayload subclass per event type. The manifest is built from the plan models (PlanNode, PlanSource, PlanMetadata). Run results and unit states are plain dicts: a results row is ROW_DEFAULTS in artifacts/results.py plus the fields a unit fills, and the unit-states reader in runtime/finalize_run.py checks the document by hand.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Schemas from pydantic only. One source, but run results and unit states have no model, and adding models only to describe them would be a second source for the same rows.
  • Schemas written by hand only. Full control of the text, but the event payloads would drift from the classes that emit them.
  • Per artifact: generated where a model exists, written by hand where none does. Chosen. A test ties each hand-written schema to the code that writes the document.
  • Closed objects (additionalProperties: false). A consumer's validator catches every unexpected field, but any field a 1.x release adds breaks every consumer that validates. That would make every addition a new major schema.
  • Open objects. Consumers ignore fields they do not know, so 1.x can add fields. The published schema cannot catch a field pipeloom emits by mistake, so pipeloom's own tests use a closed variant. Chosen.
  • Unit graph in a new command, in compile, or in graph. graph already prints the model graph as text, DOT and JSON; a --units flag on it adds one concept to an existing command instead of a new one.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Five schemas. pipeloom 1.0 publishes a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) per artifact, under the same base URL as the config schemas, https://emanuel-luis.github.io/pipeloom/latest/schema/v1/:

Document Tag Schema manifest.json pipeloom.manifest/1 manifest.json run_results.json and attempt files pipeloom.run_results/1 run_results.json one event (a JSON line, a jsonl file line) pipeloom.event/1 event.json --unit-states / --unit-states-json pipeloom.unit_states/1 unit_states.json graph --units --output json pipeloom.unit_graph/1 unit_graph.json

Every document has a required schema property whose value is its tag (a const in the schema). run_results.json, event.json and unit_states.json were published first; manifest.json was published once the 0.9 config changes had landed, and unit_graph.json came with the command below. All five are part of 1.0.

Generation. pipeloom.artifacts.schema.artifact_schemas() returns the schemas by file name, and the docs build (tools/docs_hooks.py) writes each to schema/v1/<name> with the same formatting as the config schemas. The event schema is the Event envelope plus, for every EventPayload subclass defined in pipeloom.events.model, an if type == <TYPE> then data: <payload> rule; an event type without a rule keeps an open data object. The manifest schema has a hand-written top level and $defs generated from PlanNode, PlanSource and PlanMetadata. The run results and unit states schemas are written by hand; a test asserts that the row properties are exactly the keys of ROW_DEFAULTS. UNIT_STATES_SCHEMA moves to pipeloom.artifacts.schema, and runtime/finalize_run.py keeps re-exporting it. pipeloom schema export still exports only the config schemas.

Attempt files. An attempt file (units/<unit_id>/attempt-<n>.json) is one run_results/1 row and is validated with run_results.json#/$defs/result. It has no tag of its own.

Open objects and the strict variant. The published schemas leave objects open: the generator removes the additionalProperties: false that pydantic emits for extra="forbid". A consumer must ignore fields it does not know. pipeloom's tests validate against a strict variant (close() adds additionalProperties: false to every object schema with properties, except the parts of a conditional), so a field emitted by mistake fails CI. pipeloom's own readers stay strict where they are today, since a newer core reads files an older one wrote.

What stays within /1.

  • A new field is optional and never enters required. It has a default or may be absent.
  • Event types and skip reasons (the row skip_reason and the unit.skipped data.reason) are open strings: a consumer must accept a value it does not know.
  • Every other enumerated value is a closed enum, and a new value is a breaking change that needs /2: status of a results row, of the run, of run.completed and of a unit state; the event level; materialized (manifest); ErrorInfo.category (the row error and the unit.failed and unit.retrying events); unit.cancelled reason; model.input_read kind; model.schema_changed action; run.started boundary; state.watermark_committed source; model.log level.
  • Within manifest/1 the plan hash and node checksum formulas are frozen. A field added to the manifest stays out of the hash and has a default, so an older manifest keeps its hash.
  • Anything a consumer must understand to act correctly needs /2.

The unit graph. pipeloom graph --units prints the execution units, and only with --output json (other outputs exit 2). A new --manifest PATH reads the plan from that file, so the plan hash in the output equals the manifest's; without it graph compiles. Selection works like finalize: a unit is in scope when its persisted node is selected. The output, tagged pipeloom.unit_graph/1, has pipeloom_version, project, target, plan_hash, selectors, the placeholders list and three parts:

  • units, in topological order with ties broken by id. Each has unit_id, unique_id, nodes, materialized, relation, relation_name, assets, parents, tags, the retry settings (retries, retry_delay_s, retry_on, timeout_s) and argv, the command line that runs it.
  • edges, {"from": parent, "to": child}, only among selected units; parents likewise.
  • finalize.argv, the command line that closes the run.

An argv is a list with the placeholders {project_dir}, {manifest} and {run_id}; the unit id, target and plan hash are literal, and the selectors are copied into the finalize command. finalize has no --state, so when a selector uses state: or result: the finalize command instead selects each selected unit with --select unit:<id>, in unit order, or gets --exclude * when no unit is selected. The --plugin specs given to graph are repeated at the end of every argv, since plugins named that way load only from the command line. Assets are pipeloom://{project}/{target}/{relation_name}, percent-encoded like the Airflow plugin's default; intermediates and models without a relation get none. The pydantic models live in pipeloom.artifacts.unit_graph.

The orchestrator protocol. A docs page states what any orchestrator does, all of it behavior that exists today:

  1. Prepare: compile --stable --out manifest.json, then graph --units --output json --manifest manifest.json.
  2. Pick one run id per orchestrator run, matching [A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64} (ADR-0013), and keep it across retries and repairs. Give every invocation the same --run-started-at (or PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT).
  3. Run each unit with its argv, which already carries any --plugin given to graph. Optional: --orchestrator-id, --log-format json, --cancel-grace, --full-refresh. A plan hash mismatch is PLX103; exit 1 with no new attempt file is a setup failure and is not retried.
  4. Exit codes: 0 succeeded; 2 is a usage error and never retried; 130 was cancelled and may be retried; for 1 the orchestrator reads the newest attempt file's error.category and retries when attempts remain and the category is transient or the unit's retry_on is any. The orchestrator owns retries, their delay and the timeout (timeout_s plus the cancel grace plus a margin), and stops a unit with SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace. Unit invocations never retry inside pipeloom (retries=0 in unit mode).
  5. Order: a unit starts only after its parents succeeded, and the same unit never runs twice at once. Unit invocations take no lock.
  6. Storage: every invocation sees one artifacts root, state store and catalog (ADR-0038).
  7. Finalize always runs (ADR-0034), with --unit-states or --unit-states-json for units that left no attempt file. It exits 0, 1 or 130, a failure wins over a cancellation, a rerun is safe (replay), and PLX105 means a full pipeloom run holds the run.

The docs carry one recipe: a GitHub Actions workflow with one job and ordered steps that runs the TPC-H example through this protocol. One job is enough to prove it, because hosted runners share no filesystem and the protocol needs one artifacts root.

Amendments. This ADR amends ADR-0010: the event envelope and the artifacts it lists now have published JSON Schemas, and the compatibility rules above govern changes to them. It amends ADR-0034: the pipeloom.unit_states/1 document it defines is published as unit_states.json, and graph --units gives an orchestrator the per-unit command lines it previously built from the manifest.

Amendment (1.2): required sets are frozen. The required list of a run_results row (and so of an attempt file), of run and of metadata is the explicit 1.0 set (ROW_REQUIRED, RUN_REQUIRED, METADATA_REQUIRED in artifacts/schema.py), not every property. A field added later is optional in the schema, as the manifest config keys already are. The 1.0 schemas and representative 1.0 documents live under tests/frozen/v1.0.0/; CI checks that they validate against the current schemas and that the current goldens validate against the frozen 1.0 schemas. This enforces the stability rule that 1.x output validates against 1.0 schemas and the reverse. No behavior of what pipeloom writes changes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The artifacts become a published contract that tools in any language can validate. Every golden run results document and event, and the output of a real run (events, run_results.json, attempt files), are checked against the strict variant in CI, and the schemas themselves are golden files, so a change to a payload class or to ROW_DEFAULTS shows up as a golden diff in review. Branches that add fields must update the schema in the same change, which is the intent. The published schema cannot catch an extra field; only pipeloom's tests can. A new orchestrator needs a recipe, not a plugin. A future /2 of any document is a breaking change under the stability policy of ADR-0016.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0050: Python-first model authoring
docs.text: Architecture: Section 4, Configuration, with changes in sections 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 12, 13 and 15

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Since 0.1 a model is declared in YAML (ADR-0003): a model file lists the model, its inputs, its config and either a SQL body or a python: module:function pointer, and folder _defaults.yml files and defaults.models cascade settings onto it. A Python model is therefore written twice, once as an entry in YAML and once as a function whose parameters must match that entry (PLK602), and the config sits in a different file from the code it configures.

The maintainer reversed that choice for 0.9, before 1.0 freezes the config:

  • A model is defined in code, with a decorator on a function, as in the author's earlier prototype. YAML keeps what it is good at, as in dbt: the project file holds project and folder defaults, vars, sources and targets, and properties files describe and configure models. Precedence follows dbt: the decorator wins over properties YAML, which wins over folder and project defaults. YAML alone no longer creates a model.
  • Every model is a Python function. There are no sql: models and no .sql files. SQL runs through ctx.sql(query), which runs the query on the target engine against the model's inputs and returns an engine frame.
  • The pivot is the 0.9 headline and is designed first, here. Contracts and the parked test and build work are then adapted to the decorator, followed by OpenLineage, sample data and the Airflow WATCHER mode; 0.9.0 ships with all of it.
  • The decorator, its model spec and the module loader may be adapted from the author's earlier prototype, renamed to pipeloom's modules and conventions.
  • Discovery is hybrid. A benchmark on Windows with polars models (cold: 50, 200 and 1,000 models) measured 1.9, 3.3 and 11.3 s to import every module against 0.07, 0.22 and 1.4 s to parse them with ast; with a per-file cache and one changed file, parsing took 0.05 to 0.22 s and importing 1.2 to 1.5 s. Reading the decorator from the AST keeps compiles fast and runs no user code, but forbids dynamic config; importing allows it. The chosen design parses every file and imports only the modules whose decorator arguments are not static. Dependencies stay declared, never traced, and Airflow keeps the manifest load mode by default.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Keep YAML-first (ADR-0003). Validates without running code, but every Python model is declared twice and SQL models need a second body kind on every engine.
  • Python-first, static discovery only. The compiler reads the decorator with ast and never imports. Fast and safe, but every argument must be a literal: no config computed from a loop, a helper or a constant module.
  • Python-first, import every model module. Any Python value works and the code is simple, but a cold compile of 1,000 models takes over 11 s and every compile runs user code, including in the Airflow DAG processor.
  • Python-first, hybrid discovery. Static where the decorator is static, imported where it is not, with a per-file cache. Fast for the common case, dynamic where needed, at the cost of two code paths that must agree on locations and results.
  • Decorator arguments. Typed objects only (verbose in simple cases), plain dicts only (no completion or type checking), or both.
  • SQL. Keep SQL model files beside Python models, or run SQL only through ctx.sql inside a Python model.
  • Migration. A user-facing pipeloom migrate command and a deprecation release, or a hand-written guide and removal before 0.9.0.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Python-first authoring with hybrid discovery. Every numbered point below is part of the decision.

  1. @model. Keyword-only. Bare @model and @model(...) both work (two overloads). It returns the same function object with a frozen __pipeloom_model__ = ModelSpec(kwargs) that holds only the arguments given, so the function stays callable in a user's own tests; None means not set. Nested config accepts plain dicts with the YAML keys or the pydantic config models re-exported under short names: Write, Incremental, Column, Expectation, Quality, Deletes (pydantic's dataclass_transform gives typed constructors under mypy --strict). Helpers: ref(name), source(group, table), var(name, default=...), and the check helpers not_null(*cols), unique(*cols), accepted_values(col, values), between(col, min=, max=) (the range check), regex(col, pattern), row_count(min=, max=) and freshness(col, max_age), which return a CheckConfig. var(name, default=...) returns a Var marker whose value is resolved at resolve time from the project vars and --vars. A Var is accepted as a top-level @model keyword value and anywhere inside a plain list or dict argument (for example write={"unique_key": var("keys")}); the typed constructors and check helpers reject it when called, with a hint to use the plain mapping form, so they stay strictly typed. An explicit None argument means not set and is dropped from the spec; var() without a default is distinct from default=None. Plain values and mappings are validated at resolve time, with located diagnostics. Typed constructors and helpers validate when called: in a static module the AST resolver evaluates them itself and maps a pydantic error to PLS102 (or the matching PLS code) at the call's line and column; in a dynamic module the error is raised during import and is PLY005 at the innermost frame in that file. Applying @model twice raises.

  2. Discovery (hybrid).

  3. Where models come from. A model_paths entry is a directory (every *.py below it, skipping dot entries, __pycache__ and virtualenvs) or a glob containing *. The new model_packages: [dotted.name] locates each top-level package with importlib.util.find_spec and walks it as files. Python models and properties YAML come from the same scan.
  4. AST resolver. Each file is parsed. It records the top-level imports from pipeloom import model [as m], import pipeloom [as pl] (used as pl.model) and from pipeloom.authoring import ..., and recognises the helpers the same way. A static expression is a literal accepted by ast.literal_eval; a list, tuple, set or dict of static expressions; or a call to a known pipeloom helper or re-exported config class (Write, Incremental, Column, Expectation, Quality, Deletes, also in their pipeloom. and alias-qualified forms) whose positional and keyword arguments are all static. A decorator on a top-level def is static when every argument is static; pipeloom's helpers and classes are then called on the literal values, and no user code runs. Anything else makes the module dynamic. A module is dynamic, and is imported, when any @model argument is not static, when model is used other than as a static decorator on a top-level def (factories, loops, model(...)(fn)), on from pipeloom import *, or when it rebinds a helper name. A file that never imports pipeloom is skipped. Keyword names are always checked from the AST, also in dynamic modules: an unknown keyword is PLS101 with a suggestion, and that module is then not imported.
  5. Import fallback. pipeloom.discovery.loader.ModuleLoader is a context manager grown from today's CallableLoader and adapted from the author's earlier prototype loader. The module name is the file path relative to the longest python_paths root that contains it. It takes a process-wide lock, puts the roots first on sys.path, imports only the dynamic modules and collects the marked functions from vars(module) with their bound global name. A function object seen in several modules is kept where __name__ == fn.__module__, else first in path order. On exit it removes the roots and purges, by path, every module whose __file__ or __path__ lies under them (namespace packages too), except pipeloom, __main__ and __mp_main__, so the case harness can load about a hundred projects in one process without one seeing another's modules.
  6. Load summary. Loading never stops at the first failure. Each module that cannot be loaded is one PLY005: a syntax error, an exception during import, a file outside every python_paths root, or a module name that resolves to a different file. The location is the innermost traceback frame inside that file, or SyntaxError.lineno and offset.
  7. Cache. <project>/.pipeloom/cache/discovery.json (already git-ignored), written to a temporary file and then replaced. The key per file is its POSIX path, mtime_ns, size, the pipeloom version, the Python minor version and the cache schema. For a static file it stores the discovered models as JSON (arguments, parameters, locations), with a var() argument stored as its Var marker, never a value, so changing vars never invalidates the cache; for a dynamic file the dynamic flag and its decorator sites (parse data only), because import results are never cached; for a file without models none. Deleted files are dropped. A schema or version mismatch, or a corrupt cache, means a cold run; a failed write (a read-only file system on Airflow or Databricks) is ignored. The cache is never part of the manifest or the plan hash.
  8. Reload. Discovery.refresh() stats the files again, re-parses changed static files, and purges and re-imports every dynamic module (a changed helper module purges them all). docs serve calls it on each index request and regenerates the site when the snapshot changed.

  9. Seam. Discovery returns DiscoveredModel(name, module, attr, file, line, col, kwargs, kwarg_locations, params, dynamic) records plus a list of failures. A file may hold several models. The default name is the function name; two models with one name are PLR202 at the second decorator.

  10. Parameters become inputs. Each function parameter is bound in this order: (1) an inputs= entry, whose value is ref(...), source(...) or a bare name (a string, resolved by steps 3 and 4); (2) a parameter with a default is never an input unless inputs= lists it; (3) a model with that name, never the model itself; (4) a source table with that name, when exactly one source group has it; (5) otherwise PLR201 with fuzzy suggestions over models and sources. A table name found in two source groups is PLR210. ctx is reserved and optional: it is passed only when the signature has it, and a model named ctx is PLS102. *args, positional-only parameters, and an inputs= key that is not a parameter (unless the function takes **kwargs) are PLK602. A model never reads its own name, so a bronze orders model with an orders parameter binds the source. incremental.input names an input alias exactly as today, so the incremental filter applies to a source input and to a model input alike.

  11. Sources in pipeloom.yml. sources maps a group name to a group with format, location, schema, options, tags, meta and tables, and each table may set location or table, format, options and the other group keys. A table location is joined to the group location; a table table is qualified by the group schema. A table entry whose merged result has no location and no table uses its key as table, qualified by the group schema; one with both is PLS108. targets.<t>.sources.<group> deep-merges over the group, and an explicit null removes a key. The unique id is source.<project>.<group>.<table>. Sources in properties files are rejected for now.

  12. The models: tree in pipeloom.yml. It mirrors the model folders, with config keys prefixed by + as in dbt. Root-level +keys are project defaults and folder keys nest; for a model found through model_packages the folder path is the dotted module path. vars, targets, default_target and the ~/.pipeloom/profiles.yml overrides stay, with no separate profiles file. _defaults.yml, defaults.models and model files with sources: or models: lists are removed (see point 19). python_paths stays, with the default ["."], and every model file must lie under one of its roots (PLY005 otherwise).

  13. Properties YAML. Any *.yml or *.yaml file under model_paths except pipeloom.yml, with any file name. Its shape is a models list whose entries have name, description, config (model settings), columns (the contract), data_tests and unit_tests. An entry never sets inputs. An entry that names no model, or a model that another entry already describes, is PLR209 (error), suppressed while any PLY005 exists. schema export writes project.json and a new properties.json; models.json and defaults.json stop being published under latest/ (older version folders keep them). The modeline is $schema=https://emanuel-luis.github.io/pipeloom/latest/schema/v1/properties.json.

  14. Precedence. Decorator, then properties, then the models: tree from the folder nearest the model up to the root, then the project root +keys, then built-in defaults. The merge rules do not change: mappings deep-merge, lists replace, tags is an ordered union, and an explicit null removes a key (in YAML only). columns is a model key, so the folder tree cannot set it, and decorator columns replace properties columns whole. ResolvedModel.origins maps each top-level key to the layer and Location it came from, and locate_model(m, field) uses it. Origins are not in the manifest.

  15. ctx.sql(query, *, dialect=None, inputs=None). The query sees the model's inputs by alias, as read (after the incremental filter); inputs= adds or replaces frames by name. It returns the native frame, or a Narwhals frame under frame_api: narwhals. The dialect is the dialect argument, then the inheritable setting sql_dialect, then the engine's own. sqlglot transpile runs only when the chosen dialect differs from the engine's, in pipeloom.runtime.sql, imported lazily (one more import-linter ignore entry). Translation needed with sqlglot missing is PLC513 (L5). Translation happens only when a dialect is declared and differs from the engine's, so sqlglot stays an optional extra and no core dependency is added; validation tells the user when a model's SQL will be translated. pandas raises SqlUnsupportedError at run time, reported as PLX101 with a hint, and L6 warns with PLK606 when a function's source contains ctx.sql and the engine has no SQL. EngineCapabilities.sql_dialect: str | None = None joins plugin API (0, 5), which is unreleased, so the version does not change. polars has no sqlglot dialect; it maps to the closest one and tests cover the mapping.

  16. Views. A view model is a function that returns ctx.sql(...). The runner calls it in view mode: input parameters are placeholders, any use of them other than passing them to ctx.sql raises, and ctx.sql returns a ViewQuery, a new internal type, for the unchanged create_view. Input aliases are bound to physical relations as SQL views are today: the runner passes the query with one ReadSpec per alias, and the engine binds each alias to that relation (Spark as a CTE over the table name or path). inputs= frames are rejected in view mode (PLX120), and returning anything other than the ViewQuery is PLX120. PLP409 narrows to "a view cannot inline an ephemeral model". Ephemeral models are unchanged: they are computed inside the consuming unit.

  17. Manifest. The schema stays pipeloom.manifest/1; the change is breaking before 1.0 and the CHANGELOG says so. A node body is PythonBody{kind: "python", callable: "module:attr", file}; node.file is the .py file and node.line the decorator line. SqlBody is removed with the legacy path, after which an old manifest with kind: sql is PLX107. The checksum formula does not change (resolved config, callable, NUL, module file bytes, plus columns without description), so editing any function in a file marks every model of that file modified, which is accepted as conservative. Plan hashes change once. Dynamic config must be deterministic, and PLX103 guards it. meta values must be JSON (PLS102).

  18. Diagnostics. A finding in Python carries the file, the decorator line and column and, for a keyword argument, that argument's own line and column from the AST when the @model(...) call is written directly on the def, in a static or a dynamic module. A model created any other way (factories, loops, model(...)(fn)) is located at the function's file and __code__.co_firstlineno, column 1, with no per-argument location, so a diagnostic on an argument points at the function. The JSON pointer reads /@model/write/unique_key. Pydantic errors map through DecoratorSite.locate(pointer), which has the same interface as LoadedDocument.locate, so from_validation_error is reused. CodeInfo.status gains "retired" with a retired version; the catalog page says "Retired in 0.9: no longer emitted", and a retired code has no case file (test_catalog changes accordingly). Codes:

    Code Layer, severity Title Status PLY005 L0 E Model module cannot be loaded new PLR209 L2 E Properties entry names no model, or describes one twice new PLR210 L2 E Input name matches a table in several source groups new PLC513 L5 E SQL translation needs the sqlglot extra new PLK606 L6 W ctx.sql on an engine without SQL new PLX120 Runtime E View model did not return ctx.sql(...), or passed it inputs= new PLK602 L6 E Parameters do not match inputs reused, same meaning PLK603, PLK605 L6 W Applied to literal ctx.sql queries reused PLP409 L4 E A view cannot inline an ephemeral model narrowed PLR201, PLR202, PLR203, PLS101, PLS102, PLS108, PLG302 Also located in Python reused PLK601, PLK604, PLC502 retired in 0.9

    PLM209, PLX116, PLX119, PLC511, PLC512, PLA008 and PLA009 stay free for other 0.9 items, and PLR208, PLX114, PLX115, PLP415 and PLQ303 for the test and build work.

  19. Layers. L0: YAML codes and PLY005. L1: pydantic over YAML and decorator arguments. L2: references through parameters, PLR209 and PLR210. L3: unchanged. L4: unchanged, with PLP409 narrowed. L5: PLC502 retired, PLC513 added. L6: static checks on the function source: PLK602 (signature against inputs=, emitted while binding), PLK603 and PLK605 on literal ctx.sql strings, and PLK606.

  20. Runtime. Executors and tasks do not change. They read metadata.python_paths and the node's callable from the manifest, and ModuleLoader.load("module:attr") imports that one module. An executor running a unit from a manifest never runs discovery. Any invocation that compiles runs it, including pipeloom run without --manifest and Airflow PROJECT mode, whose unit tasks each compile, so dynamic modules are imported there too. The function is called by keyword: the input aliases, plus ctx when it is a parameter. ModelContext keeps its fields and gains sql(), backed by a private callable that the runner sets.

  21. Contracts. columns comes from the decorator (Column(...)) or from properties. ColumnConfig.description is optional and stays out of the node checksum and the plan hash: columns is hashed without description. Where descriptions appear in the manifest and on the docs site is settled later in 0.9, outside the plan hash. ADR-0044 gets an amendment for the sources of columns, their precedence and description; PLP414 does not change.

  22. Test and build shape (for the later ADR-0045). data_tests (the parked DataTestConfig, whose check is a DataCheckConfig with not_null, unique or relationships, not a CheckConfig, so the expectation check helpers do not apply there) is a model key that the decorator (a keyword added by the ADR-0045 change) and properties can set, and a list that replaces. unit_tests live only in properties, with given keyed by input alias (the parameter name) and expect. Plain pytest calls on the function also work.

  23. init and new model (ADR-0041 amendment). pipeloom new model NAME [--sql|--python] [--folder] writes models/<folder>/<name>.py. With --sql the body returns ctx.sql("select 1 as id"), with --python a frame stub; the default is --python on pandas and --sql otherwise. The usage error for a missing python_paths goes away. init writes one .py per layer, the models: tree instead of _defaults.yml, models/silver/_properties.yml, and a .vscode/settings.json that maps properties.json to models/**/*.yml.

  24. Airflow and Databricks. MANIFEST stays the default Airflow load mode and imports nothing at parse or run time except the one module of the unit being run. PROJECT imports only the dynamic modules, inside the DAG processor and again in every unit task, which compiles (point 13), and its cache key adds the model_packages directories (ADR-0037 amendment). The Databricks upload set is pipeloom.yml, the nodes' .py files and every *.py under python_paths, plus the manifest; properties YAML is uploaded too, for parity. Modules from model_packages must be installed in the job environment, and the docs say so (ADR-0035 amendment).

  25. Docs. A migration section in the CHANGELOG under 0.9.0 and a new guide, docs/guide/migrate-0.9.md, both written with the removal of the legacy path.

  26. Transition. The legacy YAML models: path and the new path coexist on main, with no warning code, until the change that removes the legacy path; one project may mix both. That change lands before 0.9.0, and 0.9.0 ships Python-first only.

Migration and scope decisions.

  • There is no user-facing pipeloom migrate command. The migration guide shows the mapping from YAML to the decorator by hand. The repository's own fixtures, cases and examples were migrated by an internal converter, described in the amendment below.
  • Amendment (migration work): the converter becomes a test support utility, tests/legacy_models.py, kept after the legacy path is removed. The shared test project builders use it to turn compact YAML-style models written by tests into Python-first projects on write; it stays out of the package, so there is still no user-facing pipeloom migrate.
  • 0.9.0 drops YAML models with no deprecation release. Removal before 1.0 is allowed by pre-1.0 SemVer and by ADR-0016.
  • ctx.sql translates only when a dialect is declared (dialect= or sql_dialect) and differs from the engine's (point 8).
  • ADR-0019 does not change; its YAML dialect now covers the project file and properties files only.

Rejected.

  • Keeping YAML-first: the double declaration of Python models is the problem this ADR solves.
  • Static-only discovery: forbids any computed config, which the maintainer wants to allow.
  • Importing every module: over 11 s for 1,000 models cold, and user code on every compile.
  • Typed objects only, or dicts only, for decorator arguments: the first is verbose for simple cases, the second has no completion. Both are accepted.
  • SQL model files beside Python models: two body kinds on every engine for no gain over ctx.sql.
  • A module-level registry of decorated functions: the decorator only marks the function, and discovery collects marked functions into the project being compiled (principle 3).
  • sqlglot as a core dependency, or translating every query: translation runs only when a declared dialect differs from the engine's.
  • A user-facing pipeloom migrate command and a deprecation release (see above).

Example. The stub of the decorator:

F = TypeVar("F", bound=Callable[..., Any])

@overload
def model(fn: F, /) -> F: ...
@overload
def model(*, name: str | None = None, description: str | None = None,
          inputs: Mapping[str, str | Ref | SourceRef] | None = None,
          materialized: Literal["table", "incremental", "view", "ephemeral", "intermediate"] | None = None,
          incremental: Incremental | Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
          write: Write | Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
          partition_by: Sequence[str] | None = None, cluster_by: Sequence[str] | None = None,
          columns: Sequence[Column | Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None,
          expectations: Sequence[Expectation | Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None,
          quality: Quality | Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
          tags: Sequence[str] | None = None, retries: int | None = None,
          retry_delay: str | float | None = None, retry_on: Literal["transient", "any"] | None = None,
          timeout: str | float | None = None, frame_api: Literal["native", "narwhals"] | None = None,
          sql_dialect: str | None = None, schema: str | None = None, catalog: str | None = None,
          meta: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> Callable[[F], F]: ...
# ADR-0045 adds: data_tests: Sequence[DataTest | Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None

models/silver/orders_enriched.py:

import polars as pl
from pipeloom import Column, Expectation, ModelContext, Write, model, not_null, source

@model(
    materialized="incremental",
    inputs={"customer": source("tpch", "customer")},
    incremental={"input": "orders", "column": "o_orderdate", "lookback": "3d"},
    write=Write(strategy="merge", unique_key=["order_key"]),
    columns=[
        Column(name="order_key", dtype="int64", nullable=False),
        Column(name="customer_name", dtype="string"),
        Column(name="order_date", dtype="date"),
        Column(name="total_price", dtype="decimal(15,2)"),
    ],
    expectations=[Expectation(name="keys", check=not_null("order_key"), on_violation="fail")],
)
def orders_enriched(ctx: ModelContext, orders: pl.LazyFrame, customer: pl.LazyFrame) -> pl.LazyFrame:
    return ctx.sql("""
        select o.o_orderkey as order_key, c.c_name as customer_name,
               o.o_orderdate as order_date, o.o_totalprice as total_price
        from orders o join customer c on o.o_custkey = c.c_custkey
    """)

orders binds to the source table tpch.orders by parameter name (point 3, step 4) and customer through inputs=. orders is both a source input and the incremental input, and the incremental filter applies to it as it does today. Every argument is static, so this file is resolved without being imported.

pipeloom.yml:

models/silver/_properties.yml:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://emanuel-luis.github.io/pipeloom/latest/schema/v1/properties.json
models:
  - name: orders_enriched
    description: One row per order with its customer name.
    config:
      retries: 2
    data_tests:
      - name: order_key_unique
        check:
          unique: [order_key]
        on_violation: fail
    unit_tests:

        given:
          orders:
            rows:
              - o_orderkey: 1
                o_custkey: 7
                o_orderdate: 2024-01-02
                o_totalprice: 10.5
          customer:
            rows:
              - c_custkey: 7
                c_name: Ana
        expect:
          rows:
            - order_key: 1
              customer_name: Ana

              total_price: 10.5

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A model is written once, in one file, with completion and type checking from the decorator's signature. SQL users write a one-line function around ctx.sql.
  • Most projects compile without running user code: only modules with dynamic decorator arguments are imported, and the per-file cache keeps warm compiles fast. Where a module is imported, compiling runs user code, in Airflow PROJECT mode and in docs generate in CI among other places, so the non-goal becomes "user code runs at compile time only for modules with dynamic decorator arguments". Airflow's default MANIFEST mode still imports nothing.
  • The engine contract shrinks: SQL model bodies are gone, and engines declare a sql_dialect instead.
  • Every existing project must be rewritten before it runs on 0.9.0, every manifest and plan hash changes once, and models.json and defaults.json stop being published. The migration guide covers the mapping.
  • Two discovery paths (AST and import) must produce the same DiscoveredModel records and the same locations; the case harness covers both for every Python-located code.
  • Editing any function in a module marks every model of that module modified under state:modified.
  • ADR-0003 is superseded. ADR-0035, 0037, 0040, 0041, 0042, 0044 and 0047 carry amendments for this change.

Risks:

  • polars has no sqlglot dialect, so translation to polars maps to the closest dialect and may differ on edge cases; tests cover the mapping.
  • The cache misses an edit that keeps both mtime and size; a cold run fixes it.
  • Non-deterministic dynamic config trips PLX103 and can go stale in the Airflow PROJECT compile cache.
  • A model folder named like an installed package is shadowed by it; PLY005 must say why.
  • Importing a dynamic module at compile time runs user code (Airflow PROJECT mode, docs generate in CI). In PROJECT mode every unit task compiles, so dynamic modules are also imported on workers.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Supersedes ADR-0003.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: pipeloom 1.1 adds pipeloom-duckdb, an in-tree engine distribution released in lockstep with the others. DuckDB runs SQL in process, reads Parquet and CSV natively and Delta through its delta extension, and since 1.4 supports MERGE INTO (announcement). The engine needs a place for its tables, a mapping of pipeloom relations onto it, an extension policy that works offline in CI, and a state store. The plugin API stays at (1, 0) in 1.1. Every design input here comes from the public DuckDB documentation.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• A DuckDB database file as the catalog. Tables and views are DuckDB objects; writes are SQL inside DuckDB transactions, so a write and its idempotency token commit together. Only one process may open a file for writing.
  • An attached lakehouse (Delta or Iceberg files). Tables readable by other engines, but DuckDB writes neither format with transactions across files, and merge or scd2 would leave DuckDB.
  • The filesystem catalog, as polars uses. Reuses fs_write, but every strategy runs in Python over frames instead of pushing down to SQL.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Target. The duckdb catalog holds tables in one DuckDB database file (path, default target/pipeloom.duckdb, relative to the project), or :memory: for tests. The engine works only with this catalog; any other catalog is rejected when the session opens.
  2. Relations. A target without a catalog is "<database>"."<schema>"."<name>" in that file. A target catalog <name> (+catalog in the models: tree) is the database file <name>.duckdb next to path, attached as <name> on first use and created by ensure_namespace; with :memory: it is an in-memory database. Existing sibling files are attached when a session opens, so a view that reads another catalog binds. Schemas are DuckDB schemas, created by ensure_namespace.
