  3. Sessions. A session opens one connection with TimeZone=UTC. The unit threads share it under a lock: DuckDB parallelizes each query, and a connection must not run two statements at once. Process boundaries (boundary: task) open the file from several processes and DuckDB refuses a second writer, so they are not supported.
  4. Sources. parquet and csv read through read_parquet and read_csv, with the source options passed as named parameters; a directory reads every file of that format in it. delta is read only, through delta_scan. A missing source fails at read (PLM204).
  5. Extensions. autoinstall_known_extensions is always off. Extensions load from the engine's extension_directory (pinned in the project). extensions lists the ones to load at session open; delta loads on the first Delta read. When an extension is missing and install_extensions is off (the default), the engine raises an error that carries PLX121; the read, write or model that needed it fails with that text in its message (PLM204, PLM201 or PLX101), permanent. The plugin API has no channel for plugin codes in 1.x, so the code travels in the message. A session still opens: a listed missing extension fails the first data operation, not the run start. With install_extensions: true, the engine installs from the network into that directory.
  6. Writes. The batch is staged in a temporary table first, outside any transaction, so a failing relation never touches the target and a model can read its own table. Then one transaction runs the strategy and inserts the token into <database>._pipeloom.commits: overwrite is CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, append an INSERT ... BY NAME, replace_partitions a DELETE of every partition in the batch (null is a partition value) then an insert, merge one MERGE INTO (hard deletes as WHEN MATCHED ... THEN DELETE, update_condition in DuckDB SQL over source and target), and scd2 a MERGE INTO that closes changed or deleted current rows at the run start, then an insert of the new versions (hard deletes only; NaN compares as null). Counts come from a query over the staged batch and the target before the change. A repeated token returns the stored result and writes nothing. A schema change the core allowed rebuilds the table with CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT from itself, so column order follows the decided schema.
  7. Capabilities. Formats parquet, csv, delta; strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions, scd2; materializations table, view, ephemeral, incremental, intermediate; SQL models and views; idempotent writes; cancel (through the connection's interrupt); portable (Narwhals accepts DuckDB relations); quality; sql_dialect="duckdb"; no bytes metrics. Views are DuckDB views over CTEs of their inputs. Intermediates are one Parquet file per model under the run's artifacts, with a token file.
  8. State. The engine pairs with the core sqlite or json state stores. There is no DuckDB state store.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Merge, scd2 and replace_partitions run where the data is, in one transaction with the token.
  • Tables are DuckDB-only: another engine reads them by attaching the file, not as open table formats. Writing Delta or Iceberg from DuckDB is out of scope, as are remote databases (MotherDuck, attached Postgres) and a DuckDB state store.
  • One writer process per database file; units run on threads.
  • CI preinstalls delta into a directory and runs the plugin tests without network on Linux; macOS and Windows run the same Delta read test with installs off. Revisit PLX121 as a first-class diagnostic when a plugin API minor adds a way for engines to raise coded errors.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Three places built dataset names on their own: the unit graph (assets), the Airflow plugin (asset URI template) and the OpenLineage sink (namespace and name, with its own path parsing). The 1.4 Dagster plugin needs the same names for its asset keys. Two copies of a naming rule drift, and a drift renames a dataset in a user's lineage graph.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Keep one copy per integration. No change, but each new integration adds a copy.
  • One pure function in the core. Every integration calls it. The core stays free of plugin imports.
  • Rename datasets to a new scheme. Cleaner names, but it breaks every lineage graph and Airflow asset dependency built on 1.0.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The rule moves to pipeloom.plan.identity and every integration calls it. The module is pure: no disk, no engine, no plugin.

  • asset_uri(template, ...) fills the Airflow URI template, percent-encoding each value. The unit graph uses it with the default template through default_asset_uri.
  • relation_name, relation_dataset, source_dataset and location_dataset give the OpenLineage namespace and name of a model relation or a source.
  • unit_inputs, input_assets and output_assets name what a unit reads and writes. Ephemeral models are inlined in the unit, so an ephemeral input resolves to the persisted models and sources behind it.

Names stay byte-identical to 1.0.0. A hash suffix applies only to a name 1.0 produced but the consumer rejects. The only such case is an asset URI above 1500 characters, which Airflow refuses: it is cut to 1491 characters and ends in _ and 8 hex of the sha256 of the full URI. No other 1.0 name changes, and 1.0 rejected no OpenLineage name.

The unit graph gains no input_assets or output_assets fields in this release. Its assets already lists the output URIs, and the Python functions serve the Dagster plugin. Adding the fields later is additive.

A golden computed from the 1.0.0 code (tests/goldens/identity/dataset-names-1.0.json) covers the shop fixture and the TPC-H polars, pandas and Spark examples: Airflow asset URIs with the default and an all-placeholder template, unit graph assets, and OpenLineage inputs and outputs with and without a dataset namespace.

Provenance: designed from the OpenLineage naming spec and the Airflow asset documentation, and from the behavior of pipeloom 1.0.0. No code from other projects was used.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: One edit changes a dataset name everywhere. The golden makes that edit visible in review. Within 1.x the module only grows. Airflow naming.asset_uri is gone from the plugin; it was internal.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0067: Conformance kit as an opt-in pytest plugin
docs.text: Architecture: Section 3, Architecture overview

docs.title: Context
docs.text: pipeloom.testing ships the engine and state store contract suites, and the in-tree plugins subclass them in their own tests. A third-party engine author could do the same, but nothing named the supported entry point, nothing printed which version of the suite ran, and the capability declarations were only visible in code. The 1.1 roadmap asks for a kit that an outside project can run in CI.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• A separate distribution (pipeloom-conformance). Keeps pytest out of the core, but pytest is already imported by pipeloom.testing.contract, which nothing outside tests imports, and a second distribution has to be released and kept in lockstep.
  • A pytest11 entry point in the core. No flag, but the plugin would load in every pytest run of every user that has pipeloom installed.
  • An opt-in plugin module in the core, loaded with -p.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• pipeloom.testing.pytest_plugin is a pytest plugin loaded only with -p. pipeloom declares no pytest11 entry point and does not depend on pytest: the module is imported only by a project that already runs pytest. It sits inside pipeloom.testing, which the import-linter contracts already isolate, so no layer or isolation rule changes.
  • --pipeloom-harness MODULE:CALLABLE names a function that takes a tmp_path and returns an EngineHarness, the value the in-tree engine_factory fixtures already return. When it is given, the plugin replaces the collection arguments with pipeloom.testing.kit, which binds EngineContract to that function. A bad value is a pytest usage error.
  • KIT_VERSION (pipeloom.testing.contract) is printed in the report header with the pipeloom version. Within pipeloom 1.x the kit changes only additively: a minor kit version may add cells (for a new capability or for behavior the docs already describe) and new optional EngineHarness fields. A required EngineHarness field, a removed cell or a cell that changes meaning needs a pipeloom major, and with it a kit major.
  • Subclassing EngineContract and StateStoreContract stays supported unchanged. The plugin and the classes are on the stability list.
  • The capability matrix is generated at docs-build time by tools/docs_hooks.py from the specs of the built-ins and the installed entry points. The core gains no code for it and imports no plugin.
  • CI builds the wheels, installs only pipeloom and pipeloom-polars in a fresh venv and runs the kit from a directory outside the repository.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An engine author needs a harness function and pytest, and nothing else from this repository.
  • Adding cells to the contract is a kit minor and can turn a green third-party build red, which is why the version is in the header and the stability page says to pin it.
  • Only the engine suite has a plugin option. A state store option can follow the same shape.

docs.title: Alerts with the webhook sink
docs.text: The built-in webhook sink posts selected events as JSON to a URL, which is enough for a Slack or Teams incoming webhook or a pager. By default it posts once when a run fails. It uses the Python standard library for HTTP and adds no dependency. Decided in ADR-0047.

docs.title: Configure it
docs.text:
events:
  sinks:
    - kind: webhook
      secret_url: ${secret:env/PIPELOOM_ALERT_URL}
      buffered: true

The URL carries its own credentials, so it is a secret: give it as ${secret:provider/path} (here the env provider reads the variable PIPELOOM_ALERT_URL). A literal URL is rejected with PLS104. pipeloom never prints or logs the URL, and an error names only the HTTP status or the exception type. Only http and https URLs are accepted.

Keep buffered: true: the posts then run on a background thread, so a slow endpoint never holds up the run.

Option Default Meaning secret_url required the webhook URL, as a secret reference events [run.completed] event types to post statuses [failed] a run.completed event is posted only with one of these statuses (succeeded, failed, cancelled) min_level none also post every event at or above warning or error; off by default, so a failed run posts exactly once timeout 10 seconds to wait for each post, as 10 or 30s max_failures 3 failed posts in a row before the sink stops posting

failure_budget, buffered and buffer_size work as for every sink.

docs.title: What it sends
docs.text:
One POST per selected event, with Content-Type: application/json:

{
  "text": "pipeloom run 20261106T101500Z-1a2b failed: fct_orders PLM201",
  "event": {"schema": "pipeloom.event/1", "type": "run.completed", "...": "..."}
}

text is a one-line summary that Slack and Teams render as the message. event is the whole event envelope, with secrets masked, for anything that wants more. Any 2xx answer counts as delivered.

docs.title: When the endpoint is down
docs.text:
A failed post is a sink failure. After max_failures failed posts in a row, the sink stops posting for the rest of the invocation, and the bus disables it and reports one sink.disabled warning (PLE401). The run itself is never affected.

An orchestrator that retries pipeloom finalize for a failed run does not cause a second post: the retry's run.completed carries replay: true, and the sink skips it.

Commands that do not run anything (validate, compile) build the sink without resolving secrets, and then it posts nothing.

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
pipeloom docs generate renders your project as one HTML file. It shows the lineage graph, every model and source, and the result of the last run. The file has no external resources, so you can open it from disk, attach it to a ticket or host it on any static server. The site is read only: it never starts, schedules or changes a run.

$ pipeloom docs generate
target/docs/index.html
$ pipeloom docs serve
serving target/docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/

docs.title: What the page shows
docs.text:
• The header: project, target, pipeloom version and a short plan hash. With results, also the last run's id, status, end time and counts.
  • The graph, drawn left to right. Sources and models are boxes; ephemeral models have a dashed border. A box is colored by the model's last status (succeeded, failed, skipped, cancelled, timed out, or none). Click a box to jump to its section. The +, - and 100% buttons zoom the graph.
  • A table of models: name, path, materialization, write strategy, relation, tags, last status, rows written and duration. The filter box above it narrows the rows as you type.
  • One section per model: relation, materialization, strategy, tags, inputs (each linked to the model or source it reads), parents and children, expectations, the contract columns when declared, the resolved config as JSON, and the body (the SQL text, or the Python callable and its file). With results it adds status, rows, bytes, duration, attempt and, for a failure, the error code and message with the pipeloom explain CODE command that describes it.
  • One section per source.

The zoom buttons and the filter box need JavaScript. With JavaScript off, everything else still works.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text:
pipeloom docs generate compiles the project the way pipeloom compile does, so it takes --project-dir, --target, --vars, --plugin and --log-format. Diagnostics go to stderr, and any error exits 1. It prints the path of the file it wrote on stdout.

Flag Meaning --out DIR Output folder, relative to the project dir unless absolute. Default target/docs. The folder gets one file, index.html. --manifest PATH Render this manifest instead of compiling. A manifest that cannot be read is PLX107 and exit 1. --run-results PATH Show this run_results.json. The file must exist.

Without --run-results, the page uses the run_results.json at the root of the target's artifacts root (target/run_results.json by default), if it exists. With --manifest and no --run-results, the page has no results. A results file that is not a pipeloom.run_results/1 document, or that belongs to another project, is a usage error (exit 2) that names the file.

When the results come from a different plan than the one shown, the page still matches rows to models by id and adds a note that the plan changed since that run.

The output depends only on its inputs and holds no wall-clock time, so the same manifest and results give the same bytes.

docs.title: Serve
docs.text:
pipeloom docs serve serves the folder with the Python standard library. It never opens a browser.

Flag Meaning --project-dir DIR Directory that holds pipeloom.yml. --target, --vars, --plugin As in docs generate; the rebuild compiles with them. --dir DIR Folder to serve, relative to the project dir unless absolute. Default target/docs. --host HOST Address to listen on. Default 127.0.0.1. --port N Port. Default 8000; 0 picks a free one.

When a model module, a properties file or pipeloom.yml changes, the next request for the page compiles the project again and rewrites index.html. If the project does not resolve when the command starts, it prints one line on stderr and serves the page as it is. If index.html is missing, the command exits 2 and asks you to run pipeloom docs generate first. Press Ctrl+C to stop it; it exits 0.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The graph is a static drawing, not an interactive one. Pan and zoom are the scroll area and the buttons. An interactive viewer over the artifacts root is planned as pipeloom ui, in its own distribution.

docs.title: Incremental models
docs.text:
An incremental model processes only the input rows that are new since its last run. pipeloom keeps a watermark, the largest value of one input column seen so far, and filters the input with it. The watermark is saved after the write succeeds, so a failed run never skips rows.

An incremental run: the watermark is committed only after the write. Source: incremental.d2.

docs.title: A first incremental model
docs.text:
Project pipeloom.yml:

config_version: 1
name: shop
targets:
  dev:
    engine:
      kind: polars
    catalog:
      kind: filesystem
      root: target/warehouse
    state:
      kind: json
      path: .pipeloom/state
sources:
  raw:
    format: csv
    location: raw
    options:
      try_parse_dates: true   # read updated_at as a timestamp, not text
    tables:
      raw_orders:
        location: orders.csv

raw/orders.csv:

id,customer_id,amount,status,updated_at
1,10,5.0,paid,2026-01-01T10:00:00
2,10,2.5,new,2026-01-01T11:00:00
3,11,7.0,paid,2026-01-02T09:00:00

models/orders.py:

from pipeloom import model


@model(
    materialized="incremental",
    incremental={"input": "raw_orders", "column": "updated_at", "lookback": "2h"},
    write={"strategy": "merge", "unique_key": ["id"]},
)
def orders(ctx, raw_orders):
    return ctx.sql("select id, customer_id, amount, status, updated_at from raw_orders")

The incremental block names the input to filter (it must be one of the model's inputs), the column that moves forward, an optional lookback and where the watermark lives. Run it twice, adding rows to the CSV in between:

$ pipeloom run
... state.watermark_committed {'column': 'updated_at', 'dtype': 'timestamp[us]', 'before': None, 'after': '2026-01-02T09:00:00', ...}
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ incremental/merge   3 rows
$ printf '4,12,9.0,new,2026-01-03T09:00:00\n' >> raw/orders.csv
$ pipeloom run
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ incremental/merge   2 rows

The second run read only rows at or after 2026-01-02T07:00:00 (the watermark minus two hours), so it wrote 2 rows: the new order 4 and a re-merge of order 3 that falls inside the window.

docs.title: How a unit decides what to read
docs.text:
A unit runs incrementally when the materialization is incremental, the target table exists, the run is not a --full-refresh and a watermark is known. Otherwise it reads the whole input and writes the full result (the first build, or a rebuild).

  • Strict bound. With no lookback the filter is column > watermark. A row equal to the watermark is not read again.
  • Lookback. With lookback above zero the filter is column >= watermark - lookback. The value takes a duration (2h, 1d, or seconds). On a date column it is rounded up to whole days. Use it for data that arrives late. A lookback needs a timestamp or date column; on any other type the unit fails with PLM205.
  • Types. The column's type family (timestamp with a zone, timestamp without one, date, integer, decimal, float, string) must match the stored watermark, or the unit fails with PLM205. A column missing from the input is PLM205 too.
  • New watermark. After a successful write the watermark becomes the larger of the old one and the largest value in the batch. It never moves back, even when the lookback window returns older rows than the watermark.

A Python model sees the decision on its context:

def build(ctx, raw_orders):
    if ctx.is_incremental:
        ctx.log("incremental run", watermark=str(ctx.watermark), lower_bound=str(ctx.lower_bound))
    return raw_orders

ctx.is_incremental is true only on an incremental run. ctx.watermark and ctx.lower_bound are None otherwise. The input it receives is already filtered.

docs.title: Where the watermark lives
docs.text:
watermark_source has two values.

Value Behavior state (default) The watermark is stored in the state store under the project, target and model. If it is missing but the target table exists, pipeloom reads the maximum of the column from the target, uses it and records watermark_seeded: target in the unit's warnings. target The watermark is the maximum of the column in the target table, read on every run. The state store is never written.

Use target when the table itself is the truth, for example after restoring it from a backup, and you do not want a state store entry to disagree with it.

docs.title: Appending with a lookback
docs.text: With strategy: append and a lookback above zero, rows inside the window are written again on every run. pipeloom validate warns with PLP410. Use merge with a unique_key instead (see Merge, replace_partitions and schema changes). The default strategy of an incremental model that sets none is append.

docs.title: Full refresh and the first build
docs.text: pipeloom run --full-refresh ignores the watermark, reads the whole input and writes the table as an overwrite, whatever the strategy. The new watermark is the batch maximum. The first build (the target does not exist) also reads everything, and it keeps the declared strategy: into an absent table every strategy writes the same rows, and merge still checks its key.

docs.title: Retries, reruns and the watermark
docs.text:
The write stores the watermark it intends to commit, together with its idempotency token. If a run dies after the write and before the watermark is saved, rerunning with the same --run-id finds the token, skips the read, the body and the write, and commits that stored watermark. New rows that arrived in between are not skipped, because the retry never looked at them.

If the stored watermark changed while the unit ran, which usually means a second run on the same target, the unit fails with PLM203. The data is already written. Do not use --no-lock to run two runs of one target at once.

docs.title: What the run records
docs.text:
• Event state.watermark_committed with the column, type, before and after values, the source and whether the value was seeded.
  • In run_results.json: is_incremental, watermark_before and watermark_after, plus rows_inserted, rows_updated and rows_deleted for merge. See Run artifacts.
  • Engines that can run incremental models: polars and pandas (and the in-memory test engine).

docs.title: Migrating from 0.8 to 0.9
docs.text: In 0.9 every model is a Python function marked with @model. YAML is still where the project lives (pipeloom.yml) and where you describe models (properties files), but a YAML file no longer declares a model. There is no deprecation release and no pipeloom migrate command: you rewrite each model once, by hand, with the mapping below. The decision is ADR-0050.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
0.8 0.9 A model entry with sql: in a model file A function that returns ctx.sql(...) A model entry with python: module:function The same function, decorated with @model inputs: on the model entry The function's parameters, bound by name, or inputs= Model settings on the model entry @model(...) keywords, or config: in a properties entry description: and columns: on the model entry @model(...) keywords, or a properties entry A flat sources: list in a model file Source groups under sources: in pipeloom.yml _defaults.yml in a folder +key settings for that folder in the models: tree defaults.models in pipeloom.yml Root +key settings of the models: tree models.json and defaults.json schemas properties.json (and project.json, unchanged) A manifest body with kind: sql Every body is kind: python; recompile old manifests

What fails, and how:

  • A properties entry with sql, python or inputs, a sources: list in a properties file and a defaults: block in pipeloom.yml are PLS101 (unknown field), with a hint to this page.
  • A model setting left at the top of a properties entry (materialized, tags, retries and the like) is PLS101 too. A properties entry takes only name, description, config, columns, data_tests and unit_tests, so the setting moves under config:.
  • A _defaults.yml file is now read as a properties file, so its models: mapping is PLS102.
  • A manifest written by 0.8 does not load (PLX107). Compile it again with 0.9.
  • PLK601, PLK604, PLC502 and PLR205 are retired: the checks they made have no subject left.

Plan hashes and node checksums change once, so the first state:modified selection after the upgrade selects every model.

docs.title: Keyword mapping
docs.text:
Every key a YAML model entry accepted is a keyword of @model, with the same name and the same values. Nested settings take a plain dict with the YAML keys, or the typed classes Write, Incremental, Column, Expectation, Quality and Deletes.

YAML key on the model entry @model keyword name name= (defaults to the function name) description description= materialized materialized= inputs: {alias: {ref: m}} a parameter named alias bound to model m: inputs={"alias": ref("m")}, or just a parameter named m inputs: {alias: {source: s}} inputs={"alias": source("group", "table")}, or a parameter named like the table incremental incremental=Incremental(...) or a dict write write=Write(...) or a dict partition_by, cluster_by, tags the same keyword, a list columns columns=[Column(...), ...] or a list of dicts expectations expectations=[Expectation(...), ...]; checks with not_null, unique, accepted_values, between, regex, row_count, freshness quality quality=Quality(...) or a dict retries, retry_delay, retry_on, timeout the same keyword frame_api, sql_dialect, schema, catalog, meta the same keyword ${var:name} in a setting var("name", default=...)

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Move flat sources into source groups in pipeloom.yml (see below). The unique id of a source becomes source.<project>.<group>.<table>.
  2. Replace each _defaults.yml and defaults.models with +key settings in the models: tree.
  3. For each model entry, write a function in a .py file under model_paths and move its settings to @model(...). A python: model keeps its function; add the decorator where it is defined and make sure the file lies under model_paths and a python_paths root.
  4. Keep description, columns and other documentation in a properties file if you prefer YAML for them, as a models: list of entries without sql, python or inputs. Settings such as materialized or tags go under config: in the entry; at the top of an entry they are PLS101.
  5. Update the schema modelines: properties files use properties.json; drop models.json and defaults.json.
  6. Run pipeloom validate, then pipeloom compile to write a new manifest.

docs.title: SQL models
docs.text:
A SQL model becomes a function that returns ctx.sql(...). The query reads the inputs by their parameter names.

Before, in models/silver/silver.yml:

models:
  - name: orders_clean
    sql: select * from orders where o_totalprice > 0
    inputs:
      orders:
        source: raw_orders
    tags: [silver]

After, in models/silver/orders_clean.py:

from pipeloom import ModelContext, model, source


@model(inputs={"orders": source("tpch", "orders")}, tags=["silver"])
def orders_clean(ctx: ModelContext, orders):
    return ctx.sql("select * from orders where o_totalprice > 0")

When the parameter has the name of a model, or of a table in exactly one source group, it binds without inputs=: def orders_clean(ctx, orders) reads the source table orders on its own. ctx is optional; take it only when the function needs ctx.sql or the run context.

The query is written in the engine's dialect. Set sql_dialect (a keyword, or +sql_dialect in the tree) to write it in another dialect; pipeloom translates it with sqlglot, which is the pipeloom[sqlglot] extra. pandas has no SQL: write those models with frames.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a function that returns ctx.sql(...) with materialized="view". The runner calls it in view mode and stores the query, so the function may not use its input frames for anything other than passing them to ctx.sql, and ctx.sql may not take inputs= (PLX120).

@model(materialized="view")
def active_customers(ctx, customers):
    return ctx.sql("select * from customers where active")

docs.title: Python models
docs.text:
Before:

models:
  - name: enriched
    python: shop_models:enriched
    inputs:
      orders:
        ref: orders_clean
    retries: 2

After, in the same module:

from pipeloom import model


@model(retries=2)
def enriched(orders_clean):
    ...

The parameter orders_clean binds to the model of that name. To keep the old alias, write inputs={"orders": ref("orders_clean")} and name the parameter orders. Inputs are passed by keyword, so *args and positional-only parameters are PLK602.

docs.title: Properties and the models: tree
docs.text:
Settings resolve, highest first: the decorator, the model's properties entry (its config), the models: tree from the model's folder up to the root, the root +keys, the built-in defaults.

Before, models/silver/_defaults.yml and pipeloom.yml:

models:
  schema: silver
  tags: [silver]

defaults:
  models:
    materialized: table

After, in pipeloom.yml:

models:
  +materialized: table
  silver:
    +schema: silver
    +tags: [silver]

A properties file is any *.yml or *.yaml under model_paths:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://emanuel-luis.github.io/pipeloom/latest/schema/v1/properties.json
models:
  - name: orders_clean
    description: Orders with a positive total.
    config:
      retries: 2
    columns:
      - name: o_orderkey
        dtype: int64
        nullable: false

Decorator columns replace properties columns whole.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Before, in a model file:

sources:
  - name: raw_orders
    format: parquet
    location: data/tpch/orders.parquet
  - name: raw_customer
    format: parquet
    location: data/tpch/customer.parquet

After, in pipeloom.yml:

sources:
  tpch:
    format: parquet
    location: data/tpch
    tables:
      orders:
        location: orders.parquet
      customer:
        location: customer.parquet

A table location is joined to the group location; a table table is qualified by the group schema. A table may set one of location and table, not both (PLS108). A target can override a group under targets.<name>.sources.<group>, and null removes a key.

docs.title: Lineage with OpenLineage
docs.text:
The openlineage sink sends pipeloom runs to an OpenLineage backend such as Marquez: one job per persisted model, its input and output datasets, and facets for the schema, row counts, data quality results and errors. Decided in ADR-0046.

From a pipeloom run to the lineage graph in Marquez. Source: openlineage.d2.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
$ pip install "pipeloom[openlineage]"

The extra installs pipeloom-openlineage, which brings openlineage-python. The core never imports either.

docs.title: Configure the sink
docs.text:
events:
  sinks:
    - kind: openlineage
      transport:
        type: http
        url: http://localhost:15000

transport is an openlineage-python transport config: type plus that transport's keys (http, kafka, file, console and the others the client knows). Without transport the client reads OPENLINEAGE_URL or an openlineage.yml the way openlineage-python always does. A transport that needs credentials takes them as secret references, for example api_key: ${secret:env/OPENLINEAGE_API_KEY}; commands that run nothing (validate, compile) do not resolve them and send nothing.

Option Default Meaning namespace pipeloom.{target} namespace of the jobs; {project} and {target} are filled in dataset_namespace the job namespace namespace of catalog relations; sources with a location follow the OpenLineage naming: s3://bucket and raw/s for s3://bucket/raw/s, file and the absolute path for local files, dbfs and the path for dbfs:/... transport none an openlineage-python transport config inside_airflow skip skip leaves Airflow tasks to the Airflow OpenLineage provider; emit reports them here too

failure_budget, buffered and buffer_size work as for every sink.

docs.title: What it sends
docs.text:
• The run is the job <project>; each persisted model is the job <project>.<model>, whose runs carry a parent facet pointing at the pipeloom run.
  • Run ids are uuid5 values derived from the project, the run id, the unit and the attempt, so every process of one run (unit tasks, pipeloom finalize, an Airflow task) reports the same ids. Each attempt of a retried unit is its own run.
  • Inputs come from the manifest: the model's catalog relations and sources, minus the ephemeral models it inlines. The output is the model's relation.
  • Facets: jobType, sourceCodeLocation (the model's file and line), schema (the written columns, else the contract), outputStatistics (rows and bytes written), dataQualityAssertions (the model's expectations) and errorMessage (the error code, message and traceback of a failed unit or run).

docs.title: Under Airflow
docs.text:
The Airflow OpenLineage provider already reports every task, with the DAG run as parent. To avoid two copies of every unit, the sink ignores the events of a unit that an Airflow task runs (inside_airflow: skip), and the pipeloom operators hand the provider the datasets and facets instead, through get_openlineage_facets_on_start, ..._on_complete and ..._on_failure:

Execution mode What the provider gets LOCAL, VIRTUALENV the datasets and facets built from the child's events, as the sink would build them KUBERNETES the static datasets of the manifest: the pod's events stay in the pod WATCHER each watcher reports the static datasets of its unit from the manifest, and a watcher that reruns its unit reports the facets of its own child, as LOCAL does; the producer's child carries the Airflow ids, so the sink stays silent DATABRICKS nothing from the operators: the sink in the Databricks task reports the units, since its events carry no Airflow ids

Install apache-airflow-providers-openlineage and pipeloom-openlineage in the Airflow image; without either, the hooks return nothing. Set inside_airflow: emit only when the provider is not installed.

docs.title: Try it with Marquez
docs.text:
examples/marquez/compose.yml starts Marquez locally (API on port 15000, web UI on 13000), and tools/marquez_check.py runs the TPC-H polars example against it and checks the jobs, the lineage edges, the schema fields, the quality assertions and the parent run ids. From the repository root:

$ uv run examples/tpch_data.py
$ docker compose -p pipeloom-marquez -f examples/marquez/compose.yml up -d
$ uv run --all-packages python tools/marquez_check.py
$ docker compose -p pipeloom-marquez -f examples/marquez/compose.yml down -v

Wait until curl -fs http://localhost:15000/api/v1/namespaces answers before the check. Each fact prints as CHECK <name> ok or CHECK <name> FAIL <detail>, and the tool exits 1 on any failure. --keep keeps the example's run artifacts. Then open http://localhost:13000 and pick the namespace pipeloom.dev.

docs.title: Orchestrator protocol
docs.text:
An orchestrator runs a pipeloom plan one unit at a time and closes the run when the units are done. Airflow and Databricks do it through plugins. Anything else (GitHub Actions, Kestra, Argo, a shell script) can follow the same protocol with only the command line and the files pipeloom writes. The protocol is ADR-0049; this page is the short version, and the GitHub Actions recipe is a working example.

Prepare once, run each unit, always finalize. Source: orchestrator.d2.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
• Run: one orchestrator run of the plan, named by a run id. It has one folder, <artifacts root>/runs/<run_id>/.
  • Unit: the smallest thing the orchestrator schedules, one persisted model plus the ephemeral models inlined into it. The unit id is the model name.
  • Artifacts root: the folder that holds the runs, target/ in the project by default.
  • Attempt file: units/<unit_id>/attempt-<n>.json in the run folder, written by every unit invocation. It is one row of run_results.json.

docs.title: 1. Prepare
docs.text:
Compile once, then read the unit graph from that manifest, so every unit runs the same plan:

$ pipeloom compile --project-dir <dir> --target <target> --stable --out /tmp/plan/manifest.json
$ pipeloom graph --units --output json --project-dir <dir> --target <target> --manifest /tmp/plan/manifest.json > units.json

--stable leaves the timestamps out of the manifest, so the same project always gives the same bytes. Use an absolute manifest path: compile --out resolves a relative path against the project directory, while every --manifest option (and so the {manifest} placeholder) resolves it against the working directory. The unit graph (pipeloom.unit_graph/1) has the plan hash, the units in topological order, the edges, and finalize.argv. Each unit lists its parents, its retries, retry_delay_s, retry_on and timeout_s, and its argv.

docs.title: 2. Run id
docs.text: Pick one run id per orchestrator run: 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens (ADR-0013). Use the same id for every unit, for the finalize call, and for every retry or repair of that run. Prefix it with the orchestrator so ids do not collide, such as gha-<run_id>-<attempt>.

docs.title: 3. Start time
docs.text: Give every invocation the same start time, with a UTC offset. Either pass --run-started-at to each command or export PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT once. Engines use it to make writes idempotent. Once a run has recorded its start, a retry or repair must pass the same value or leave it out (the recorded one is kept); a different value stops run and finalize with PLX108 (exit 2). So compute the start time once per orchestrator run, never per attempt. The option needs --run-id.

docs.title: 4. Run a unit
docs.text:
The argv of a unit is a command line with three placeholders: {project_dir}, {manifest} and {run_id}. Replace them as whole values and run the result. The unit id, the target and the plan hash are already in it. For the example in the recipe a unit looks like this:

$ pipeloom run --project-dir examples/tpch_polars --target dev --manifest /tmp/plan/manifest.json \
    --select unit:orders --run-id gha-1-1 --expect-plan-hash <sha256>

You may add these options to a unit command: --orchestrator-id KEY=VALUE (repeatable, stored in the attempt file, the run results and every event), --log-format json, --cancel-grace DURATION and --full-refresh. A unit invocation takes no run lock, writes no run_results.json and never retries on its own.

docs.title: 5. Plan hash mismatch and setup failures
docs.text: --expect-plan-hash stops the unit with PLX103 when its plan is not the one you prepared. That is an orchestrator bug, not a data problem, so do not retry it. More generally, a unit that exits 1 without writing a new attempt file failed during setup (a bad config, a missing plugin, an unreachable catalog). Treat it as permanent and do not retry it.

docs.title: 6. Exit codes and retries
docs.text:
Exit code Meaning What the orchestrator does 0 The unit succeeded. Go on. 1 The unit failed. Read the newest attempt file. 2 Usage error. Never retry. 130 The unit was cancelled. May retry.

For exit 1, read error.category in the newest attempt file. Retry when attempts remain and the category is transient, or when the unit's retry_on is any. The orchestrator owns the retry count, the delay and the timeout: use retries, retry_delay_s and timeout_s from the unit graph. Pipeloom does not retry inside a unit invocation, so retries are never counted twice. Enforce timeout_s by stopping the process with SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the cancel grace. Allow timeout_s plus the grace plus a margin before you stop it. More on the settings in Retries, timeouts and cancellation.

docs.title: 7. Order
docs.text: Start a unit only after all its parents succeeded. Never run the same unit twice at once. Units that do not depend on each other may run in parallel. A unit whose parent failed or was skipped is not started; tell finalize about it (see below).

docs.title: 8. Shared storage
docs.text: Every invocation, including finalize, must see the same artifacts root, the same state store and the same catalog (ADR-0038). On one machine that is a folder. Across machines it takes a shared volume and a remote catalog and state store. Pipeloom does not copy artifacts between machines for you.

docs.title: 9. Finalize
docs.text:
Always run finalize, also when a unit failed: it is the call that writes run_results.json and closes the run (ADR-0034). Use finalize.argv from the unit graph, with the same placeholders. Options you may add: --orchestrator-id KEY=VALUE and --run-started-at.

For each unit in scope, finalize takes the newest attempt file. A unit that left none takes the state you pass with --unit-states PATH (a JSON file) or --unit-states-json TEXT (the same document inline), and a unit with neither is recorded as skipped with not_run, which does not fail the run. The states document is pipeloom.unit_states/1: a map from unit id to status (skipped, cancelled, failed or excluded) plus an optional reason, code, message and orchestrator_ids. An excluded unit gets no row.

Finalize exits 0 when the run succeeded, 1 when any unit failed, and 130 when it was cancelled. A failure wins over a cancellation. Run it again and it rewrites the same results; the second run.completed event carries replay: true. PLX105 means a full pipeloom run holds the run, so a run is driven either by the orchestrator or by one pipeloom run, never both.

docs.title: 10. Outputs
docs.text:
Everything lands in <artifacts root>/runs/<run_id>/: manifest.json, run_results.json, the attempt files under units/, the logs, and one event file per invocation under events/. Each document has a JSON Schema, so a consumer in any language can validate it:

Document Tag Schema manifest.json pipeloom.manifest/1 manifest.json run_results.json, attempt files pipeloom.run_results/1 run_results.json one event pipeloom.event/1 event.json unit states pipeloom.unit_states/1 unit_states.json unit graph pipeloom.unit_graph/1 unit_graph.json

See Run artifacts for the fields.

docs.title: 11. Stability
docs.text: The protocol and the five schemas are part of pipeloom 1.0. A new field is optional, so a consumer must ignore fields it does not know. Event types and skip_reason are open strings. status values are a closed set, and a new one needs a new schema version. Anything a consumer must understand to act correctly is a breaking change. The full policy is in Stability and deprecations.

docs.title: Portable models
docs.text:
A portable model is one Python function that runs unchanged on polars, pandas, DuckDB and Spark. You opt in with frame_api="narwhals" on the model. The function then receives Narwhals frames, and whatever it returns is converted back to the engine's own frame. pipeloom uses narwhals.stable.v2, the API Narwhals promises not to break, and imports it in one module only, pipeloom.engine.portable.

The engine must declare portable frames. All four do. On an engine that does not, such as the memory engine, pipeloom validate stops with PLC508.

One model, four engines, the same rows. Source: portable-models.d2.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
import narwhals.stable.v2 as nw
from pipeloom import model, ref


@model(
    frame_api="narwhals",
    inputs={"orders": ref("stg_orders"), "customers": ref("stg_customers")},
)
def revenue_by_region(ctx, orders, customers):
    paid = orders.filter(nw.col("status") == "paid")
    joined = paid.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="inner")
    doubled = joined.with_columns((nw.col("amount") * 2).alias("amount_x2"))
    return doubled.group_by("region").agg(
        nw.col("order_id").count().alias("orders"),
        nw.col("amount_x2").sum().alias("total"),
    )

Filters, joins, with_columns, select and group_by(...).agg(...) behave the same everywhere. Return the Narwhals frame as it is; there is nothing to convert. Returning the engine's native frame (nw.to_native(frame)) also works.

The repository tests exactly this shape of model on every engine, with the same input rows, and requires the same output rows on each (tests/portable/test_matrix.py, plus a Spark leg in the spark CI job).

docs.title: Lazy and eager frames
docs.text:
What the function receives depends on the engine:

Engine Frame Kind polars LazyFrame lazy DuckDB relation lazy Spark DataFrame lazy pandas DataFrame eager

Write for the lazy case and the model works on both. A lazy frame is a query plan: nothing runs until the engine writes the result. That rules out anything that needs the data in hand, such as indexing a row by position or to_list(). Collecting inside the model defeats the engine, so leave the result lazy and let pipeloom materialize it.

docs.title: Rows have no order
docs.text:
A lazy frame makes no promise about row order. A table has no first row, and a Spark or DuckDB plan may return the same rows in a different order on every run. A portable model therefore never relies on the order its input arrived in, and its output is a set of rows.

An operation that needs an order must say which one. Narwhals refuses the rest on a lazy frame:

Fails on a lazy frame Works nw.col("a").cum_sum() nw.col("a").cum_sum().over(order_by="day") nw.col("a").shift(1) or diff() nw.col("a").shift(1).over(order_by="day") nw.col("a").first() or last() nw.col("a").first().over(order_by="day") frame.unique(keep="first") frame.unique(subset=["id"], keep="any")

Add partition_by to over for a window per group, for example .over("customer_id", order_by="day"). A sort() earlier in the chain does not count: on a lazy frame Narwhals still refuses, so name the order on the operation itself. pandas runs these without order_by, which is how a model can pass on pandas and fail on DuckDB. Test a portable model on a lazy engine before you trust it.

Fix the order in the output only if a consumer needs one, and then sort at the end. Rows written to a table have no order either; the sort is for what you return, not a guarantee about storage.

docs.title: PLX122
docs.text: When Narwhals refuses an operation for lack of an order, the unit fails with PLX122 instead of a bare traceback. The message names the model and carries Narwhals' own explanation, and the hint points here. The exception behind it is narwhals.exceptions.InvalidOperationError with an order_by hint. The fix is in the model: name the order with over(order_by=...) or first(order_by=...), or rewrite without it. The failure is permanent, so retries do not repeat it.

docs.title: When to drop to ctx.sql
docs.text:
Not every operation exists in the Narwhals API, and some are cheaper to say in SQL: window functions with frames, QUALIFY, engine-specific functions. Use ctx.sql for those. Under frame_api="narwhals" it returns a Narwhals frame, so you can mix the two:

@model(frame_api="narwhals", inputs={"events": ref("stg_events")})
def sessions(ctx, events):
    ranked = ctx.sql(
        "select *, row_number() over (partition by user_id order by ts) as n from events"
    )
    return ranked.filter(nw.col("n") == 1)

The query is written in the dialect of the engine, or in the sql_dialect the model declares, and pipeloom translates it when they differ (this needs the sqlglot extra, otherwise PLC513). pandas has no SQL: a model that calls ctx.sql is not portable to it, and the validation warns with PLK606. If you need all four engines, stay in the frame API; if you need windows over an explicit order, over covers most of it.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Set frame_api="narwhals" and import narwhals.stable.v2 as nw.
  • Use expressions (nw.col), not engine methods. Do not call .collect(), .to_pandas() or .to_native() on an input.
  • Give every order-dependent operation an order_by.
  • Never rely on the order of rows going in or out.
  • Run the model on a lazy engine (polars, DuckDB or Spark) as well as on pandas.

docs.title: Data quality
docs.text: Expectations check a model's output before it is written. Each one has an action: warn, drop or fail. Dropped rows can go to a quarantine table so you can look at them later. The polars and pandas engines support all of it.

docs.title: Declare expectations
docs.text:
Project and source as in the quickstart, with this raw/orders.csv:

id,amount,status,updated_at
1,5.0,paid,2026-01-01T10:00:00
2,-2.5,paid,2026-01-01T11:00:00
3,7.0,refunded,2026-01-02T09:00:00
,4.0,new,2026-01-02T10:00:00

The source group in pipeloom.yml:

sources:
  raw:
    format: csv
    location: raw
    options:
      try_parse_dates: true
    tables:
      raw_orders:
        location: orders.csv

models/orders.py:

from pipeloom import model


@model
def orders(ctx, raw_orders):
    return ctx.sql("select id, amount, status, updated_at from raw_orders")

models/orders.yml, its properties file:

models:
  - name: orders
    config:
      expectations:
        - name: id_present
          check:
            not_null: [id]
          on_violation: drop
        - name: status_known
          check:
            accepted_values:
              column: status
              values: [new, paid, shipped]
          on_violation: drop
        - name: amount_non_negative
          check:
            range:
              column: amount
              min: 0
          on_violation: warn
        - name: unique_id
          check:
            unique: [id]
          on_violation: fail
        - name: not_empty
          check:
            row_count:
              min: 1
          on_violation: fail
      quality:
        quarantine: true
        max_drop_ratio: 0.5

The same settings can go in @model(expectations=[...], quality={...}) instead.

$ pipeloom run
... WARN   orders: id_present (not_null) dropped 1 of 4 rows
... WARN   orders: status_known (accepted_values) dropped 1 of 4 rows
... WARN   orders: amount_non_negative (range) failed on 1 of 4 rows
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ table/overwrite   2 rows

Two rows were written, two went to orders__quarantine, and the negative amount only produced a warning. The unit still succeeded. on_violation defaults to fail.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Row checks look at each row. check takes one of these (or use expr instead of check):

Check Passes when not_null: [a, b] the columns are not null accepted_values with column and values the value is one of the list (exact comparison) range with column, min and max the value is within the bounds, inclusive; either bound may be left out regex with column and pattern the pattern is found anywhere in the string (an unanchored search); the column must be a string expr: "amount >= 0" the expression is true

A null passes every check except not_null, and NaN counts as null. A row check can warn, drop or fail.

Aggregate checks look at the whole batch and can only warn or fail (a drop is PLP403):

Check Fails when unique: [a, b] a key appears more than once (rows with a null key part are not counted) row_count with min and max the number of rows is outside the bounds freshness with column and max_age the newest value is older than max_age; an all-null column fails

Aggregates see the rows that are left after drops. For an incremental model that means the new rows of this run, not the whole table.

docs.title: The expr dialect
docs.text: An expr is written in the dialect of the engine and never runs code. On polars it is a SQL expression (amount >= 0 and amount < 1e6). On pandas it is a restricted Python expression: column names, literals, comparisons, and, or, not, arithmetic and in with a list. Function calls, attributes and @name are rejected with PLQ302. Prefer the named checks when a model has to run on several engines.

docs.title: Drops, quarantine and the drop ratio
docs.text:
A row that fails any drop check is removed from the output. With quality.quarantine: true the removed rows are appended to <target>__quarantine: the model's columns plus

Column Content _pipeloom_run_id the run that dropped the row _pipeloom_failed the names of the failed drop checks (a list; JSON text on a csv catalog) _pipeloom_ts when it happened, a UTC timestamp

quality.max_drop_ratio (0 to 1) fails the unit when the share of dropped rows is larger. In the example, 0.25 fails the unit because half of the rows are dropped:

FAIL   orders ... PLQ301
  model 'orders' failed expectation(s): max_drop_ratio
  hint: fix the data, or relax on_violation or quality.max_drop_ratio

A failed fail check or an exceeded ratio stops the unit before it writes: the target and its quarantine are left as they were. The counts are still recorded. Quarantine rows are written once per run even if the unit is retried. If the model output changes, the quarantine table follows (new columns are added); an incompatible type change fails with PLM202 naming the quarantine table.

A view or an ephemeral model cannot carry expectations (PLP411), and no other model may be called <model>__quarantine in the same catalog and schema (PLP412). An engine that does not declare the quality capability is rejected with PLC510.

docs.title: Model contracts
docs.text:
A model can declare its exact output columns with columns. Each entry has a name, a logical dtype (the type names engines report, such as int64, string, decimal(18,2) or timestamp[us, UTC]) and nullable (default true).

@model(
    columns=[
        {"name": "order_id", "dtype": "int64", "nullable": False},
        {"name": "amount", "dtype": "decimal(18,2)"},
    ],
)
def fct_orders(ctx, stg_orders):
    return ctx.sql("select order_id, amount from stg_orders")

A properties entry can declare the same columns in YAML; decorator columns replace them whole.

Before every write, pipeloom compares the batch with the contract:

  • the column names must match exactly (case-sensitive, any order), with no column missing and none extra;
  • each logical type must equal the declared dtype. Nothing is widened or cast, so cast in the body. Engines report fixed forms: Spark timestamps are always timestamp[us, UTC]. On pandas, an integer column with a null is float64 unless it uses the nullable Int64 dtype, and a column of Python Decimal objects is unknown; use pd.ArrowDtype(pa.decimal128(18, 2)) to get decimal(18,2). To see what an engine reports, run once: PLM208 names the reported type of every column whose type differs;
  • a column with nullable: false must hold no null (NaN counts as null), counted with one pass over the batch.

The check runs after the expectations, on the rows they keep, and before the schema-change policy, the quarantine write and the table write. A drop expectation can therefore remove null rows before the contract sees them. A mismatch fails the unit with PLM208, writes nothing and is never retried under retry_on: transient. on_schema_change still compares the batch with the existing table as before.

columns is a model key; the models: tree cannot set it. An unknown dtype or a repeated name is PLS102 at validation, and a contract on a view or an ephemeral model is PLP414. Declared columns appear as nodes[].columns in manifest.json and on the docs site model page. See ADR-0044.

docs.title: What the run records
docs.text:
• model.quality_evaluated event: total rows, one result per expectation, dropped and quarantined counts, the drop ratio and the names of the failures.
  • run_results.json: expectations[] (name, kind, action, passed, failed and, for aggregates, a value), rows_dropped, rows_quarantined and warnings[]. See Run artifacts.
  • The console prints a WARN line for every check that warned, dropped or failed rows.

Counts are kept for fail checks too, so you can see how bad a failing batch was.

docs.title: Recipe: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
This workflow runs the TPC-H polars example through the orchestrator protocol on a GitHub Actions runner. A shell loop plays the orchestrator: it reads the unit graph, runs each unit with its own command line, finalizes the run and checks the result. Nothing in it is specific to the example except the project folder and the count of nine units. The same file runs in this repository's CI, so it stays correct.

name: orchestrate-tpch

# The orchestrator protocol on a CI runner: a shell loop plays the orchestrator and runs the TPC-H
# polars example one unit at a time, from the unit graph. See docs/guide/recipe-github-actions.md.

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "src/**"
      - "plugins/pipeloom-polars/**"
      - "examples/**"
      - "uv.lock"
      - ".github/workflows/orchestrate-tpch.yml"
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "src/**"
      - "plugins/pipeloom-polars/**"
      - "examples/**"
      - "uv.lock"
      - ".github/workflows/orchestrate-tpch.yml"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions: {}

concurrency:
  group: orchestrate-tpch-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  orchestrate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    permissions:
      contents: read
    env:
      PROJECT_DIR: examples/tpch_polars
      # fills the placeholders of an argv from the unit graph
      FILL: '.argv[] | gsub("\\{project_dir\\}"; $p) | gsub("\\{manifest\\}"; $m) | gsub("\\{run_id\\}"; $r)'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@07a047e608db84b3d8c06cd9a7c7dcc9c355c18e # v10.3.2

      # The only step tied to this repository. Outside it, install the released packages instead:
      #   pip install "pipeloom[polars]"
      - name: Install pipeloom
        run: |
          uv sync --locked --all-packages
          echo "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/.venv/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

      - name: Generate the TPC-H data
        run: uv run examples/tpch_data.py

      # One run id and one start time for every invocation of this orchestrator run.
      - name: Pick the run id and start time
        run: |
          echo "RUN_ID=gha-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          echo "PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Prepare the plan and the unit graph
        run: |
          pipeloom compile --project-dir "$PROJECT_DIR" --target dev --stable --out "$RUNNER_TEMP/manifest.json"
          pipeloom graph --units --output json --project-dir "$PROJECT_DIR" --target dev --manifest "$RUNNER_TEMP/manifest.json" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/units.json"

      # A unit starts after all its parents succeeded; a unit with a failed or skipped parent is
      # skipped. Units run one at a time here, in the graph's topological order. Retries are the
      # orchestrator's job: this graph sets none, so a failed unit stays failed.
      - name: Run the units
        run: |
          : > "$RUNNER_TEMP/not-ok"
          while read -r unit; do
            id=$(jq -r '.unit_id' <<< "$unit")
            blocked=""
            for parent in $(jq -r '.parents[]' <<< "$unit"); do
              if grep -qxF "$parent" "$RUNNER_TEMP/not-ok"; then blocked="$parent"; fi
            done
            if [ -n "$blocked" ]; then
              echo "skip $id: parent $blocked did not succeed"
              echo "$id" >> "$RUNNER_TEMP/not-ok"
              continue
            fi
            mapfile -t argv < <(jq -r --arg p "$PROJECT_DIR" --arg m "$RUNNER_TEMP/manifest.json" --arg r "$RUN_ID" "$FILL" <<< "$unit")
            echo "run $id"
            if ! "${argv[@]}" < /dev/null; then
              echo "::error::unit $id failed"
              echo "$id" >> "$RUNNER_TEMP/not-ok"
            fi
          done < <(jq -c '.units[]' "$RUNNER_TEMP/units.json")
          test ! -s "$RUNNER_TEMP/not-ok"

      # Always runs, so a failed run still gets its run_results.json.
      - name: Finalize the run
        if: always()
        run: |
          mapfile -t argv < <(jq -r --arg p "$PROJECT_DIR" --arg m "$RUNNER_TEMP/manifest.json" --arg r "$RUN_ID" ".finalize | $FILL" "$RUNNER_TEMP/units.json")
          "${argv[@]}" --orchestrator-id "gha_run_id=${{ github.run_id }}"

      - name: Check the results
        run: jq -e '.run.status == "succeeded" and .run.counts.succeeded == 9' "$PROJECT_DIR/target/runs/$RUN_ID/run_results.json"

      - name: Upload the run folder
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:
          name: tpch-run
          path: examples/tpch_polars/target/runs
          if-no-files-found: warn
          retention-days: 7

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Install pipeloom. The workflow installs this checkout with uv sync --locked --all-packages and puts .venv/bin on the path. This is the only step you replace in your own repository, with pip install "pipeloom[polars]" or whatever your project needs.
  2. Generate the data. The example ships a script that writes the five TPC-H tables as parquet. Your pipeline reads its own sources, so you drop this step.
  3. Pick the run id and start time. gha-<run_id>-<attempt> is a valid run id and changes when someone reruns the workflow. The start time is exported as PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT, so every later command sees the same one.
  4. Prepare. compile --stable writes the manifest. graph --units --output json --manifest writes the unit graph with the plan hash of that manifest.
  5. Run the units. The loop reads the units in topological order. A unit with a parent that failed or was skipped is skipped. For the others, jq fills the placeholders {project_dir}, {manifest} and {run_id} in the argv and the loop runs it. A failed unit is recorded and the step fails at the end, after every unit that could run has run.
  6. Finalize. This step has if: always(), so a failed run still gets its run_results.json. It uses finalize.argv from the unit graph and adds the id of the workflow run with --orchestrator-id.
  7. Check. jq -e fails the job unless the run succeeded with nine succeeded units.
  8. Upload. The run folder, with the manifest, results, attempt files, logs and events, is attached to the workflow run even when the job failed.

The loop does not retry. In the example no model sets retries, and the protocol leaves retries to the orchestrator: add a retry loop around a unit that reads retries, retry_delay_s and retry_on from the unit graph and the error.category of the newest attempt file. Add a timeout around the command for a unit with timeout_s.

docs.title: Several jobs
docs.text: GitHub hosted runners share no filesystem, so one job per unit needs three things the example does not have: a remote catalog, a remote state store, and an artifacts root on shared storage that every job and the finalize job can read and write. With those in place each unit is a job that runs its argv, a final job with if: always() runs finalize, and units that failed or were skipped are passed to it with --unit-states-json. This variant is not tested in CI.

docs.title: Other orchestrators
docs.text: Kestra, Argo Workflows and Airflow without the plugin follow the same protocol. A task runs a unit's argv, task dependencies come from edges, and a last task runs finalize whatever happened before it. The orchestrator's own retry and timeout settings come from the unit graph.

docs.title: Retries, timeouts and cancellation
docs.text:
A unit can fail for a reason that goes away on its own, run for too long, or be stopped together with the run. pipeloom has a setting for each case.

A retry, then a graceful cancel. Source: retry-cancel.d2.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
from pipeloom import model
from pipeloom.engine.errors import TransientError


@model(
    retries=2,  # extra attempts after the first; the default is 0
    retry_delay="1s",  # base delay; the default is 1s
    retry_on="transient",  # or "any"
    timeout="5m",
)
def orders(ctx, raw_orders):
    if ctx.attempt == 1:
        raise TransientError("the first attempt fails")
    return raw_orders

The model above fails once with a TransientError and then succeeds:

$ pipeloom run
... 1/1 FAIL   orders ........ PLX101 pipeloom.engine.errors.TransientError
... RETRY  orders attempt 1 failed PLX101 (transient), next in 0.7s
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ table/overwrite   2 rows

Each attempt writes its own file (units/orders/attempt-1.json, attempt-2.json), and the result row has attempt: 2 and retries_used: 1. While a unit waits for its next attempt it holds no worker slot, and every attempt emits unit.retrying with the attempt that failed, the next one and the delay.

retries, retry_delay, retry_on and timeout can be set in the decorator, in a properties entry's config, and as +key settings in the models: tree of pipeloom.yml.

docs.title: What is retried
docs.text:
With retry_on: transient (the default) only transient failures are retried. A failure is transient when:

  • the model or an engine raised pipeloom.engine.errors.TransientError, directly or as the cause of another exception;
  • the engine says so (for example a table commit conflict);
  • a ConnectionError or TimeoutError is in the cause chain;
  • an OSError happened while reading, writing or touching state, except file not found, permission denied and the directory errors (a Windows sharing violation counts as transient);
  • a unit process exited without a result (PLX106).

Everything else is permanent: an exception from your code, a validation error and a failed expectation. A rejected schema change, a lost watermark race, a bad watermark and a bad write key are always permanent. With retry_on: any every failed attempt is retried, including deterministic ones, so use it only when you know that a rerun can change the outcome.

An append model on an engine without idempotent writes cannot have retries (PLC505), because a retry could write the same rows twice. The polars and pandas engines have idempotent writes.

docs.title: Delay between attempts
docs.text: For retry number n the delay is a random value between half and all of min(max(retry_delay, 300 s), retry_delay * 2^(n-1)). With the default of one second that is up to 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on, capped at five minutes. The random part is seeded by the run id, the unit and n, so the same run waits the same time.

docs.title: Who retries
docs.text: Whoever schedules the unit. With boundary: process or task under pipeloom run, the parent scheduler retries. A single unit run with --select unit:<id>, which is what an orchestrator task does, never retries on its own: the orchestrator owns the retry.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
timeout is a limit per attempt. A unit that exceeds it ends as timed_out with PLX102, its downstream units are skipped and the run fails. A timeout is never retried.

... 2/2 TIMEOUT slow_orders ... PLX102 after 2s (attempt 1)

pipeloom cannot kill a Python thread. On the thread executor (boundary: process) the attempt is asked to stop and then abandoned: the unit is marked timed_out at once and whatever the thread reports later is dropped. The engine's cancel is called once. The model stops at the checkpoints before reading, after the body and before the write; a long call in the middle of your code is not interrupted. If the thread is still working when the run ends, run.completed reports it in abandoned_threads, and the thread ends with the process. In the rare case where an abandoned thread still commits its write, the attempt file says timed_out and the unit gets a late_result: <status> warning. With boundary: task the child process is killed after timeout plus the grace period, together with everything it started.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C (or send SIGTERM; on Windows, Ctrl+C or Ctrl+Break) to stop a run:

  1. The first signal is a graceful stop. Nothing new starts, pending, queued and retrying units are cancelled, and running units are asked to stop. They get cancel_grace seconds to finish, and a unit that finishes in time keeps its real result. The rest end as cancelled (PLX104). The run emits run.cancel_requested, ends with status cancelled and exits with 130.
  2. A second signal is a hard stop: no more grace; running units are cancelled at once.
  3. A third signal raises KeyboardInterrupt.

cancel_grace is 30 seconds by default. Set it per target, or override it for one run:

targets:
  dev:
    engine:
      kind: polars
    catalog:
      kind: filesystem
      root: target/warehouse
    state:
      kind: json
      path: .pipeloom/state
    cancel_grace: 10s

$ pipeloom run --cancel-grace 5s

From Python, pass a RunControl to Project.run(..., control=control) and call control.request_stop().

With boundary: task each child runs in its own process group, so a Ctrl+C in your terminal reaches only the parent, which then stops the children. A graceful stop is SIGTERM on POSIX and Ctrl+Break on Windows, followed by a kill after the grace. The kill ends the child and every process it started: its process group on POSIX, its job object on Windows. When a child exits on its own, the parent sweeps the same group or job, so a grandchild it left behind does not outlive the run.

Run IDs are reusable after a stop. Rerun with the same --run-id and the units that already committed are skipped through their write tokens.

docs.title: Run history
docs.text: pipeloom runs lists past runs and shows one run with its units. It reads the state store of the target by default, or the run_results.json files under the artifacts root with --artifacts. It takes no lock and changes no run; building the store may create an empty one, as every command does. Decided in ADR-0047.

docs.title: List runs
docs.text:
pipeloom runs ls --target dev

prints one tab-separated line per run, newest first: run id, status, start time, duration and unit counts.

20261106T101500Z-1a2b   failed  2026-11-06T10:15:00+00:00   12.4s   failed=1 skipped=2 succeeded=5 total=8
20261106T090000Z-9f8e   succeeded   2026-11-06T09:00:00+00:00   10.1s   succeeded=8 total=8
  • --limit N lists at most N runs (default 20).
  • --before RUN_ID lists the runs older than that one, so passing the last run id of a page gives the next page.
  • --output json prints a JSON list of run records instead.
  • --artifacts reads <artifacts root>/runs/*/run_results.json instead of the state store. Use it when the store is gone or lives on another machine. A run that is still running, or crashed, has no run_results.json and is not listed.

Runs are ordered by start time, then by run id. Only the runs of the selected project and target are listed.

docs.title: Show one run
docs.text:
pipeloom runs show 20261106T101500Z-1a2b --target dev

prints the status, the start and end times, the parent run (set by pipeloom retry --from) and one line per unit attempt: unit id, attempt and status. --output json prints {"run": ..., "units": [...]}, and --artifacts reads the run's run_results.json.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Code When PLX117 the configured state store has no list_runs (a plugin written before plugin API 0.5); use --artifacts PLX118 runs show or --before names a run that this project and target do not have

docs.title: For plugin authors
docs.text: StateStore.list_runs(project, target, limit, before=None) is part of plugin API (0, 5). pipeloom.state.types.page_runs orders and pages any sequence of RunRecords, so a store can read its run records and hand them to it. The StateStoreContract suite in pipeloom.testing.contract.state checks the ordering and the paging.

docs.title: Running a pipeline
docs.text:
pipeloom run executes the selected models of a project and writes the run artifacts.

$ pipeloom run --target polars

The command validates the project, compiles the plan, takes a run lock, runs every selected unit in dependency order and finalizes the artifacts. Exit codes: 0 when every unit succeeded, 1 when a unit or a check failed, 2 for bad usage and 130 when the run was stopped.

Select models with -s/--select and --exclude (see pipeloom ls). A unit whose upstream failed is skipped with the reason upstream_failed. With --fail-fast the first failure stops the scheduler from starting more units; the units still waiting are skipped with the reason fail_fast. Independent branches keep running without it.

docs.title: Executors and the boundary
docs.text:
The target's boundary decides how units are executed. You can override it with --boundary.

Boundary Executor What it does process (default) thread Every unit runs on a thread of the invocation. One engine session serves all of them, and an ephemeral model shared by several units is computed once. task process Every unit runs as its own pipeloom run --select unit:<id> process, so each unit could be an orchestrator task. Events of the child are relayed to the parent, and its logs go to logs/.

--workers N (or PIPELOOM_WORKERS) sets how many units run at once. The default is the target's workers setting, else the smaller of 4 and the CPU count.

With boundary: task the units share nothing in memory, so the state store must be shared between processes: the json store qualifies, sqlite does not (PLC503). Starting a child process costs about a second per unit.

docs.title: Run ids and reruns
docs.text:
Each run has an id: --run-id, or a timestamp and a short suffix such as 20261104T014938Z-3fa91c. Ids use 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens.

Reusing a run id continues that run. Every write carries the idempotency token <run_id>:<unit_id>, and the filesystem catalog remembers the last tokens of each table, so a unit that already committed under that token is not written twice. Rerunning a finished run with the same id leaves the data byte-identical. Attempt files keep counting up (attempt-2.json, and so on), and run_results.json reports the newest attempt of each unit.

Every engine sees one start time for the run. By default it is the time the run began, and a reused run id keeps the start recorded the first time. --run-started-at ISO8601 (or PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT) sets it instead, for an orchestrator that wants every task to share the job's start time. The value needs a UTC offset (2026-11-05T03:00:00+00:00 or a trailing Z) and needs --run-id. Giving a different value for a run id that already has a start is PLX108 and exit code 2. The Spark engine derives its Delta write version from this time.

--full-refresh rebuilds append tables from scratch. It takes an optional true or false, so an orchestrator can pass a templated value.

To run exactly the plan you compiled earlier, pass --manifest target/runs/<id>/manifest.json. Add --expect-plan-hash <sha256> to stop with PLX103 when the plan changed.

docs.title: Retrying a run
docs.text:
pipeloom retry --from RUN_ID runs again what that run did not finish: the units that failed, timed out, were skipped or were cancelled. Fix the model, then retry.

$ pipeloom run --run-id nightly-1        # bad fails, its child is skipped
$ pipeloom retry --from nightly-1        # runs bad and its child, nothing else

The retry is a new run with its own id (--run-id sets it and must differ from --from). Its run_results.json and its state record name the original in parent_run_id. The project is compiled again, so the fix is picked up. The retry inherits the vars (--vars wins), --full-refresh (--full-refresh or --no-full-refresh wins), --state and --defer of the run it retries. It takes no --select or --exclude: the parent's rows already say what to run. When nothing failed, it prints run nightly-1 has nothing to retry and exits 0 without a run folder.

The parent must be a finished run of the same project and target in the artifacts root; anything else is PLX113 (for another target, the hint says which --target to use). A unit that failed after its write committed is written again if it appends, because the new run id gives it a new idempotency token. To continue the same run instead, run it again with its own --run-id.

docs.title: Selection by state and defer
docs.text:
Compile production once with a stable manifest and keep it as the reference:

pipeloom compile --target prod --stable --out state/manifest.json

--state DIR on run, compile, ls and graph reads DIR/manifest.json (and DIR/run_results.json when it is there). target works too, because every run copies both files to the artifacts root. A relative DIR is relative to the project dir. A missing folder, or a manifest or run results of another project, is PLX110.

  • state:modified selects the models that are new or whose body, config or inputs differ from the reference, and the persisted models that inline a modified ephemeral model. The comparison ignores the target, so a dev project and a prod reference match when nothing changed.
  • state:new selects the models the reference does not have.
  • result:fail, result:skip, result:cancelled and result:succeeded select by the status of the model in the reference run results (fail includes timeouts). They need the run results (PLG308).

The graph operators work as usual, so state:modified+ is the models that changed and everything downstream. A state or result atom without --state is PLG307. A change to a variable or an environment value interpolated into a model's config counts as a change; a change to a source does not.

pipeloom run --state state --defer reads every parent the run does not build from the relation the reference manifest records for it, so a dev run of one model reads the production upstreams. The plan and its hash stay the same. The relation is not checked first: a table that is missing, or that your target cannot read, fails the child with PLM204 and a hint that names the relation. An intermediate parent, or one the reference lacks, is read from this target and PLX112 warns. --defer is refused (PLX111) for -s unit: runs, for boundary: task and when the reference was compiled for another catalog kind. With a filesystem catalog the reference's root must be the same as yours.

The dev loop:

pipeloom run --target dev --state state -s "state:modified+" --defer

docs.title: Intermediates
docs.text:
A model with materialized: intermediate is persisted for the length of the run, so units in other processes (boundary: task) can read it. The result goes to <artifacts.root>/runs/<run_id>/intermediate/<model> and relation_name in run_results.json is that location. An intermediate takes no incremental block, no partition_by and no strategy other than overwrite (PLP413).

The intermediate_ttl key of the target's artifacts block (default 1d) says how long the data stays. With 0 the folder is deleted at the end of a run that succeeded; a failed run keeps it. At the end of every run, finalize also deletes the intermediates of other runs once they are older than the TTL those runs recorded. A run that left no results, or was resumed and stopped again, is deleted after it has been idle for the longer of the TTL and one hour. A deletion that fails is a warning in run.warnings, never a failed run.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text: A run takes a lock named <project>/<target> in the state store, so two runs of one target do not overlap. The lock is a lease of 60 seconds that a heartbeat renews every 20 seconds. A run that dies frees the lock within a minute. A second run that finds the lock held stops with PLX105 and names the holder, its run id and when the lease expires. --no-lock skips the lock.

docs.title: Unit mode for orchestrators
docs.text:
pipeloom run --select unit:<id> runs a single execution unit and nothing else: no lock, no run.* events, no run_results.json. Use it when an orchestrator owns the schedule and the retries. Each invocation writes its own attempt file and event file under the run folder, and the invocation that owns the run merges them when it finalizes. The unit ids are in the manifest.

Pass the ids the orchestrator gave the run with --orchestrator-id KEY=VALUE, repeated as needed, for example --orchestrator-id job_run_id=42. Keys match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63} and values are 1 to 256 printable characters; a later duplicate wins.
