The ids go into every attempt file, the orchestrator_ids of each result row and of the run, and the context of every event as orchestrator_id.<key>.

docs.title: Closing the run: pipeloom finalize
docs.text:
When the orchestrator ran each unit itself, nothing merged the results. pipeloom finalize --run-id <id> does it as the last task of the job. For each unit in scope (the whole plan, or what -s/--select and --exclude leave) it takes, in this order:

  1. the unit's attempt file;
  2. else the state the orchestrator reports in --unit-states PATH, a JSON file (or the same document inline in --unit-states-json TEXT, not together with the file), {"schema": "pipeloom.unit_states/1", "units": {"<unit id>": {"status": "failed", ...}}}. status is skipped, cancelled, failed or excluded; reason (for skipped, default upstream_failed), code, message and orchestrator_ids are optional. excluded drops the unit from the results;
  3. else the unit is skipped with the reason upstream_failed when one of its upstreams failed, otherwise not_run, which does not fail the run.

The run is failed when any unit failed, timed out or was skipped as upstream_failed, else cancelled when any unit was cancelled, else succeeded. The exit code is 0, 1 or 130. A file that cannot be read or does not match the schema is exit 2. Finalize records the run in the state store, deletes expired intermediates and emits run.completed. Running it again with the same inputs rewrites the same results. It also takes --manifest, --expect-plan-hash, --orchestrator-id, --run-started-at and the project options of run.

Finalize refuses with PLX105 (exit 1, as run does) while a pipeloom run of the same run id is still live, that is, its lock is held and its run record says running.

On a file system without hard links (some network volumes), attempt files are created with an exclusive open instead of a link, which is still exclusive but not atomic.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The console prints one line per unit, a summary, the failure block for each failed unit and the paths of the files written. See Run artifacts for the files.

Each failure block has an explain: line after the hint. pipeloom explain <CODE> (for example pipeloom explain PLX101, any case) prints what the code means and links to its entry on the error codes page.

docs.title: Inspecting a project
docs.text:
These commands write no data. The flags of each are in the command line reference.

  • pipeloom validate runs the checks from YAML syntax to engine capabilities (layers L0 to L6) and prints each finding with its code. It exits 1 on an error, and with --warn-error on a warning too.
  • pipeloom compile validates the same way, then writes the plan to a manifest (--out, default target/manifest.json). --stable blanks the timestamp, the invocation id and the selection, so the same project and target always give the same file.
  • pipeloom ls prints the names of the models that -s/--select and --exclude choose, one per line, or a JSON list with --output json.
  • pipeloom graph prints the selected models in dependency order as text (name <- parents), Graphviz dot, Mermaid or JSON. --units --output json prints the execution units instead; see the orchestrator protocol.
  • pipeloom plugins list lists the installed plugins by group and kind from their metadata, without importing them. --group keeps one group, --output json prints JSON, and --check imports each plugin and adds its plugin API version and a status. A kind that two distributions provide is PLU002 and exit 1.
  • pipeloom schema export --out DIR writes the JSON Schemas of pipeloom.yml and the properties files; see JSON Schema.

docs.title: Testing models
docs.text: A unit test runs a model body on rows you give it and compares the output with rows you expect. It needs no warehouse and writes nothing: pipeloom test builds the inputs in memory on the target's engine, runs the model function, and reads the result back. The design is in ADR-0045.

docs.title: A first case
docs.text:
Take a model:

from pipeloom import model, ref


@model(inputs={"orders": ref("stg_orders")})
def orders_enriched(ctx, orders):
    return ctx.sql("select o.id, o.amount * 2 as doubled from orders o")

Its cases live in its properties entry, in any YAML file under model_paths. Rows are data, so they never go on the decorator. Every input alias (a parameter name of the function) needs given rows, and expect lists the rows the function should return.

models:
  - name: orders_enriched
    unit_tests:
      - name: doubles_the_amount
        given:
          orders:
            rows:
              - id: 1
                amount: 10
              - id: 2
                amount: null
        expect:
          rows:
            - id: 2
              doubled: null
            - id: 1
              doubled: 20

$ pipeloom test
12:00:01 PASS   orders_enriched: doubles_the_amount
12:00:01 unit tests: 1 passed, 0 failed

docs.title: How rows compare
docs.text:
• Only the columns that expect names are compared. Extra output columns are ignored; a missing one fails the case.
  • Order does not matter, but duplicates do: two expected copies of a row need two in the output.
  • Expected values are cast to the type of the output column, so amount: 3 matches a float64 3.0.
  • Null equals NaN, floats compare to 12 significant digits, a timestamp without a time zone is read as UTC, and decimals compare exactly.

When rows differ, the case fails with PLX114 and a row diff: - lines are expected rows the output lacks, + lines are output rows nobody expected.

12:00:01 FAIL   orders_enriched: doubles_the_amount PLX114 1 missing, 1 unexpected row(s)
         - {"id": 1, "doubled": 21}
         + {"id": 1, "doubled": 20}

The console shows 10 rows of each side, the unit_test.failed event holds up to 50.

docs.title: Rows from CSV files
docs.text:
csv replaces rows in a given or in expect. The path is relative to the project dir. The file needs a header row; an empty field is null.

given:
  orders:
    csv: tests/data/orders.csv

docs.title: Column types
docs.text:
A given column takes its type from, in order:

  1. the columns of the given block,
  2. the contract columns of the upstream model,
  3. inference.

Inline values infer boolean, int64, float64, string, date and timestamps from their YAML type. CSV values infer int64, then float64, then string, so declare dates, timestamps and string ids:

given:
  orders:
    csv: tests/data/orders.csv
    columns:
      - name: id
        dtype: string
      - name: ordered_at
        dtype: timestamp[us, UTC]

A column that holds only nulls and declares no type cannot be typed; the case fails with PLX115.

docs.title: Keeping cases in their own files
docs.text:
A properties file can live anywhere under model_paths, and each model has one properties entry. To keep cases in a tests folder, add it to model_paths in pipeloom.yml and put the model's properties entry there:

models:
  - name: orders_enriched
    unit_tests:
      - name: doubles_the_amount
        given:
          orders:
            csv: tests/data/orders.csv
        expect:
          csv: tests/data/doubled.csv

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
pipeloom test takes --select, --exclude, --state, --target, --vars, --plugin, --project-dir and --log-format, like compile. It takes no lock, records no run and writes no artifacts. Exit codes: 0 when every case passed, 1 when one failed or the project does not validate, 2 for a usage error, 130 when interrupted.

Unit tests never change the manifest or the plan hash, so adding one selects nothing under state:modified.

docs.title: Data tests
docs.text:
Expectations judge each batch before it is written. Data tests judge the whole written table afterwards, which is where a foreign key check belongs. Like unit tests, they go in the model's properties entry:

models:
  - name: orders
    data_tests:
      - name: customer_exists
        check:
          relationships:
            column: customer_id
            to:
              ref: customers
            field: id
      - name: order_id_unique
        check:
          unique:
            - order_id
        on_violation: warn

A check is one of not_null (a list of columns), unique (a list of columns) or relationships. A relationships violation is a row whose non-null column matches no field value of the parent named in to (a ref or a source); NaN counts as null, and parent nulls never match. on_violation is fail (the default) or warn.

Data tests run under pipeloom build, inside each unit after its write and its watermark commit, and again when a retry replays a write. They read the whole table, incremental models included, so set on_violation: warn where a full scan on every build is too slow. The parent is read like an input, so --defer reads it from the reference. Each result is an entry of results[].expectations in run_results.json with scope: table (expectations carry scope: batch). A failed warn test adds a warning; a failed fail test is PLQ303: the unit fails, its descendants are skipped and the run exits 1, but the data stays written.

Tables, incremental, intermediate and view models take data tests. On an ephemeral model they are PLP415, as is a relationships parent that is the model itself, one of its descendants, an ephemeral model, an intermediate model, or a model that closes a cycle among input and relationship edges.

docs.title: Data tests on the decorator
docs.text:
data_tests also has a decorator keyword, which takes DataTest objects or plain dicts. The check is one of not_null, unique or relationships, as in YAML. It is not an expectation check, so helpers such as not_null() from pipeloom do not apply there:

from pipeloom import DataTest, model, ref


@model(
    data_tests=[
        DataTest(name="id_unique", check={"unique": ["id"]}, on_violation="warn"),
        DataTest(
            name="customer_exists",
            check={"relationships": {"column": "customer_id", "to": ref("customers"), "field": "id"}},
        ),
    ],
)
def orders(raw_orders):
    ...

In a relationships check, to takes ref("name") or source("group", "table") as well as the mapping {"ref": "name"} or {"source": "group.table"}; they resolve to the same config.

A model that sets data_tests in both places keeps the decorator's list, which replaces the properties list whole. unit_tests live only in properties.

docs.title: build
docs.text: pipeloom build takes the flags of run. It runs the unit tests of the selected models first; if one fails it stops with exit 1 before a run id exists and before anything is written. Then it runs the selection with data tests on, ordering each model after its relationship parents. run_results.json records args.data_tests: true, and pipeloom retry --from keeps it.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Code Meaning PLP415 Data tests on an ephemeral model, or a relationships parent that is the model itself, a descendant, an ephemeral model, an intermediate model, or closes a cycle among input and relationship edges PLQ303 A data test with on_violation: fail found violations; the data stays written PLR208 A case gives an alias that is not an input, leaves an input without rows, or reuses a case name PLX114 The output differs from expect PLX115 The case cannot run: a CSV is missing, a value does not cast, an untyped all-null column, the body raised, or the engine has no from_rows or to_rows

docs.title: Merge, replace_partitions, scd2 and schema changes
docs.text: write.strategy decides how a batch meets the rows already in the target table. 0.3 adds merge and replace_partitions next to append and overwrite, and a policy for batches whose columns differ from the table. The polars and pandas engines support all of it on filesystem tables. 0.9 adds scd2 on polars, pandas and Spark.

docs.title: merge
docs.text:
Rows are matched on unique_key. Matched rows are updated, unmatched rows are inserted.

from pipeloom import model


@model(
    materialized="incremental",
    incremental={"input": "raw_orders", "column": "updated_at", "lookback": "2h"},
    write={
        "strategy": "merge",
        "unique_key": ["id"],
        "update_condition": "source.updated_at > target.updated_at",
        "deletes": {"column": "status", "value": "cancelled", "mode": "hard"},
    },
)
def orders(raw_orders):
    return raw_orders
  • update_condition is optional and written in the engine's dialect (a SQL expression on polars, a restricted Python expression on pandas). source.x is the batch, target.x the table, and a bare name means the source. A matched row whose condition is false or null is left unchanged.
  • deletes marks batch rows as deletions: a row where column equals value removes the matched target row with mode: hard, or writes the batch row with mode: soft so you can keep a flag. A delete for a key that is not in the table is ignored. The update_condition applies to deletes too.
  • A batch with a repeated key, or without the key column, fails with PLM206 before anything is written. A row with a null key never matches and is inserted.
  • run_results.json reports rows_inserted, rows_updated and rows_deleted; rows_written counts inserts, updates and soft deletes.

In 0.3 a merge reads the whole table, merges in memory and rewrites it, so its cost grows with the table. Row order is not preserved.

docs.title: replace_partitions
docs.text:
replace_partitions swaps the partitions present in the batch and leaves the others alone. It needs partition_by; without it pipeloom validate reports PLP407.

@model(
    partition_by=["event_date"],
    write={"strategy": "replace_partitions", "on_schema_change": "append_new_columns"},
)
def daily_clicks(ctx, raw_events):
    return ctx.sql("select event_date, user_id, clicks from raw_events")

With partition_by every strategy writes one part file per distinct partition value. A replace_partitions write drops the files of the partitions in the batch and adds the new ones without reading the other files. rows_deleted reports how many old rows went away. A table written by 0.2 has no partition values in its files, so the first replace reads and rewrites those files once. An empty batch changes no files. A null is a partition value like any other.

docs.title: scd2
docs.text:
scd2 keeps the history of each key as a type 2 slowly changing dimension. The table holds the model's columns followed by three system columns: valid_from and valid_to (timestamp[us, UTC]) and is_current (boolean).

@model(
    write={
        "strategy": "scd2",
        "unique_key": ["id"],
        "tracked_columns": ["name", "tier"],
        "deletes": {"column": "status", "value": "closed", "mode": "hard"},
    },
)
def customers_history(ctx, raw_customers):
    return ctx.sql("select id, name, tier, status from raw_customers")

The same settings can live in the model's properties entry under config:, as block YAML.

  • The first load, and every --full-refresh, writes each batch row as the current version and drops any earlier history.
  • On later runs a batch row for a new key opens a version. A row whose tracked columns differ from the key's current version closes that version and opens a new one. Tracked columns are compared null-safely, and NaN counts as null. A change in any other column is ignored.
  • tracked_columns defaults to every column except unique_key and the delete column. An empty list or a key column in the list is PLP416, and so is a system column named in unique_key, tracked_columns, partition_by, cluster_by, deletes.column or the model's columns.
  • Versions open and close at the run's start time, the same on every retry of the run, so a rerun with an unchanged batch adds no version.
  • deletes supports mode: hard only (soft is PLP416). A delete row closes the key's current version without opening a new one; a delete for an unknown key is ignored, and a key that comes back later opens a new version. Keys missing from the batch stay current.
  • A null or repeated key in the batch, or a batch column named like a system column, fails with PLM206 before anything is written.
  • run_results.json reports rows_inserted (versions opened), rows_updated (versions closed by a change) and rows_deleted (versions closed by a delete); rows_written is their sum.

The schema policy applies to the model's columns only; old versions read a new column as null. A target without the system columns fails with PLM206 until you run with --full-refresh. On filesystem tables an scd2 write rewrites the whole table like a merge; on Spark it is one Delta MERGE INTO. The memory engine does not support scd2 (PLC501).

docs.title: Schema changes
docs.text:
write.on_schema_change says what happens when the batch's columns differ from the target's. The default is fail.

Policy Result fail Any added, removed or retyped column is PLM202. ignore The table keeps its columns. Extra batch columns are dropped, missing ones are filled with nulls, values are cast to the table's types (a failed cast is PLM201). append_new_columns The table's columns plus the new ones, which are nullable. Removed columns stay. A type change is PLM202. sync_all_columns The batch's columns. A type change is accepted only if it widens.

Widening means a wider integer, an integer to float64, float32 to float64, a decimal that keeps every digit, a finer timestamp unit in the same zone, or a null column to any type. A batch that differs from the table only by such a widening of the table's type is cast to the table's type under every policy.

The policy applies to append, merge, replace_partitions and scd2 on an existing table. overwrite, --full-refresh and the first build use the batch's schema, and report the difference with the action replaced.

With fail, adding a column to the model fails like this:

FAIL   daily_clicks ... PLM202
  schema change rejected for model 'daily_clicks' (on_schema_change: fail): the batch schema
  differs from the target: added extra (int32)
  hint: change the model, or set write.on_schema_change to ignore, append_new_columns or sync_all_columns

With append_new_columns the same run succeeds and prints one line:

daily_clicks: schema changed on main.daily_clicks (policy append_new_columns, applied): +device string

Each change is an event model.schema_changed (relation, policy, action and the list of changes), and schema_changes[] of the unit in run_results.json carries the same diff. The filesystem catalog reads every old file through the table's current schema, so adding a column or widening a type never rewrites existing files. A key column (unique_key or partition_by) missing from the batch is PLM206, whatever the policy.

docs.title: Safe concurrent writes
docs.text: A filesystem table commit takes a lock file with a 30 second lease and checks that nobody committed since the table was read. If another writer got in first, the second fails with a transient error and can be rerun from the new version. Do not run two writers on one table on purpose; the run lock exists to prevent it.

docs.title: Airflow
docs.text:
pipeloom-airflow turns a compiled plan into an Apache Airflow 3 DAG (or a task group inside one): one Airflow task per execution unit, plus a finalize task that closes the pipeloom run. Four execution modes are supported: local, virtualenv, kubernetes and databricks. The design is in architecture section 13 and ADR-0037 to ADR-0039. For another orchestrator, the same per-unit protocol is described in Orchestrator protocol.

from datetime import datetime

from pipeloom_airflow.config import ExecutionConfig, ExecutionMode, ProjectConfig, RenderConfig
from pipeloom_airflow.dag import PipeloomDag

shop = PipeloomDag(
    dag_id="shop_daily",
    schedule="@daily",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    project_config=ProjectConfig(
        project_dir="/opt/pipelines/shop",
        manifest_path="/opt/pipelines/shop/target/manifest.json",
    ),
    target="prod",
    render_config=RenderConfig(select=("tag:daily",), group_by="folder", emit_assets=True),
    execution_config=ExecutionConfig(mode=ExecutionMode.LOCAL),
)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Airflow is not a hard dependency. The extras pull what each mode needs:

Extra Adds airflow apache-airflow>=3.2,<4 kubernetes the above and apache-airflow-providers-cncf-kubernetes>=10.25,<11 databricks the first and pipeloom-databricks (not the Databricks Airflow provider)

Install Airflow the way its project recommends, with a constraint file for your Airflow and Python versions, so the resolver does not pick versions Airflow was never tested with:

$ AIRFLOW_VERSION=3.4.0
$ PYTHON_VERSION=3.12
$ pip install "pipeloom-airflow[airflow]" \
    --constraint "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apache/airflow/constraints-${AIRFLOW_VERSION}/constraints-${PYTHON_VERSION}.txt"

Tested range: Airflow 3.2.2 (the floor), the 3.3 line and 3.4.0, which is the version the lock pins. The floor is Airflow 3.2, the first release with Python 3.14 support. An older or missing Airflow is reported as PLA005 when the DAG file is parsed, never as an ImportError. Installing the plugin also needs the engine plugins your project uses (pipeloom[polars] and so on) on every machine that runs a unit.

In DATABRICKS mode the triggerer must have pipeloom-airflow[databricks] installed too, since the trigger code runs there. The workers that run the launch task need the project files and pipeloom-databricks.

Importing pipeloom_airflow imports nothing from Airflow. The DAG classes live in pipeloom_airflow.dag and the configs in pipeloom_airflow.config.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Three frozen dataclasses describe a DAG. Paths are strings and must be absolute; they are never touched at parse time unless a load method reads them.

ProjectConfig says where the DAG file reads the project.

Field Default Meaning project_dir required Project directory as the parser sees it. manifest_path None Stable manifest. Required by the manifest load method. vars {} Project variables, passed to every unit as --vars JSON. cache_dir None Compile cache of the project load method.

RenderConfig shapes the task graph.

Field Default Meaning load_method LoadMode.MANIFEST MANIFEST or PROJECT, see below. select, exclude () Selectors applied to the plan. A selection that renders no unit is PLA003. group_by "none" none, folder or tag: visual task groups only. Every unit is still one task. Has no effect in DATABRICKS mode. emit_assets False Each model task declares an Asset outlet. asset_uri pipeloom://{project}/{target}/{relation} Template; placeholders project, target, model, relation, unique_id. Values are percent-encoded.

ExecutionConfig says how and where units run.

Field Default Meaning mode ExecutionMode.LOCAL LOCAL, VIRTUALENV, KUBERNETES, DATABRICKS, WATCHER. DOCKER is PLA001. project_dir, manifest_path those of ProjectConfig Where units execute, when that differs from where the DAG is parsed (a pod, for example). virtualenv_dir None Required by VIRTUALENV: a virtualenv created on every worker. kubernetes None Required by KUBERNETES: KubernetesConfig(image, namespace=None, python="python", pod_kwargs={}). env {} Extra environment for the unit process, or the pod environment. databricks_conn_id "databricks_default" Airflow connection of the workspace. databricks_pipeline "main" Which deploy pipeline to run. databricks_ensure_job False Deploy the job from the project when it is missing or stale. databricks_poll "per_task" per_task or shared, see Poll modes. databricks_poll_interval 30.0 Seconds between polls. databricks_timeout 86400.0 Seconds any single wait on the job run may last. watcher_workers None WATCHER: --workers of the producer's run. None keeps the target's. watcher_poll_interval 10.0 WATCHER: seconds between reads of a unit's files. watcher_timeout 86400.0 WATCHER: the producer's execution timeout and each watcher's deadline for one try. watcher_artifacts_root None WATCHER: absolute path that replaces the artifacts root read from pipeloom.yml.

PipeloomDag takes project_config, target, render_config, execution_config, an optional operator_args mapping that goes to every operator, and the usual DAG keywords. PipeloomTaskGroup(group_id, ...) takes the same configs inside an existing DAG. A configuration error raises PipeloomAirflowError, which Airflow shows as the DAG file's import error; warnings go to the pipeloom_airflow logger. operator_args may not set task_id, retries, retry_delay, trigger_rule, outlets, execution_timeout or deferrable, nor (in DATABRICKS mode) the arguments the pipeloom operators set themselves; that is PLA002.

docs.title: Load methods
docs.text:
• MANIFEST (recommended) reads a stable manifest written by pipeloom compile --stable. Parsing reads one JSON file, imports no engine and runs no user code. The manifest must be for the same target (PLX107).
  • PROJECT discovers the models on the parse path (ADR-0050): an AST pass resolves static @model decorators without importing, and only modules whose decorators have dynamic arguments are imported. The result is cached on disk, keyed by a hash of the installed pipeloom versions, the target, the variables and the path, size and modification time of pipeloom.yml and every file under model_paths and python_paths. An entry also stores a fingerprint of the environment variables the plan read, so a secret never lands on disk, and a hit needs the same fingerprints. The default directory is pipeloom-airflow-cache under the system temporary directory; the 8 newest entries per project are kept. A cache that cannot be written is PLA006: the project still compiles, only slower.

Airflow 3 parses the DAG file before every task, so a PROJECT cache miss costs a compile at task start-up. Each unit still compiles and checks the plan hash itself, so no worker-local cache path crosses a process boundary. Prefer MANIFEST for large projects.

docs.title: Execution modes
docs.text:
Mode A unit runs as Needs LOCAL python -m pipeloom run in a child process group of the worker, with the worker's interpreter pipeloom and the engine installed where the worker runs VIRTUALENV the same, with the interpreter of virtualenv_dir the virtualenv on every worker (a missing interpreter fails the task without retry, PLA002) KUBERNETES a pod from KubernetesPodOperator an image with pipeloom; see below DATABRICKS a task of the Databricks job that pipeloom-databricks renders see below WATCHER one pipeloom run for the whole selection, reported by one deferrable watcher per unit pipeloom on the worker and the triggerer, one artifacts root shared with both; see below

In LOCAL and VIRTUALENV, killing the task sends SIGTERM to the child's process group and SIGKILL after the cancel grace. The grace is the core default of 30 seconds, not the target's cancel_grace, because the manifest does not carry that setting. Child events are logged line by line to the task log.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: image, namespace and pod_kwargs go to KubernetesPodOperator: volumes, mounts, resources, service account. ExecutionConfig.env becomes the pod environment, and the cancel grace (the core default of 30 seconds, not the target's cancel_grace) the pod termination grace period. project_dir and manifest_path of the execution config are paths inside the pod. Pods are never deferrable and push no XCom; the keys cmds, arguments, image, name, do_xcom_push and deferrable in pod_kwargs are PLA002.

docs.title: Databricks
docs.text: The DAG has pipeloom_launch, one sensor per Databricks task key (with the plan's edges) and a pipeloom_finalize sensor on the job's finalize task. The launch compiles the project on the worker, checks its plan hash against the DAG's (PLX103), and starts the job run named after the DAG run. A missing job is PLD007 and a job deployed from other settings is PLD008, unless databricks_ensure_job=True deploys it. A retried or cleared launch finds the same run: it attaches to it, or repairs it when a task failed. Databricks owns the task retries.

docs.title: Watcher
docs.text:
LOCAL starts one Python process per unit. On a wide DAG of short models that start-up dominates. WATCHER runs the whole selection once and keeps one Airflow task per model for its state, retries, logs and asset events.

execution_config=ExecutionConfig(
    mode=ExecutionMode.WATCHER,
    watcher_workers=4,
    watcher_poll_interval=10.0,
)

The DAG has a root task pipeloom_run (the producer), one watcher per unit and pipeloom_finalize. The producer has no edge to the watchers. Watchers follow the plan's edges, so a failed unit leaves its descendants upstream_failed. Finalize runs after the producer and every leaf. virtualenv_dir is optional, as in VIRTUALENV.

  • The producer runs python -m pipeloom run with the rendered selection (--select name:* when it is empty), the plan hash, the run id and --workers when watcher_workers is set. Exit 0 or 1 is a success for the producer: the results belong to the watchers, and finalize fails the DAG run when the pipeloom run failed. Exit 2 or 130 fails it. Once the child exits, the producer checks that runs/<run id>/run_results.json is visible under the artifacts root, and raises PLA008 if it is not. A producer try above 1 is skipped, so it runs once per DAG run.
  • Each watcher defers on a trigger that only reads the unit's attempt files. It succeeds when the latest attempt succeeded, and fails (without Airflow retry) when the attempt failed and the unit's retries and retry_on allow no more, or timed out, or was cancelled. If the producer ended and left no run results, the watcher raises PLA009 after a short grace, and a retry runs again.
  • The watcher's log shows the attempt summary and the last 200 lines of the unit's log, or the error code, message and trace excerpt. A unit has a log of its own only with boundary: task; otherwise the watcher says that the unit's output is in the producer task's log.
  • To rerun a unit, clear its failed watcher with Downstream. At try 2 or later, when the producer is no longer running the unit, the watcher runs the unit itself (same run id, one attempt), and the cleared descendants follow. Finalize then merges the new attempt.
  • The watchers have no execution_timeout. watcher_timeout bounds one try, and a watcher that waits longer raises an Airflow exception and retries.
  • The artifacts root is read at parse time from <project_dir>/pipeloom.yml as plain YAML: targets.<target>.artifacts replaces the top-level block, root falls back to target, and a relative root joins the execution project_dir. An unreadable file, or a ${...} reference in the root, is PLA008 unless watcher_artifacts_root is set. The project is not bound in the worker for this.
  • PLA002 covers watcher_workers below 1, a non-positive interval or timeout, and a selection made only of unit: selectors. PLA007 is not reported.
  • Limit: a producer worker that dies can leave its child running, so PLA009 and a watcher retry may run a unit twice. A retry after a watch timeout can rerun a unit the producer finished meanwhile.

docs.title: Artifact store
docs.text:
All units of a run and the finalize task must see one artifacts.root directory: unit result files are how the finalize task learns what happened. pipeloom 0.6 supports a shared POSIX path only; URI stores such as fsspec are not supported, because create-once files and atomic replace are not portable across their backends. State stores and filesystem catalogs need shared storage anyway.

Setup What artifacts.root can be LocalExecutor Any local path. CeleryExecutor A network mount at the same path on every worker: NFS, EFS or SMB. Kubernetes pods A ReadWriteMany persistent volume claim, or a CSI object-store mount, given in pod_kwargs as volumes and volume_mounts. Databricks Not an Airflow concern: the units run inside the job, which has its own artifact location.

A unit task that Airflow saw succeed, with no attempt file visible under the root, fails the run with PLA004. That is the sign of a root that is not shared. PLA007 warns when the target's boundary is not task, since each unit runs in its own process.

In WATCHER mode the triggerer reads the unit files too. It needs pipeloom-airflow installed and the artifacts root mounted at the same path as on the workers. On NFS, a stale directory listing can hide a fresh attempt file, so the watcher also opens attempt-1 up to attempt-<retries + 1> by name and treats partial JSON as not visible. Mount with lookupcache=positive and a low acdirmax (a few seconds) to keep the delay short. A file still hidden after the grace of 120 seconds is PLA004.

docs.title: Run id
docs.text: All tasks of a DAG run share one pipeloom run id: af- plus the first 16 hex characters of the sha256 of dag_id, the Airflow run_id and, inside a PipeloomTaskGroup, the group id, joined by a NUL byte. Joining with NUL keeps two different inputs from hashing alike, and the group id keeps two groups of one DAG run apart. The id is stable across task retries, so a retry or a clear and rerun continues the same pipeloom run and increments the unit's attempt. Each unit also records the DAG id, run id, task id and try number as orchestrator ids.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
Mode Who retries Rule LOCAL, VIRTUALENV Airflow The model's retries and retry_delay become the task's. A unit invocation never retries by itself. Exit 2 fails without retry. Exit 130 retries. Exit 1 fails without retry when the unit's error is permanent and retry_on is transient; otherwise it retries. KUBERNETES Airflow The same counts and delay. retry_on is not enforced: Airflow sees only the pod's result, so every failure retries. DATABRICKS Databricks Sensors have no retries. A sensor fails once the task's last attempt failed or the run is over. The launch retries twice and attaches to the same run. WATCHER The core scheduler, then Airflow The producer has retries=0 and the core applies the model's retries inside the one run. A watcher gets the model's retries and retry_delay: a failure the producer already reported fails it without retry, while PLA004, PLA009 and a watch timeout retry. A rerun at try 2 or later maps exit codes as LOCAL does.

The task execution timeout is the model timeout plus the cancel grace plus 300 seconds, so the core times a unit out before Airflow does. The grace here is the core default of 30 seconds, since the manifest does not carry the target's cancel_grace.

docs.title: full_refresh
docs.text: PipeloomDag adds the boolean param full_refresh (default false) unless you define it. Trigger the DAG with full_refresh set to true to run every incremental model as a full refresh. A value that is not a boolean is PLA002 at run time. Task groups read the param of the enclosing DAG and use false when it is missing.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text: With emit_assets=True, each model task (in WATCHER mode, each watcher) declares Asset(name=uri, uri=uri) outlets, one per persisted model of the task. The URI comes from asset_uri. In DATABRICKS mode the sensor of a task carries them.

docs.title: Finalize and DAG failure
docs.text:
pipeloom_finalize runs with trigger rule all_done after every leaf task. In LOCAL, VIRTUALENV and KUBERNETES it has one retry; in DATABRICKS it is a sensor with no retries. In LOCAL and VIRTUALENV it reads the states of the unit tasks from Airflow and passes them to pipeloom finalize --unit-states. An attempt file always wins. Without one, a task that succeeded or failed becomes a failed unit with PLA004, upstream_failed becomes skipped, and a skipped task becomes skipped with not_run. The finalize task merges the unit files into run_results.json and fails the DAG run when the pipeloom run failed (exit 1, no retry).

In KUBERNETES the finalize pod gets the states inline (--unit-states-json). In DATABRICKS the finalize task of the job does the merge and the pipeloom_finalize sensor mirrors its result.

docs.title: Databricks connection
docs.text:
The Airflow connection named by databricks_conn_id is read by pipeloom itself; the Databricks Airflow provider is not used, so an existing databricks_default connection works.

Field Meaning Host Workspace URL. https:// is added when missing. Password Personal access token. extra.token works as well. Extra service_principal_oauth When true, OAuth machine-to-machine: login is the client id and password its secret.

No profile, ~/.databrickscfg or DATABRICKS_* variable is read, so a worker's environment cannot change the authentication. A connection that cannot be used (no host, no token, Azure-only extras) is PLD010; the message names the connection id and never a value. Secrets are masked in task logs and a trigger serializes only the connection id.

docs.title: Poll modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior API cost per_task (default) The launch returns right after run-now or repair. Each sensor makes one get_run call and, with no verdict yet, defers on its own trigger. One call per waiting sensor per interval. shared The launch defers on one trigger that polls the whole run. Sensors read its final snapshot and make no call. One call per interval in total, but a task's result shows only when the whole run is over.

The trigger retries a transient API error (429, 5xx, no answer) up to 5 times in a row, with sleeps of one, two and then four intervals, and fails the task at once on any other API error (an authentication error, for example) or when the retries run out. The same holds for a sensor's first call, except that a transient error there defers instead of failing the task. After a repair, a sensor with no verdict yet waits until the run reports the repair, so it never decides on the failed run from before the repair. Every deferral stops after databricks_timeout (24 hours by default). A wide DAG should raise databricks_poll_interval or use shared.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Airflow does not run on Windows, so neither do the DAG classes. The pure modules (configs, rendering, ids) do.
  • No DOCKER mode: it is PLA001.
  • No deferrable pods. deferrable is PLA002 for the Kubernetes mode.
  • retry_on is enforced only in LOCAL and VIRTUALENV.
  • group_by has no effect in DATABRICKS mode.
  • The cancel grace of a unit is the core default (30 seconds), not the target's cancel_grace.
  • The artifact root must be shared (see above). There is no fsspec store.
  • The finalize pod takes the unit states inline, capped at 120 KiB because one Linux exec argument is limited to 128 KiB. Above that it fails with PLA002; split the project with select.
  • A DATABRICKS-mode DAG needs the project files on the worker that runs the launch, and each wait is bounded by databricks_timeout.
  • On Airflow 3.2, dag.test() fails in the finalize task and in WATCHER sensors: they read task states through the Task SDK, and the in-process Execution API that dag.test() starts on 3.2 answers that call with a server error. A real deployment on 3.2 is not affected, and dag.test() works from Airflow 3.3.0.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
PLA001 unsupported mode or missing extra, PLA002 invalid configuration, PLA003 the selection renders no unit, PLA004 a task ended without a unit result, PLA005 unsupported Airflow version, PLA006 the compile cache is unusable, PLA007 the target boundary is not task, PLA008 the WATCHER artifacts root is not resolved or the producer's run left no run_results.json under it, PLA009 the WATCHER producer ended without run results. See the error code reference.

LOCAL, VIRTUALENV and KUBERNETES modes: one Airflow task per unit. Source: airflow-task-per-unit.d2. DATABRICKS mode: launch, mirror sensors, finalize; repair stays in Databricks. Source: airflow-databricks.d2. WATCHER mode: one producer, one watcher per unit. Source: airflow-watcher.d2.

docs.title: Databricks plugin
docs.text:
pipeloom-databricks deploys a compiled plan as a Databricks job and runs, repairs and finalizes it from the command line. It also adds a Unity Catalog catalog and a Databricks secret provider. The design is in ADR-0035 and ADR-0036; section 12 of the architecture has the overview.

One plan, one Databricks job. Source: databricks.d2.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
$ pip install "pipeloom[databricks]"       # on your machine, to deploy and run

The extra pulls pipeloom-databricks, pipeloom-spark and databricks-sdk (0.50 up to, not including, 1.0). On a Databricks cluster or serverless environment, install pipeloom-spark without extras: the runtime ships its own pyspark, and a second copy breaks it. The job's own environment installs pinned versions of the pipeloom distributions for you (see Compute).

docs.title: Connection rules
docs.text:
Commands that talk to a workspace pick the connection in this order, and never guess:

  1. --profile NAME, an option of the pipeloom databricks group.
  2. A profile you set yourself in DATABRICKS_CONFIG_PROFILE.
  3. DATABRICKS_HOST with DATABRICKS_TOKEN, or with DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET.
  4. Runtime authentication, when DATABRICKS_RUNTIME_VERSION is set (inside a Databricks task).
  5. Otherwise PLD010.

pipeloom never selects the DEFAULT profile of ~/.databrickscfg, and without a profile the SDK is told that no config file exists. The group option comes before the command:

$ pipeloom databricks --profile prod-workspace deploy --target prod

deploy --dry-run and bundle connect to nothing.

docs.title: The deploy block
docs.text:
A target gets a deploy block of kind databricks. It needs a shared state store (for example table) and an absolute artifacts.root on a volume, because the tasks of one run share both.

targets:
  prod:
    engine:
      kind: spark
    catalog:
      kind: unity
      catalog: main
    state:
      kind: table
      table: ops._pipeloom_state
    artifacts:
      root: /Volumes/main/ops/pipeloom
    deploy:
      kind: databricks
      pipelines:
        main: {}
        daily:
          select: ["tag:daily"]
      compute:
        default:
          kind: serverless
          environment_version: "5"
        big:
          kind: job_cluster
          new_cluster:
            spark_version: "16.4.x-scala2.12"
            node_type_id: "Standard_D8ds_v5"
            num_workers: 4
      compute_rules:
        - select: ["tag:heavy"]
          compute: big
      task_grouping: none
      settings:
        schedule:
          quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 * * ?"
          timezone_id: "UTC"
Key Meaning pipelines One job per entry. select and exclude take selectors; empty means the whole plan. Default: one pipeline main. compute Named computes: serverless or job_cluster. default_compute The compute no rule matches (default default). compute_rules Selector rules; the first rule that matches a model wins. task_grouping none, by_tag or by_folder. workspace_root Where a direct deploy uploads the project. Default /Workspace/Users/<you>/.pipeloom. settings Job settings passed through (schedule, notifications, run_as, tags, ...).

A job is named pipeloom_<project>_<pipeline>_<target>. Rendering is pure and byte-for-byte deterministic, so a rendered job can be reviewed and diffed. A pipeline job runs only its own units: an upstream model in another pipeline is read from its persisted output, so schedule that pipeline first.

settings cannot set what pipeloom owns: tasks, job_clusters, environments, parameters, max_concurrent_runs, queue, format, git_source, deployment, name, or a tag that starts with pipeloom_. A ${secret:...} reference in the block is refused. All of these are PLD004.

docs.title: Compute and compute rules
docs.text:
A serverless compute becomes one job environment named pipeloom_<compute>. Its environment_version is a string from 2 to 6 (default "5", Python 3.12); version 1 runs Python 3.10, below the floor, and is PLD004. A job holds at most 10 environments.

dependencies lists pip requirements. Unset, the environment installs pinned distributions: pipeloom, pipeloom-databricks and every plugin in the plan, as name==version, sorted. Set it to install from somewhere else, for example wheels on a volume. A job_cluster compute becomes a shared job cluster, with libraries defaulting to the same pins from PyPI.

compute_rules choose the compute per model. A rule with no matching model is the warning PLD005. All models of one task group must resolve to the same compute (PLD004).

Each model keeps its own retries, retry_delay and timeout: they become max_retries, the retry interval and timeout_seconds (the model timeout plus the cancel grace plus 300 seconds). Databricks retries any failure, so retry_on: transient cannot be enforced there. Serverless tasks are rendered with disable_auto_optimization: true: serverless auto-optimization would otherwise retry a failed task on top of max_retries, so a model with retries: 0 would still run twice.

docs.title: Task grouping
docs.text: With task_grouping: none every unit is one task, named by its unit id. by_tag groups models by their first tag (tag_<tag>, or tag_untagged) and by_folder by the folder of the model module (dir_<folder>, or dir_root). Grouping applies whenever it is set, so the job's shape does not change when the project grows. A group runs its models with the in-process scheduler. Groups that wait on each other in a cycle are PLD003. Task keys are sanitized to [A-Za-z0-9_-]; a key above 100 characters, or one that collides, gets a short hash suffix.

docs.title: Bundle and direct deploy
docs.text:
Two ways to create the same job.

Bundle. pipeloom databricks bundle --target prod --out resources writes one job file and one stable manifest per pipeline into a Declarative Automation Bundle. The output folder must lie inside the bundle, next to databricks.yml, and the job files must be in its include. Paths use ${workspace.file_path}. --check writes nothing and exits 1 when a file is stale. Running databricks bundle deploy stays your step.

Databricks CLI versions. The generated job files use only Jobs API fields, which both the Terraform and the direct deployment engine accept. They were checked with databricks bundle validate on CLI 1.18.0, with no unknown-field warning. CLI 1.20.0 removed the Terraform engine, so a bundle that sets bundle.engine: terraform fails there; remove the setting or pin CLI 1.19. pipeloom does not set a CLI floor. To require one, set bundle.databricks_cli_version in your own databricks.yml; an included file overrides the root's value, which is why pipeloom writes none. pipeloom never runs the CLI: deploy, run and repair use the Databricks SDK, so it has no CLI version check.

Direct deploy. pipeloom databricks deploy --target prod uploads the project and creates or resets one job per pipeline. The job is found by its pipeloom_job tag (two matches are PLD006). The upload is content addressed, under <workspace_root>/<project>/<pipeline>/<target>/<hash>, and holds pipeloom.yml, the properties files, the model modules and the *.py files below python_paths. Modules found through model_packages are not uploaded: install those packages in the job environment. Other files below python_paths are not uploaded, so a Python model that reads a file next to it works locally and not on Databricks; keep such data in a table or a volume. Notebooks and files above 10 MB are refused (PLD012). When the settings hash tag already matches, deploy changes nothing. reset overwrites edits made in the Databricks UI; use settings instead. --dry-run prints the settings as JSON and connects to nothing.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
$ pipeloom databricks run --target prod --pipeline daily

run starts the deployed job with run-now. A missing job is PLD007, and a job whose settings differ from what the project renders now is PLD008, unless you pass --ensure, which deploys first. The command prints one JSON line with the job id, the job run id, the run id and the run page URL.

  • --select and --exclude choose units. Their tasks plus finalize run (only); the others are excluded. A group that is partly selected runs whole, with the warning PLD015. A selection that matches nothing is exit 2.
  • --run-id RID names the run and makes the start idempotent. Without it the run id is dbx-<job run id>. --full-refresh is passed to the tasks.
  • --ephemeral uploads the project and submits a one-time run with no saved job. It is for development: serverless compute only, and the same 1,000-task limit.
  • --wait (the default) polls every 15 seconds, prints task transitions, then lists the failed units from run_results.json and exits 1 unless the run succeeded. --no-wait returns after the start. --timeout SECONDS (default 24 hours) stops the wait with exit 1; the run keeps going.

docs.title: Repair
docs.text:
$ pipeloom databricks repair --target prod --pipeline daily --run-id RID

Name the run with --run-id (the pipeloom id) or --job-run-id (the Databricks id), exactly one. Repair reruns the tasks that failed, timed out, were cancelled or were skipped, plus finalize. The run keeps its run id, and each rerun unit writes the next attempt: the repair passes the run's job parameters again, since without them {{job.parameters.pipeloom_run_id}} would resolve to its empty default and start a new pipeloom run. A run that is still active is PLD014. With nothing to repair the command says so and exits 0. --wait, --no-wait and --timeout work as in run.

docs.title: Finalize and task states
docs.text:
Every job ends with the task pipeloom__finalize. It depends on every leaf task, runs with run_if: ALL_DONE, and calls pipeloom finalize, which merges the unit files into run_results.json and closes the run.

A task that dies, times out or is cancelled can leave no attempt file. Finalize therefore reads how each task ended from the Jobs API and hands core the state of every unit without an attempt:

Task state Unit state EXCLUDED, DISABLED excluded (no row); serverless reports a task left out by only as DISABLED UPSTREAM_FAILED, UPSTREAM_CANCELED skipped, reason upstream_failed CANCELED, TIMEDOUT cancelled FAILED failed, with PLD011 and the termination message

If the API cannot be read, finalize prints one warning and judges by the attempt files; units with neither get not_run, which does not fail the run. A job run's result comes from its leaf tasks, so a succeeding finalize would hide a failure: finalize exits 1 when the run failed. A one-time run has no job run id in its parameters, so it gets no task states.

docs.title: Task values
docs.text: After a unit task, the wrapper sets the task value pipeloom: the run id, the run status and, per unit, status, attempt, rows written, duration, target version, error code and warning count. Values above 32,768 bytes lose units from the end and carry truncated: true; Databricks caps a value at 48 KiB. Task values are documented for notebooks only, so setting one is best effort: a failure prints one line on stderr and never changes the exit code.

docs.title: Secrets provider
docs.text: ${secret:databricks/<scope>/<key>} in plugin options reads a Databricks secret scope at run time, with the connection rules above (no profile is chosen, so it works inside a job). The value is masked like any resolved secret. A bad path, a missing connection or an API error is PLX109, naming the path and never the value.

docs.title: Unity Catalog
docs.text: A catalog block with kind: unity and catalog: main works with the Spark engine only. Tables and views are addressed as `catalog`.`schema`.`name`; the option fills in the catalog when the target's naming leaves it empty. A model's catalog setting (or a folder's +catalog in the models: tree) wins over both, so each layer can write to its own catalog. pipeloom never creates a catalog: every catalog a model names must exist, and the principal needs USE CATALOG on it. A schema is created only when it does not exist yet, so a principal without CREATE SCHEMA can write to an existing one.

docs.title: Limits and unconfirmed facts
docs.text:
• A job has at most 1,000 tasks, finalize included (PLD001; set task_grouping or split the pipelines). runs/submit shares the limit, so PLD002 stays reserved and is never emitted.
  • A task value is at most 48 KiB; pipeloom stays under 32 KiB.
  • Tasks run the plugin wrapper pipeloom_databricks_task, a python_wheel_task entry point, in the task's own process, so an existing Spark session is reused. When none is active on a Databricks runtime, the Spark engine attaches with builder.getOrCreate() and no conf.
  • An unresolved {{...}} in a task parameter stops the task with PLD013.

Some behaviors cannot be confirmed from public documentation, so the code guards them and a manually dispatched workflow, databricks-live, checks them against a real workspace (see CONTRIBUTING). It passed all its checks on serverless environment version 5 on 2026-11-05 (pipeloom 0.6.1). Until it has passed for your runtime, treat these as unconfirmed:

  • dynamic value references such as {{job.run_id}} inside wheel task parameters;
  • an empty parameter default resolving to dbx-<job run id>;
  • only with an ALL_DONE finalize whose dependencies are excluded;
  • disable_auto_optimization stopping the serverless automatic retry, in a job and in a one-time run (--ephemeral);
  • os.link and os.replace on /Volumes (attempt files fall back to an exclusive open);
  • a Spark session being available in a wheel task;
  • task values set from a wheel task (not checked by the workflow today);
  • workspace import format AUTO keeping a plain .py or .yml as a file.

docs.title: DuckDB engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-duckdb runs models on DuckDB: SQL in process, with tables in a DuckDB database file (ADR-0051).

$ pip install "pipeloom[duckdb]"

targets:
  dev:
    engine:
      kind: duckdb
      extension_directory: .duckdb/extensions
    catalog:
      kind: duckdb
      path: target/warehouse.duckdb
    state:
      kind: json
      path: .pipeloom/state

The engine needs the duckdb catalog. path is the database file that holds tables without a catalog (default target/pipeloom.duckdb), or :memory:. A model catalog (+catalog in the models: tree) is the file <catalog>.duckdb next to it, attached under that name, so pipeloom_gold.tpch.top_customers lives in target/pipeloom_gold.duckdb. Pair the engine with the json or sqlite state store.

One process writes a database file at a time, so units run on threads (boundary: process).

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Capability Value Source formats parquet, csv, delta (read only) Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions, scd2 Materializations table, incremental, view, ephemeral, intermediate Expectations and quarantine yes (expr in DuckDB SQL) SQL models and views yes, sql_dialect: duckdb Idempotent writes yes, by run token Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes Cancel yes

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Engine:

Option Default Meaning extension_directory DuckDB's default Where extensions are installed and loaded from, relative to the project. extensions [] Extensions to load when the session opens. delta loads on the first Delta read. install_extensions false Install a missing extension from the network into extension_directory. config {} DuckDB configuration for the connection, for example threads or memory_limit.

Catalog: path, as above.

docs.title: Frames and SQL
docs.text: Relations are DuckDBPyRelations on the session's connection. A Python model receives relations and returns one; with frame_api: narwhals it receives Narwhals frames. ctx.sql runs DuckDB SQL, where each input is a CTE named after its alias. A query written for another engine declares sql_dialect and is translated (needs pipeloom[sqlglot]). A view is a DuckDB view, so it sees later writes of its inputs.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text: A write stages the batch in a temporary table, then runs one transaction that changes the table and records the run token, so a failure leaves the table as it was and a repeated token writes nothing. merge is a MERGE INTO keyed on unique_key (a null key never matches); update_condition is DuckDB SQL over source and target. scd2 closes changed and deleted current rows at the run start and inserts the new versions. replace_partitions deletes every partition the batch holds, null included, then inserts the batch. Bytes written are not reported.

docs.title: Extensions offline
docs.text:
The engine never downloads an extension on its own: DuckDB's automatic install is off, and install_extensions defaults to false. Pin extension_directory in the project and fill it once on a machine with network access, for example with a run that sets install_extensions: true, or in CI:

$ python -c "import duckdb; duckdb.connect(config={'extension_directory': '.duckdb/extensions'}).install_extension('delta')"

A missing extension fails the read or write that needs it with PLX121 in the error message.

docs.title: Delta
docs.text: format: delta reads a Delta table through delta_scan. Writes to Delta are not supported. CI runs a Delta read test on Linux, macOS and Windows with the extension preinstalled.

docs.title: pandas engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-pandas runs models on pandas DataFrames.

$ pip install "pipeloom[pandas]"

targets:
  dev:
    engine:
      kind: pandas
    catalog:
      kind: filesystem
      root: warehouse
    state:
      kind: json
      path: .pipeloom/state

The engine needs the filesystem catalog: tables are directories of part files committed through _pipeloom/commit.json (ADR-0022). Any other catalog is rejected when the session opens.

A model can set catalog (and a +catalog key in the models: tree can set it for a layer). The catalog becomes a leading directory: <root>/<catalog>/<schema>/<name>/. A table with no catalog keeps <root>/<schema>/<name>/.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Value Source formats parquet, csv, json, ndjson Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions Materializations table, incremental, ephemeral Expectations and quarantine yes (expr limited to column names, literals and operators) SQL models and views no Idempotent writes yes, by run token Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes Cancel no

A model that calls ctx.sql gets a PLK606 warning at validate and fails at run time with PLX101; a view is rejected with PLC507. An intermediate materialization is supported (files under the artifacts root). incremental is supported. SQL on pandas is deferred past 0.2. The supported versions are pandas>=2.3.3,<4 and pyarrow>=22.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Relations are eager DataFrames, so rows_read is filled in run_results.json. A Python model receives DataFrame inputs and returns a DataFrame. With frame_api: narwhals the model receives Narwhals frames and returns a Narwhals or a native frame. Inputs are shared between the units that read them, so a model must not modify an input in place.

Reads use Arrow-backed columns (dtype_backend="pyarrow"): integer columns with nulls stay integers and the logical types of a table survive a round trip. String columns, object dtype in pandas 2 or the string dtype in pandas 3, are reported as string.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text: A table is written as one part file in the catalog format (parquet, csv or ndjson). Repeating a run id with the same token returns the stored result and writes nothing. A failure leaves the previous commit untouched and removes the unfinished part file. Reading a table concatenates its committed part files; csv and ndjson parts are cast back to the logical types stored in the commit file.

docs.title: Polars engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-polars runs models on Polars lazy frames.

$ pip install "pipeloom[polars]"

targets:
  dev:
    engine:
      kind: polars
    catalog:
      kind: filesystem
      root: warehouse
    state:
      kind: json
      path: .pipeloom/state

The engine needs the filesystem catalog: tables are directories of part files committed through _pipeloom/commit.json (ADR-0022). Any other catalog is rejected when the session opens.

A model can set catalog (and a +catalog key in the models: tree can set it for a layer). The catalog becomes a leading directory: <root>/<catalog>/<schema>/<name>/. A table with no catalog keeps <root>/<schema>/<name>/.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Value Source formats parquet, csv, json, ndjson Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions Materializations table, incremental, view, ephemeral Expectations and quarantine yes (expr through pl.sql_expr) SQL models and views yes, through pl.SQLContext Idempotent writes yes, by run token Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes Cancel no

incremental and intermediate are supported; an intermediate is a table of part files under the artifacts root. The polars bound is polars>=1.30,<3.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Relations are LazyFrames, so rows_read is empty in run_results.json. A Python model receives LazyFrame inputs and returns a LazyFrame or a DataFrame. With frame_api: narwhals the model receives Narwhals frames and returns a Narwhals or a native frame.

import narwhals.stable.v2 as nw


def fct_orders(ctx, enriched):
    return enriched.filter(nw.col("amount") > 1)

docs.title: SQL and views
docs.text: Each SQL model runs in a fresh pl.SQLContext that holds only its declared inputs, so aliases do not leak between models. A view stores its SQL and inputs in the commit file and is evaluated again on every read, so it sees later overwrites of its inputs. Rerunning with an unchanged definition commits nothing.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text: A table is collected and written as one part file in the catalog format (parquet, csv or ndjson). Repeating a run id with the same token returns the stored result and writes nothing. A failure leaves the previous commit untouched and removes the unfinished part file. A whole table must fit in memory in 0.2.

docs.title: Reading CSV and NDJSON tables
docs.text: Part files in csv and ndjson lose some type information, so a table is read back with the logical types stored in the commit file when this engine can name them all.

docs.title: Spark engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-spark runs models on Apache Spark DataFrames and Spark SQL and writes Delta Lake tables. It works on a local Spark, through Spark Connect, and inside a session someone else owns, such as a Databricks runtime. It also provides the table state store, which keeps run state in a Delta table.

$ pip install "pipeloom[spark]"      # local Spark: pulls pipeloom-spark[local]
$ pip install pipeloom-spark         # Databricks, Databricks Connect, or any environment with pyspark

targets:
  dev:
    engine:
      kind: spark
      mode: local
      conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"
    catalog:
      kind: delta_path
      root: warehouse
    state:
      kind: table
      path: warehouse/_state

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pyspark is not a hard dependency. Databricks runtimes and Databricks Connect ship their own pyspark, and installing another one breaks them, so pipeloom-spark depends only on pipeloom.

Where Install Local Spark (a laptop, CI) pipeloom-spark[local], or pipeloom[spark]. The extra installs pyspark[connect] (4.0.1 up to, not including, 4.3) and delta-spark (4.1 up to, not including, 4.5). A Databricks runtime or serverless pipeloom-spark with no extras. Databricks Connect pipeloom-spark with no extras, next to databricks-connect. A thin Spark Connect client pipeloom-spark and pyspark-client. Never together with pyspark: both own the pyspark package.

Local Spark needs Java 17 or 21 on the path. Spark 4 runs with ANSI mode on by default, so an invalid cast or an overflow fails the query instead of giving null. Check SQL models that relied on the old behavior.

On Windows, run Spark in WSL. Windows Python workers do not work without winutils and die with a connection reset. Install Java and uv in the WSL distribution and run the project there.

docs.title: Session modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior local Builds a session with master (default local[*]), app_name and conf, and adds the Delta jars, SQL extension and catalog unless delta: false. connect Builds a Spark Connect session from remote or SPARK_REMOTE. A URL that starts with local starts a local Connect server with the same conf. active Uses the existing session and never configures or stops it. On a Databricks runtime with no active session (a wheel task starts without one) it attaches with builder.getOrCreate() and no conf. auto (default) active when DATABRICKS_RUNTIME_VERSION is set or a session exists, else connect when remote or SPARK_REMOTE is set, else local.

Only a session the engine built is stopped. The engine sets no Spark conf on a session it did not build, and sets none at run time on any session: conf applies when the session is built, and conf with mode active is an error. Building a session when one already exists in the process fails and tells you to use mode active. Classic and Connect cannot share one Python process.

boundary: task with local Spark starts one JVM per unit. It works, and it is slow.

docs.title: Catalogs
docs.text:
• delta_path: Delta tables at <root>/<schema>/<name>, or <root>/<catalog>/<schema>/<name> when the target has a catalog (a model's catalog setting or the naming option). No metastore, and it works across processes. root may be a URI such as s3:// or abfss://. It cannot hold views.
  • spark_catalog: tables and views by name through the session catalog (catalog option, else the current catalog). The unity catalog of pipeloom-databricks builds on it. A view is created with CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW over a table, delta or parquet input. A model's catalog setting wins over the catalog option. pipeloom creates schemas, never catalogs: the catalog must exist, and on a local session it must be registered in the Spark conf (spark.sql.catalog.<name>).

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Value Source formats delta, parquet, csv, json, ndjson Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions Materializations table, incremental, view, ephemeral, intermediate Expectations and quarantine yes SQL models and views yes, inputs bound by alias; views on spark_catalog Idempotent writes yes, by token in the Delta commit Metrics rows and bytes, from the commit history Cancel yes, through Spark job tags Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes

csv reads a header and infers types; json is one multi-line document and ndjson is one document per line. Reader options pass through as strings.

docs.title: CSV sample data
docs.text:
A small CSV committed with the project works as sample data, the way dbt seeds do, without a new materialization. Declare it as a source:

sources:
  samples:
    format: csv
    tables:
      region:
        location: ${var:region_csv}

The location can be a path relative to the project directory (data/region.csv), an absolute path, a file: URI or a Databricks volume path (/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/... or dbfs:/Volumes/...). Only relative paths are resolved against the project directory; the others reach Spark as written. On Databricks the project files are not on the cluster, so copy the CSV to a volume and point the var at it, for example --vars '{"region_csv": "/Volumes/main/ops/samples/region.csv"}'.

Options are Spark's own CSV options: header and inferSchema default to true, and sep sets the delimiter. The polars and pandas engines read the same file with their defaults; their option names differ (separator and has_header for polars, sep and header for pandas). The tpch_spark example reads its region table this way.

docs.title: Write strategies
docs.text:
Every write is a DataFrameWriter option or a SQL statement. No Spark conf is touched.

Strategy What the engine does append Appends. New columns are added in the same write (mergeSchema). overwrite Overwrites data and schema (overwriteSchema), so any result of the schema policy is accepted. replace_partitions Overwrites with a replaceWhere predicate built from the distinct partition_by tuples of the batch. It works on partitioned and unpartitioned tables. More than 10,000 distinct tuples fails and recommends merge. An empty batch replaces nothing and writes only the token commit. merge A SQL MERGE INTO on unique_key, with update_condition and hard or soft deletes. Rows with a null key never match and are inserted. A key repeated in the batch is PLM206. A merge into a table that does not exist yet is the first load, written as an append.

A full refresh and a first build follow the core rules described in the write strategies guide.

docs.title: Schema changes
docs.text: The core decides the final columns from on_schema_change. The engine writes added columns in the write itself (mergeSchema); a merge first makes an empty mergeSchema append instead. When columns were removed or a type was widened, the engine first runs one migration commit: it reads the table, aligns it to the final columns and overwrites it with overwriteSchema, keeping the table's partitioning. The migration commit carries no transaction options and no token, so it is not counted in the metrics. With the guard on, the claim commit made just before it takes the write version (see below).

docs.title: Tables created by spark_catalog
docs.text: A table that saveAsTable creates does not keep the writer's commit metadata. When the target does not exist, the catalog creates it empty first, without a token, and the tokened write is an ordinary append into it.

docs.title: Idempotent writes
docs.text:
Each write has the token <run_id>:<model>, which the engine records in Delta.

  • The transaction app id is pipeloom/<project>/<model>. Quarantine and intermediate writes add the suffix #quarantine or #intermediate.
  • The transaction version is the run start in epoch milliseconds. It comes from the run start time the core passes with the write (see --run-started-at in Running a pipeline), never from the session.
  • The commit's userMetadata holds {"pipeloom": {"v": 1, "token", "commit_meta", "result"}}.

Before a write, the engine scans the last 100 commits (DESCRIBE HISTORY) for the token. A hit returns the stored result and writes nothing, so rerunning a finished run id changes no data.

For a merge, Delta applies the transaction options to a MERGE only through session conf, which would leak into other units of the same session. So the MERGE runs as plain SQL, and with the guard on it is bracketed by two empty appends:

  1. A claim commit before it, with the real transaction app id and version and the metadata {"pipeloom": {"v": 1, "claim": token}}. It has no token, so the token scan and the metrics ignore it. Delta refuses it when a later version exists, so PLM207 comes before any data changes. Any write that needs a migration commit makes the same claim first.
  2. A token commit after it, with the token and the stored result. The commits after the claim use the app id <app id>@<token> with version 1, which still keeps two attempts of the same token from both committing.

Running the same MERGE again with the same batch converges on the same table, so a crash between the commits is safe: the retry finds its own claim and continues. A claim is void once a later run of the same model has committed, so such a retry fails with PLM207 instead of merging over that run's data.

docs.title: PLM207 and its limits
docs.text:
The transaction version only grows. When Delta skips a write and no commit carries the token, the engine looks again (a racing attempt may have won), then through the full history. If the token is nowhere, a later version already exists for this model and the write fails with PLM207. Nothing was written, for every strategy: the claim commit makes the check come before any data or schema change. The causes:

  • a newer run of the same model finished first;
  • an overlapping run started with --no-lock;
  • a host clock that is behind, since the version comes from a timestamp. Clock skew between machines that write the same model can refuse a legitimate write.

PLM207 is permanent: retry_on: transient does not repeat it. To turn the guard off, set txn_guard: false on the engine. Then no transaction options are sent and only the history check applies, which still stops a repeated token, but nothing stops an older run from writing after a newer one.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Rows and bytes come from the table's commit history, so there is no extra Spark job. Before the write the engine notes the latest version. After it, the engine sums operationMetrics over the commits after that version whose token is this write's, plus the newest MERGE commit for a merge. Fields a commit does not report stay null in run_results.json.

A concurrent MERGE on the same table inside that window can be mistaken for ours in the metrics (the data is not affected).

docs.title: Expectations and quarantine
docs.text: The engine declares the quality capability. All counts and aggregates of a model's checks are evaluated in one Spark job. Rows dropped by a check go to <model>__quarantine with the usual _pipeloom_run_id, _pipeloom_failed and _pipeloom_ts columns, under the #quarantine app id. regex is a Java regular expression applied unanchored.

docs.title: The table state store
docs.text:
state:
  kind: table
  table: ops._pipeloom_state   # by catalog name
  # path: warehouse/_state     # or by path; set exactly one of the two

table keeps watermarks, runs, units and the run lock in one Delta table, partitioned by kind. It is shared, so it works with boundary: task (PLC503 passes). Compare-and-set and the lock lease are single MERGE statements, and Delta conflicts are retried up to 10 times. The store reuses the engine's session; its session option builds one only when none exists, and only a session it built is stopped. Each state call is a Spark job, so it is slower than sqlite or json. The table grows with every run, and Delta's OPTIMIZE and VACUUM apply to it. Lease times use the client clock.

docs.title: Intermediates
docs.text: materialized: intermediate writes the model's result as a Delta table under <artifacts.root>/runs/<run_id>/intermediate/<model>, under the #intermediate app id. The consumer reads it back as a Delta path. With a remote Spark Connect server, the client and the server must both see artifacts.root, so set it to a shared location such as a Volume or an object-store URI. See Running a pipeline for the TTL.

docs.title: SQL
docs.text: A SQL model's inputs are bound without session temp views: each alias becomes a common table expression over a DataFrame passed to spark.sql, so two units can use the same alias at the same time and an alias shadows a catalog table of the same name.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: Each unit adds a job tag (pipeloom:<run id>:<unit id>) for the length of its reads, body, checks and write. cancel interrupts the jobs with that tag (SparkContext job tags on classic Spark, session tags on Connect) and keeps interrupting, for up to a minute, until the unit ends. Cancellation is cooperative: Python code between jobs is not stopped, and a Delta commit either completes or does not happen.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text: The engine reads timestamps as microseconds since the epoch, so the Python process time zone never changes a value. User code that calls collect() on a classic session gets naive local datetimes for timestamp columns, converted in the time zone of the Python process. Convert in Spark (for example with unix_micros) when the exact instant matters.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text: Spark tests opt in with PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK=classic or connect and skip otherwise (pyspark, java on the path and a non-Windows host are needed). Classic and Connect run as two pytest invocations. A test that starts a second JVM also needs PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK_HEAVY=1.

docs.title: Writing an engine
docs.text:
An engine is a distribution that registers a PluginSpec in the pipeloom.engines entry-point group. This page walks through the pieces and ends with the conformance kit, which proves the engine does what the core expects. The protocols are Engine and EngineSession in pipeloom.engine.protocols; the design is in ADR-0002.

How the conformance kit judges an engine. Source: conformance-kit.d2.

docs.title: 1. Declare what the engine can do
docs.text:
EngineCapabilities is static data that the core reads without importing the engine. Declare only what the engine really does: the kit skips a cell for a capability you leave out and fails one you claim and break. Engine capabilities lists the declarations of the engines in this repository.

# my_engine/spec.py
from pipeloom.engine.types import EngineCapabilities
from pipeloom.plugins import API_VERSION, OptionsModel, PluginSpec

CAPABILITIES = EngineCapabilities(
    formats=frozenset({"parquet", "csv"}),
    strategies=frozenset({"append", "overwrite"}),
    materializations=frozenset({"table", "view"}),
    sql_models=True,
    views=True,
)


class MyOptions(OptionsModel):
    """The engine has no options."""


def _build(opts):
    from my_engine.engine import MyEngine  # import the library on first use only

    return MyEngine()


SPEC = PluginSpec(
    "my-engine", "my-engine", "engines", API_VERSION, _build, MyOptions, capabilities=CAPABILITIES
)

Register it in pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."pipeloom.engines"]
my-engine = "my_engine.spec:SPEC"

docs.title: 2. Implement the engine
docs.text: Engine.session(ctx, catalog=...) returns an EngineSession: a reader per format, a materializer per write strategy, and sql, schema, count, max_value, align and the rest of the protocol. pipeloom-polars is the shortest real example. A write takes an idempotency token: repeating a token must not write twice.

docs.title: 3. Write a harness
docs.text:
The kit cannot build your engine's frames or files, so you give it a function that takes a tmp_path and returns an EngineHarness: the engine, a catalog, and small adapters (make_native, to_rows, write_source, failing_relation, settings_snapshot, plus expr_cases and update_condition for the capabilities that need them). The field docstrings of pipeloom.testing.contract.engine.EngineHarness say what each one must do. plugins/pipeloom-polars/tests/test_contract.py has a complete harness function.

# my_engine_tests.py
from pathlib import Path

from pipeloom.builtins.filesystem import FilesystemCatalog
from pipeloom.testing.contract.engine import EngineHarness


def harness(tmp_path: Path) -> EngineHarness:
    return EngineHarness(
        engine=MyEngine(),
        catalog=FilesystemCatalog(tmp_path / "wh"),
        ...,
    )

docs.title: 4. Run the kit
docs.text:
The kit is a pytest plugin that ships in the core and does nothing until you opt in. In a project that has pipeloom, pytest and your engine installed:

$ pytest -p pipeloom.testing.pytest_plugin --pipeloom-harness my_engine_tests:harness
pipeloom conformance kit 1.0 (pipeloom 1.0.0), harness my_engine_tests:harness
  • --pipeloom-harness MODULE:CALLABLE selects the engine suite. Paths on the command line are replaced by the kit; -k, -x and the other pytest options still work.
  • The first report line carries the kit version. Keep it in your CI logs: it tells a reader which cells your engine passed. It changes when cells change meaning (major) or are added (minor), independently of the pipeloom version.
  • A cell for a capability you did not declare is reported as skipped, with the reason.

Run it in CI from a directory outside your checkout, with the built wheels installed in a fresh venv. That shows the published package passes, not just your source tree. This repository does exactly that for polars.
